resources.string: Aardvark
Orycteropus afer

The aardvark is the only living member of the mammalian order Tubulidentata. It is native to sub-Saharan Africa. Despite eating ants and termites, it is not a South American anteater; the resemblance reflects a similar diet, not close kinship.

An adult has a heavy arched body, sparse yellow-grey coat, long tapered tail, narrow snout and tall ears that fold back. It has four large digging claws on each forefoot and five on each hind foot. Its cheek teeth are enamel-free dentine tubes; adults lack incisors and canines.

Aardvarks range widely across sub-Saharan Africa, where soils are diggable and prey is available. They inhabit savanna, grassland, woodland and thicket. Hard rocky ground, waterlogged sites and hyper-arid deserts limit them because they need diggable earth for both feeding and shelter. Deep burrows provide daytime refuge.

A field study in South Africa’s Nama Karoo found ants and termites exclusively in aardvark diets, with ants predominant in every season. Termites became more important in winter, when ant numbers fell and aardvarks may have had more difficulty meeting their nutritional needs.

Radio-tracking in South Africa’s Nama Karoo found that aardvarks used a burrow for about five to nine days on average, then moved on. Nightly travel reached roughly two to four kilometres. Activity timing and duration shifted with the season, with shorter winter outings.

A female usually gives birth to one young after a gestation of roughly seven months. The newborn stays in the burrow during its first weeks, then begins to accompany its mother. Nursing continues for about three months, when it also starts eating insects. It becomes independent at around six months; the mother provides the care.

A study of aardvark burrows compared entrances, excavated soil mounds and nearby control ground. Burrowing increased variation in soil and vegetation; plant richness differed among these microsites, and the effect depended on how degraded a burrow had become. Burrowing therefore reshapes local habitat, while its effects vary over time.

The 2015 global IUCN assessment classified the aardvark as Least Concern. The 2016 southern African assessment reached the same category but noted local declines associated with habitat transformation and persecution. These dated assessments describe different geographic scales; a widespread species can still face serious local pressures.

African savanna elephant
Loxodonta africana

The African savanna elephant is an immensely large herbivore whose movement and feeding shape its surroundings while it depends on broad access to forage and water. It occurs mainly in eastern and southern sub-Saharan Africa, across open grasslands, scrub, and woodland mosaics rather than one uniform kind of savanna. It is a distinct species from the African forest elephant, Loxodonta cyclotis, which is generally smaller and adapted to closed forest; individuals in the forest–savanna transition can show mixed traits.

Adults have grey, deeply folded skin, very large triangular ears, a concave or saddle-shaped back, and a long trunk; these traits together help distinguish them from the smaller, round-eared forest species. A SANParks comparison guide lists broad adult-male ranges of 3–4 m at the shoulder and 4–6.3 tonnes; females are smaller, and size varies with age and population. Known-age Amboseli data were fitted with growth curves: the estimated sex difference widened after about ten years, with males 60–70 cm taller at age 65. The trunk is an elongated upper lip and nose made of muscle, connective tissue, nerves and skin, with no bones; it smells, breathes, touches, lifts and manipulates food. Its sensitive tip has two small opposing projections, often called fingers, which pinch small objects while the flexible trunk can also wrap around larger loads. Tusks are enlarged upper incisors, not horns; both sexes generally grow them, and males tend to have thicker, faster-growing tusks. Some populations show local exceptions: in Gorongosa, Mozambique, ivory poaching during the civil war favored female tusklessness, and researchers implicated tooth-development genes.

The species uses grassland, savanna, scrub, and open woodland, shifting among them as seasonal rains change the availability of grass, leaves, and surface water. In arid regions, waterholes anchor dry-season movements, and ranges expand when local forage and water become scarce. Their large ears help limit overheating: flapping moves air across the broad surface and exposes blood vessels on the inner surface of the ear flap, increasing heat loss.

It grazes grasses and sedges, and browses leaves, herbs, fruits, roots, twigs and bark as seasonal plant growth changes. The trunk gathers vegetation and carries it to the mouth, pinching small pieces and wrapping around larger bundles. Unlike a cow, an elephant does not ferment food in a multi-chambered foregut before digestion; microbes ferment fibrous material in the large intestine, after the small intestine. This hindgut fermentation lets food pass relatively quickly, supporting the enormous daily intake needed by a very large body, but it extracts nutrients less completely than slow retention would; elephants compensate by eating for many hours and selecting high-quality parts when available.

Females and dependent young form enduring family units, usually led by a matriarch; female group membership follows close maternal kinship and affiliative ties. These units do not remain in one fixed herd: related families may gather into larger clans, then separate into smaller parties and reunite as local conditions change, a pattern called fission–fusion. Older daughters and other females help guard and guide calves, spreading care and learned behaviour through the maternal family. Males leave the natal family as they mature and often travel alone or associate in loose bachelor groups; they still encounter female groups, especially when females are receptive. Adult bulls may enter musth, a recurring reproductive state marked by raised testosterone, urine dribbling, secretion from temporal glands and altered behaviour; it can improve access to mates, but sexual activity also occurs outside musth. Communication is multimodal: contact, posture, scent and calls work together, and low rumbles include infrasound, frequencies below human hearing that can carry social signals across open country. Experiments with recorded calls show that females can recognize familiar family voices at long range, while the exact information carried by each call depends on context.

Females usually produce one calf after a gestation of about 22 months, among the longest pregnancies of any land mammal. At birth a calf already weighs around 100 kg, and field observations show that healthy newborns generally stand and begin walking within hours, allowing them to keep pace with the family. The mother nurses for years; weaning is gradual and varies, often overlapping with a later birth rather than occurring at one fixed age. Calves learn by following and imitating adults: using the trunk to grasp, drink and feed takes practice, while allomothers provide protection and opportunities to learn social rules. Females commonly wait several years between births because pregnancy, lactation and care require sustained investment; drought and poor body condition can lengthen the interval. Males mature physically later than females and their reproductive success is strongly affected by body size, age and the competitive advantage of musth, so reaching adulthood does not mean immediate breeding access.

By browsing, grazing, pushing over trees and opening paths, elephants alter vegetation structure; the outcome depends on elephant density, rainfall, soils and the plants present, so local woodland change is not a universal result. In Hwange, elephant density was higher where artificial waterholes were more concentrated in the late dry season; density did not predict short-term vegetation heterogeneity, while long-term waterhole maintenance was associated with less woody structural variety. Elephants also move seeds in dung: in a southern African study of Balanites maughamii, seeds passed through elephant dung germinated better than intact seeds, illustrating one documented plant relationship rather than a rule for every species. In South African Sand Forest, field research found that elephant effects on smaller browsers changed with hillslope position, showing why plant-eater interactions depend on local terrain.

The IUCN assessed the savanna elephant separately on 13 November 2020 and published the assessment in 2021; a 2022 amendment retained the Endangered category. Earlier IUCN assessments treated African elephants as one taxon: it was listed as Vulnerable in the 2004 and 2008 updates, and Endangered in 1996 under older criteria. The amended assessment identifies continuing ivory poaching and human-driven habitat loss as major drivers, while noting uneven trends: some subpopulations are stable or increasing and others decline faster.

Eurasian skylark
Alauda arvensis

The Eurasian skylark is a ground-foraging songbird of open landscapes across Europe and temperate Asia, reaching North Africa. It uses natural grasslands, moors and steppes as well as cultivated fields. Streaked brown plumage conceals it on the ground, while the male’s sustained song flight makes it conspicuous over its territory. Movement varies geographically: some populations remain near breeding grounds year-round, while birds from colder or northern regions move south or west for winter.

This compact bird has streaked brown upperparts, a pale underside, marked breast and short raisable crest. The sexes look alike, though British ringing samples show males average larger. Long broad wings and white outer tail feathers show in flight. Compared with the smaller woodlark, the skylark has a longer tail and lacks its pale eyebrow. Mottled plumage conceals it as it walks and feeds among low plants; undulating flight and pale wing edges help identify it in the air.

Skylarks use open ground with low or patchy vegetation: natural steppe, heath, saltmarsh and mountain grassland as well as crops and pasture. A breeding site allows movement and display but also offers cover for a shallow ground nest. Tall crops obstruct access; bare ground conceals little. Birds may leave a field as vegetation grows too high. In winter, stubbles provide spilled grain and weed seeds. The species depends on a mosaic of open ground, low cover and food rather than on one crop.

Skylarks glean seeds, grains, leaves and small invertebrates from the ground, with proportions varying by season and habitat. Winter samples from southern Britain contained cereal grain and leaves, weed leaves and seeds, grass leaves and arthropods. Stubbles supplied grain; winter cereals supplied leaves. Weed leaves were eaten disproportionately to their cover. During breeding, invertebrates provide protein for chicks, while adults also eat plants. Harvest, herbicides and stubble removal alter access to these foods.

In breeding season a male sings while climbing on fluttering wings, circling high above its territory, then descends. The aerial display signals territorial occupation. Playback experiments found that level-flight song can help neighbours recognize individual singers; song tempo increases on ascent, perhaps reflecting respiratory demands. Skylarks also sing on the ground and walk as they forage. Territorial in spring, they gather in autumn and winter flocks. Some European populations migrate at night; others are resident, and passage can also be seen by day.

The nest is a shallow cup on the ground, often beside a grass tuft or in a low crop. The female incubates three or four eggs for about 12–14 days. Chicks usually leave the nest after eight to ten days, before they can fly; flight develops around 16–20 days after hatching. Both parents feed the dependent young. More than one brood is possible when season and habitat allow. Among 995 nests monitored in southern England, predation caused most failures; trampling and farm operations also mattered in grass. Cereal nest survival was lower near tractor tracks and later in the season.

The skylark links open-field plants with invertebrate prey, while eggs and young are vulnerable to predators and farm disturbance. Studies describe its diet and nest outcomes but do not establish broad control of insects or weeds. Crops may provide food but become too dense for nesting; winter flocks use patches where seeds and green plants persist. The bird responds to vegetation, food and disturbance together, not to farmland as a uniform habitat.

The 2018 global IUCN assessment lists the skylark as Least Concern: its range and population remain above threatened thresholds despite a decreasing trend. This does not describe every regional population. In the UK it is Red-listed; BTO monitoring records a 9% breeding-population decline from 1995 to 2024, following a sharper earlier fall. British evidence links decline chiefly to agricultural intensification, especially the shift from spring to autumn cereal sowing: dense winter crops can close nesting habitat and loss of stubbles reduces winter food. Local studies also find nest losses to predators, trampling and machinery. Open plots in cereals, spring crops, managed grass and seed-rich stubbles can maintain nesting access or winter feeding.

Razorbill
Alca torda

The Razorbill is a North Atlantic auk that breeds on rocky coasts and spends much of the year at sea. Its colonies extend from eastern North America to northern Europe. Its wings serve two functions: rapid flapping powers flight, while underwater strokes propel it after fish. Dense breeding colonies contrast with flocks at sea outside the breeding season. Because adults forage over marine waters, breeding success can depend on food conditions far beyond the nesting cliff.

A compact auk with a large head, short neck and narrow wings, the Razorbill is black above and white below in breeding plumage. Its deep black bill has a pale transverse line. In winter, the throat and face sides turn white. The sexes look alike. Compared with the Common Guillemot, it is stockier and has a heavier bill, though the species can be difficult to distinguish at sea.

Razorbills lay eggs on cliff ledges or among boulders, often in colonies shared with Common Guillemots and other seabirds. These sites provide sheltered space and immediate sea access for chicks that leave before they can fly. BTO records show British and Irish colonies follow suitable rocky coasts; in winter, birds range more widely offshore. Their annual cycle thus shifts between coastal breeding sites and marine feeding grounds.

Razorbills pursue fish underwater, using wing strokes for propulsion and their feet to steer. Buoyancy changes with depth: loggers on free-ranging auks recorded Razorbills ascending without wing strokes at depths shallower than roughly 20–30 m. Fish dominate the breeding-season diet, but prey varies by sea. At Stora Karlsö in the Baltic, clupeids, usually sprat, dominated photographed food loads; mean fish length was 115 mm. At Hornøya in the Barents Sea, chick food included capelin and sandeels, with young herring in some years.

Razorbills breed in dense colonies and often return to established sites. At sea they may feed in flocks, but tracking shows that they do not simply repeat fixed routes. In a three-year study of 18 breeders and 56 trips, foraging locations were more flexible during incubation and more focused on productive water during chick-rearing. Both parents care for the chick at the colony; after it leaves the ledge, the male accompanies and feeds it at sea.

The pair usually lays one egg on a ledge; BTO records from Britain and Ireland include occasional two-egg clutches. Both adults incubate for about 32–39 days. The downy chick leaves the ledge before it can fly, within the locally recorded 14–24-day fledging interval, and reaches the sea by walking or fluttering down.

As a fish predator, the Razorbill depends on marine prey populations and can respond to their changing distribution. At Hornøya, northeast Norway, a 1981–2013 study found annual variation in chick food and suggested warming-related shifts in fish distribution could alter future diets. At Stora Karlsö in the Baltic, the prey loads were largely clupeids, fish also targeted by industrial fisheries. These local studies document a trophic link, not a measured effect on fish stocks or a uniform relationship across the North Atlantic.

BirdLife International’s global IUCN assessment of 17 August 2021 classified the Razorbill as Least Concern and estimated 838,000–1,660,000 mature individuals. This dated global status does not exclude local declines. The assessment identifies climate-related prey shifts, entanglement in gillnets and driftnets, and unregulated hunting as threats. Bycatch risk follows from pursuit-diving; changing fish availability can affect chick provisioning. Colony counts and fishery data are needed to assess local risk.

Alpaca
Vicugna pacos

Alpacas are Andean domestic camelids, raised in herds chiefly for their fleece. Genetic studies identify the vicuña as their main wild ancestor; domestic herds also show later llama ancestry. Also known historically as Vicugna pacos, the species is currently listed as Lama pacos by the Mammal Diversity Database.

Adults usually stand about 0.8–1.0 metres at the shoulder and weigh roughly 45–90 kilograms, with size varying by sex, condition and population. Alpacas are smaller and more lightly built than llamas. Huacaya fleece is dense and crimped; Suri fibre grows in long, silky locks. Each foot has two small-nailed toes supported by broad pads, while the split upper lip and lower incisors help crop short plants.

Domestic herds are centred in the high Andes of Peru and Bolivia, with husbandry also extending into northern Chile. Alpacas graze open puna grasslands, dry slopes and wet valley meadows called bofedales, moving as forage and water change. In one Bolivian pastoral system, herders relied more heavily on wet meadows during the dry season.

They crop short plants with a split upper lip and lower incisors, then chew repeatedly. Anatomical examination found that the alpaca stomach has three compartments, rather than the four in true ruminants. Microbial fermentation occurs chiefly in the first compartment, where fibrous forage is broken down before further digestion. This digestive design helps alpacas use coarse plants, while forage quality and abundance still change with season. Herders may add hay when grazing is scarce.

Alpacas live in social herds. They communicate through posture, ear position, vocal sounds and spitting or retreating during conflict. A soft hum can accompany contact or routine activity, but also separation or distress; it does not always signal calm. A sharper alarm call can alert nearby animals to perceived danger.

Females do not follow a regular spontaneous oestrous cycle: mating stimulates ovulation, a pattern called induced ovulation. Gestation lasts about eleven months and usually produces one cria, the term for a young camelid. A cria is relatively developed at birth and soon stands to follow its mother. Mothers nurse and protect their young, which are commonly weaned near six months.

Bofedales are wet meadows within the seasonally dry puna; their water and low-growing plants provide important forage for alpacas and other livestock. A study of natural and irrigated bofedales in southern Peru found links among vegetation, soil and hydrology, with similar carbon storage and palatable plant cover in the two sites. The researchers found that cover of two nutritious alpaca forage plants tracked environmental measurements weakly, suggesting grazing may obscure those relationships.

The Mammal Diversity Database classifies the alpaca as domesticated and marks it Not Evaluated on the global Red List. A genomic study dated substantial llama-to-alpaca introgression to about 500 years ago, near the Spanish conquest; the authors suggest disrupted traditional management may explain the pattern but say its cause is unknown. In a 1995–96 Bolivian study, deferred grazing (temporarily resting pasture) reduced plant diversity in bofedales but access to reserves improved young alpaca survival. The authors caution that fencing communal pastures can bring social costs.

American alligator
Alligator mississippiensis

The American alligator is a large crocodilian native to the southeastern United States, from North Carolina to Texas. It inhabits wetlands where shallow water, cover and prey meet. Its armored body and short legs suit its life between water and bank. Though formidable as an adult, it begins as a small hatchling vulnerable to predators.

Its body is dark and armored by bony plates beneath the skin, with short legs and a flattened, muscular tail. The broad, rounded snout forms a U-shaped outline when viewed from above. When the jaws close, the large fourth tooth of the lower jaw fits into a socket and disappears from view, unlike the projecting lower tooth of a crocodile. Adults show strong size differences between sexes: typical females average about 2.6 metres long and males about 3.4 metres. Exceptional males can approach 4.5 metres, a rare maximum rather than an ordinary adult size. The forefeet have five toes and the hind feet four.

It mainly inhabits freshwater marshes, swamps, lakes and slow-moving rivers. It tolerates salt poorly because it lacks salt-excreting glands. In temperate parts of its range, it uses bank dens as a winter refuge.

This opportunistic carnivore takes prey suited to its size and locally available. Hatchlings and small juveniles eat mainly insects, crustaceans and small fish; larger individuals can tackle turtles, snakes, birds and mammals. Adults still eat fish and invertebrates, so large vertebrates are only part of the menu. They seize prey with conical teeth and swallow small items whole; a large carcass may be held underwater until softened, then torn apart. On Georgia’s barrier islands, juvenile diets differed between sites with different prey communities.

Eyes, ears and nostrils sit high on the head, so an alligator can watch and breathe while mostly submerged. Valves close its nostrils and ear openings underwater; a transparent inner eyelid protects its eyes without blocking vision. As an ectotherm, it relies on outside heat, basking in cool weather and shifting activity with temperature. In temperate regions it enters winter dormancy, or brumation; during extreme cold, adults may rest in shallow water with nostrils exposed as ice forms. The tail propels the body through water, with partly webbed feet helping. Spring brings more movement and courtship. Bellows, head slaps, postures and scent cues communicate; acoustic studies find bellow formants carry information about caller size, though how receivers interpret these cues remains under study.

Courtship and mating take place in spring, with timing varying across the range. Males bellow and slap the water with the head; pairs also touch snouts and blow bubbles. In early summer the female piles vegetation and mud into a mound nest, lays roughly 20–60 eggs, and guards it during incubation. Rotting plants warm the nest; incubation lasts about 65 days, though local conditions shift the schedule. Egg temperature during a sensitive phase of embryonic development influences sex, with a female–male–female pattern rather than a steady shift toward males. In incubation experiments, low temperatures produced females, about 32.5–33°C males, and viable temperatures near 34.5°C again produced mostly females; transition bands can yield mixed clutches. Near hatching, young call from their eggs; the mother opens the nest and may carry hatchlings to water in her mouth. She stays with the brood for months, sometimes its first year. Hatchlings are about 20–23 centimetres long; reaching breeding size takes years and depends on growth, food and climate.

In the Everglades, an alligator may excavate and maintain a water-filled depression called an alligator hole. During drought, these pools can shelter fish and other aquatic life, while birds and mammals forage around them. Excavation disturbs vegetation and enriches soil, creating habitat differences around the basin. This regional example shows how the alligator links prey, seasonal water and marsh structure as both predator and habitat shaper.

Heavy hunting and wetland loss once caused severe declines, but legal protection, habitat safeguards and regulated management enabled a major recovery. The IUCN assessment published in 2019, based on an assessment dated 7 October 2018, classifies the species as Least Concern and describes a large, stable or growing population. Regional concerns remain: habitat destruction, altered water management, contamination and conflict with people. In 1987, after recovery, the United States reclassified the alligator as threatened due to similarity of appearance. Its current federal listing classifies it as threatened because of similarity to another threatened taxon. This is an appearance-based legal status, not evidence that the alligator is biologically threatened throughout its range.

American beaver
Castor canadensis

The American beaver is a large freshwater herbivorous rodent, distinct from the Eurasian beaver (Castor fiber). Its webbed hind feet propel it through water; its broad flattened tail steers and supports the body on land. Families occupy ponds, lakes, wetlands and streams. Where they build dams, the deeper impounded water provides underwater access to food stores and shelter.

The adult has a stout brown body, small ears, a broad, scaly tail and large webbed hind feet. Its orange incisors grow continuously and cut branches or strip bark. Hard enamel on the front and faster wear behind keep their edges sharp. Dense underfur insulates the animal beneath longer guard hairs that shed water. Valves close the ears and nostrils underwater; a nictitating membrane protects the eyes, and the lips can close behind the incisors while the animal gnaws underwater.

The species ranges across much of Canada and the United States into northern Mexico. It uses fresh water beside woody or herbaceous plants, especially ponds, wetlands and slow streams with banks suitable for burrowing. A lodge of branches and mud has an underwater entrance and a dry chamber. Where lakes or rivers already hold deep, stable water, beavers may use a bank den or lodge without building a dam. Introductions have also established populations outside North America, notably in Finland and Tierra del Fuego.

Beavers eat leaves, grasses, aquatic plants, roots, buds, twigs and the soft cambium beneath bark. Aspen, willow, birch, poplar and other local trees provide woody foods; dense wood is often left for construction. Mammals cannot digest cellulose unaided, so microbes in the enlarged caecum ferment plant tissue and help release nutrients. In autumn, a colony may anchor branches underwater near its lodge. This food cache remains accessible beneath winter ice when fresh plants are scarce.

A colony is usually a territorial family with two adults and young from one or two breeding seasons. Older offspring help maintain the lodge and dams and care for kits. They remain active year-round, often at dusk or night. In water, hind feet provide thrust and the tail steers; on land, the tail can brace the body while the animal gnaws.

Mating usually occurs in winter. After about 105–107 days of pregnancy, a female gives birth in spring or early summer, often to two to four kits. Newborns are furred and can see; they soon sample solid food while continuing to nurse. Parents and older siblings shelter and tend them. Young usually disperse around age two, before or near the next litter, to establish territories. Breeding dates and litter size vary with latitude, food and local population density.

A dam slows water, raises the upstream level and may connect a stream with its floodplain. In a 2002–2005 study of two dams along 1.5 kilometres of the Colorado River in Rocky Mountain National Park, researchers measured longer inundation and a higher water table. The dams reduced summer water-table decline across parts of the 58-hectare study valley. These findings describe that reach; effects elsewhere depend on channel form and flow. In Tierra del Fuego, introduced beavers can turn native Nothofagus forest into meadows by cutting trees and flooding land.

The Mammal Diversity Database, consulted in October 2026, reports the species’ global IUCN category as Least Concern. The species recovered in many regions after historic fur-trapping declines, but local pressures persist. British Columbia’s Conservation Data Centre assigns it provincial rank S5, last reviewed on 15 January 2024; it lists urbanization, altered waterways, severe drought, trapping and conflict control as possible local pressures. These regional assessments do not establish a current continent-wide population total.

Arctic fox
Vulpes lagopus

The Arctic fox is a small northern canid whose circumpolar range follows treeless tundra from North America and Greenland across Eurasia to Iceland and other Arctic islands. Compact proportions, dense fur and furry feet help it remain active through severe winters.

Short ears, a short muzzle, low-set legs and a very full tail give it a rounded outline. Most foxes moult between a brownish summer coat and thick white winter fur; the blue morph stays charcoal or brown-grey year-round, lightening somewhat in winter. Fur also covers the foot soles.

It occupies Arctic and alpine tundra, from inland valleys to coasts, barren islands and, seasonally, sea ice. Dens are excavated in raised, well-drained ground and may be reused for generations. In Svalbard, foxes range from mountain ridges to shorelines and drifting ice.

Food changes with place and season. Inland lemming foxes depend heavily on cyclic lemmings and voles; coastal foxes also take seabirds, eggs, fish, marine carrion and terrestrial prey. Berries and cached food add variety. Coastal supplies peak in summer and become scarcer in winter.

Breeding pairs defend territories around dens, but Arctic foxes can roam widely when food is scarce and travel over sea ice. They scavenge as well as hunt, and may hide surplus food among rocks or in dens. Outside the breeding season, individuals often forage alone.

Mating generally occurs in late winter or early spring; after about 52–54 days, pups are born in a den in May or June. They first emerge at three to four weeks and are weaned around four to six weeks. Litter size responds strongly to food: inland lemming populations fluctuate more than coastal ones.

As both predator and scavenger, the fox links tundra and marine food webs. Inland populations follow rodent cycles, while coastal populations can use seabird colonies and reindeer carcasses; these alternative foods can stabilize numbers. Predation may affect ground-nesting birds, with effects depending on local prey and conditions.

The IUCN global assessment, last assessed in 2023 and published in 2025, lists the species as Least Concern. This broad category masks sharp regional differences: the 2021 Norwegian Red List classified mainland Norway’s population as Critically Endangered, while Svalbard’s was Least Concern. Fennoscandian populations receive intensive conservation measures.

Asian elephant
Elephas maximus

Elephas maximus is Asia’s largest living land mammal. Smaller than African elephants, it survives in scattered populations. Its grasping trunk and massive body support foraging across varied landscapes.

Adults have grey skin, sometimes pink on the ears, forehead or trunk; young are hairier and reddish. They have smaller, rounder ears than African elephants and one finger-like trunk tip. Only some males grow prominent tusks; many lack them, while females and some males have short tushes. Tusk frequency varies among populations.

It survives in fragmented parts of South and Southeast Asia, including India, Sri Lanka, Sumatra and Borneo. Habitats include evergreen and deciduous forests, thorn scrub, grasslands and modified landscapes. It forages in forest clearings and moves widely for food and water.

This herbivore eats grasses, leaves, roots, vines, shoots, twigs, bark and fruit. Its diet shifts with habitat and season; studies in southern India found more browse in the dry season. It feeds for much of the day because digestion extracts only part of food energy.

Related females and young form matrilineal communities; groups may split and reunite while foraging. Young males leave their natal group; adults are often solitary or associate with males. Elephants communicate through scent, touch and low-frequency calls, and explore objects with the trunk.

Females usually have their first calf in their teens. Gestation lasts about 21.5–22 months; births are usually single, though twins occur. Calves stand and nurse soon after birth, then eat vegetation at about six months. Several years separate births, depending on environmental conditions.

Elephants disperse seeds far from parent plants. In a Kerala evergreen forest, a study found viable seeds of 27 woody species in dung; ingested seeds germinated sooner than controls. This shows seed dispersal at that site, without implying identical effects across the species’ range.

The IUCN assessment published in 2020 classified the species as Endangered, based on a 2019 assessment. It inferred a decline of at least 50% over three generations, linked to habitat loss and degradation. Fragmentation blocks movement routes and brings elephants near farms and settlements. These data belong to that dated global assessment.

Atlantic puffin
Fratercula arctica

The Atlantic puffin is a small, stocky auk of the North Atlantic that spends most of the year at sea and comes ashore to breed in colonies. Its cycle links small fish at sea with sheltered burrows where it raises one chick.\nBecause adults can breed repeatedly over many years, population change reflects both their survival and the later recruitment of young birds.

Adults are generally 26–29 cm long, with a wingspan near 53 cm.\nThe black back and crown contrast with white underparts and a pale breeding-season face; the bill’s bright plates and facial ornaments fade or fall away after breeding, revealing darker facial feathers and a smaller, duller winter bill.

Puffins breed on islands, headlands, and sea cliffs, digging burrows in soft ground or nesting in rock crevices and beneath boulders where soil is shallow. The tunnel shelters egg and chick from exposure and many surface predators.\nOutside the breeding season, birds disperse across the North Atlantic; during chick-rearing, adults must find suitable prey within practical commuting distance of the colony.

The puffin hunts by pursuit-diving: it beats its short wings underwater to propel itself and uses its webbed feet to steer toward prey.
At Skomer, Wales, instrumented birds averaged 11.8 m depth and about 40 seconds per dive; most dives were shallow and V-shaped, so those measurements describe that breeding population rather than a species-wide maximum.
Small fish dominate the diet, including sandeels, herring, and capelin, although crustaceans and marine worms are also eaten. Adults can hold several fish crosswise in the bill, braced by backward-pointing spines on the roof of the mouth and tongue, and carry the catch back to a chick.
A Gulf of Maine study found that adult diets included more kinds of prey than chick meals and shifted across breeding stages and warm years; this flexibility did not fully compensate for apparent prey shortages.

Breeding colonies are dense, but each pair attends its own nest burrow. Partners renew their bond with a bill-rattling display, and males give low grunts in courtship.\nAnnual moult also changes how the bird moves: in the North Sea, flightless adults have been recorded from September to March, with peaks in October and March. The dates vary among individuals; each bird replaces its flight feathers during only part of that window.

A pair usually lays one egg in a burrow excavated with bill and feet, or in a rock crevice, and both parents share incubation for about 40–45 days. The newly hatched, dark-down chick is brooded continuously for its first week or so, then stays in the nest while adults forage.\nParents deliver whole fish until the chick fledges at roughly 38–44 days; it leaves at night and heads out to sea, then lives independently. Young birds spend several years at sea before breeding. At Hornøya, ringed immatures often returned to the natal colony at age three, while the estimated local mean age at first breeding was five; this shows that visiting a colony can precede recruitment, not that all populations share that schedule.

Puffins are both consumers of forage fish and prey for larger seabirds: gulls may rob returning adults or take eggs and chicks, while great skuas kill adults at some colonies. These interactions shape where and how safely a colony can raise young.\nOn Fair Isle, a 27-year study estimated a roughly 50% population decline from 1986 to 2012 alongside lower breeding success and fewer fish delivered to chicks, although adult survival stayed comparatively high. Across four North Atlantic populations, poor local prey supply was associated with longer trips, fewer chick feeds, and lower-energy diets.

The global IUCN assessment dated 1 October 2017 and published that year classed the puffin as Vulnerable, reporting rapid declines across much of Europe and projecting a 50–79% European population decrease over 2000–2065. A 2021 pan-European regional assessment classified it as Endangered and recorded a decreasing trend; these assessments describe extinction risk at different geographic scales. Threats include warming-driven prey shifts, fishing and bycatch, introduced predators, disturbance, and pollution, with effects varying among colonies.\nIn Maine, hunting for meat, feathers, and eggs, followed by introduced grazing and predators, had nearly eliminated puffins by 1900. Project Puffin began at Eastern Egg Rock in 1973, moving chicks from Newfoundland and using decoys and recorded calls to re-establish breeding. A separate restoration on Seal Island began in 1984. A 2003 Maine agency profile records the state’s 1997 threatened listing.

Atlantic salmon
Salmo salar

The Atlantic salmon is a streamlined fish native to North Atlantic rivers and coastal waters. Most populations are anadromous: juveniles grow in rivers, adults feed at sea, then return to spawn. Migration timing and distance vary among populations. Some naturally landlocked populations complete their cycle between streams and lakes.

At sea, adults are silvery, dark-backed and pale underneath, with sparse cross-shaped spots mostly above the lateral line. The long body, small head and upper jaw ending at the eye help distinguish them from more heavily spotted brown trout. Juveniles have dark vertical parr marks and red spots; migrating smolts become slimmer and silver. Mature males darken and develop a hooked lower jaw, the kype, during spawning. Grilse return after one sea winter and are smaller than fish that spend two or more winters at sea. In Newfoundland and Labrador, adults are usually under 70 centimetres and 4.5 kilograms; the North American fly-caught record of 32.6 kilograms is exceptional.

Eggs develop in clean gravel flushed by oxygen-rich current. Parr use shallow, cool streams with rocky bottoms, feeding in riffles and sheltering in pools. After one to several freshwater years, smolts descend rivers and estuaries to coastal or open-ocean feeding grounds. Returning adults need connected rivers and gravel beds; dams, culverts and poor water quality can block access. Landlocked populations feed and grow in lakes, then spawn in tributaries or lake outlets.

Newly emerged fry seize drifting invertebrates, especially aquatic insect larvae. Parr dart at insects carried by the current or falling onto the surface. At sea, young salmon eat planktonic crustaceans and fish larvae; larger adults prey on capelin, herring and sand lance. They swallow prey whole, and abundant marine food supports faster growth than in rivers. Adults entering rivers to spawn usually stop feeding and rely on stored energy.

Parr hold feeding territories, move between seasonal habitats, and some males mature early in fresh water. During spring smoltification, the fish becomes silver and prepares for seawater. Osmoregulation, the balancing of body water and salts, changes with salinity: at sea it drinks, absorbs water through the intestine, secretes excess sodium and chloride through the gills, and sharply reduces urine flow; in fresh water it conserves salts and produces dilute urine. Adults show strong fidelity to their natal river. Evidence supports smell as a cue: juveniles learn stream chemistry that can help adults identify their home river. Odours guide the final freshwater approach, while other cues are needed at sea and the full navigation mechanism remains unresolved. At spawning sites, males compete for females; the kype is a visible feature of this breeding phase.

In autumn, a female sweeps gravel with her tail to make a shallow nest, or redd. She releases eggs as males release sperm over them, so fertilization is external; she then covers the eggs with gravel. The eggs develop through winter among stones, where flowing water supplies oxygen. After hatching, yolk-sac alevins remain in the redd and absorb their yolk; they emerge as free-swimming fry and begin feeding after roughly a month, with timing varying with water conditions. In Maine populations, fry grow into parr, which usually spend two or three years in fresh water before smoltification; timing varies elsewhere. Depending on population, adults return to spawn after one to three years at sea. Many die afterward, but surviving kelts can return and reproduce again; death after one spawning is not inevitable.

River juveniles eat insect larvae; marine adults prey on schooling fish and are themselves eaten by larger fish, birds and marine mammals. Their return also carries marine-derived nutrients into rivers. Measurements in Atlantic rivers found these inputs in stream biofilm, invertebrates and resident fish during spawning periods. Eggs, excretion and occasional carcasses pass nutrients into the food web; because many adults survive, inputs are less dominated by mass die-offs than in semelparous Pacific salmon runs, where adults usually die after their single spawning.

The global IUCN assessment, made on 6 April 2022 and published in 2023, lists Atlantic salmon as Near Threatened. It estimates a 20–25% decline over three generations and warns the species may approach Vulnerable; river populations vary greatly. In the United States, dams, pollution and overfishing sharply reduced the historic range; the Gulf of Maine distinct population segment is listed as Endangered under federal law. The global assessment lists dams and aquaculture as ongoing threats; droughts and temperature extremes are future threats whose impacts remain uncertain. Where farms overlap wild migration routes, sea lice can raise infection risk for migrating juveniles, while escaped farm adults can breed with wild adults and reduce population productivity; effects vary by place and year. All Atlantic salmon sold in U.S. public markets are farm-raised; this production does not restore depleted wild populations or their river-specific diversity.

Axolotl
Ambystoma mexicanum

The axolotl is a mole salamander of Mexico’s highland wetlands, with its surviving natural habitat concentrated around Xochimilco. Rather than metamorphosing into a land-dwelling salamander, it reaches reproductive maturity while retaining larval features such as external gills and a finned tail. Its remarkable limb and tissue regeneration makes it a major developmental model, but laboratory findings do not promise human treatments. After a limb is amputated, a specialized wound epidermis covers the stump, where cells gather into a blastema, a growth zone that rebuilds missing structures; experiments show that nerve signals are needed for its growth.

Adults average about 20 centimetres, and some exceed 30; age, sex and rearing conditions influence size. Wild-type animals are dark brown, olive or blackish with mottling; captive lines also include pink-bodied leucistic and pale-eyed albino forms. Three pairs of feathery external gills project from the head, above a long tail edged by a low fin. Four short limbs have slender digits. Gills and vascularized skin absorb dissolved oxygen from water, while simple lungs let the axolotl breathe air at the surface. Mature males tend to have a swollen cloaca, while egg-bearing females may have a fuller abdomen.

Historically, axolotls inhabited freshwater lakes and wetlands across the Mexican Central Valley, including Xochimilco and Chalco; Lake Chalco was later drained. The canal network of Xochimilco, south of Mexico City, is the best-documented modern natural habitat; the 2019 IUCN assessment also listed records from other sites. These cool, high-altitude waters have muddy bottoms, aquatic plants and channels woven through cultivated chinampas. Chinampa refuge canals combine habitat structure with local farming and wetland restoration.

Young larvae eat zooplankton, including small crustaceans, and laboratory trials show that prey choice changes as they grow. Larger axolotls are carnivores; wild gut samples and food-web studies find varied aquatic invertebrate and fish prey, though adult field data remain limited. The axolotl approaches prey closely, then rapidly opens its mouth and lowers the floor of its mouth, drawing water and prey inward by suction. Laboratory tests with Xochimilco water found that contamination reduced feeding by axolotl larvae.

Axolotls swim through waves of bending that pass along the body and tail, a motion documented in adults. Their external gills remain functional in adulthood, and their vascularized skin also exchanges gases with water. Courtship is the clearest documented adult social interaction: a male nudges a female and leads her to a sperm packet on the bottom. Studies have detected male proteins released into the water during courtship, evidence for chemical communication.

During courtship, the male deposits a spermatophore that the female takes up with her cloaca, enabling internal fertilization. In controlled UAM Xochimilco breeding, females laid roughly 300–600 eggs, attaching them to plants or other submerged surfaces. Transparent egg coverings reveal development; one university study recorded hatching about 15 days after laying under laboratory conditions. Newly hatched larvae feed on small zooplankton, with intake changing as they grow. Their limbs develop progressively while adults retain the larval body plan and external gills. Laboratory studies place female maturity around 12–18 months; growth varies with rearing conditions, and comparable wild-age data are scarce.

As a predator, the axolotl links zooplankton and other small aquatic animals to larger consumers in the Xochimilco food web. Introduced carp and tilapia eat some of the same prey as axolotls, and carp stomach samples have also contained axolotl eggs. Vegetated chinampa edges and filtered refuge canals can shelter axolotls from invasive fish and improve local water conditions. A release study documented survival and foraging at two sites, but also recorded a great egret capturing an axolotl in Xochimilco; releases alone cannot prove population recovery.

The IUCN SSC Amphibian Specialist Group assessed the axolotl as Critically Endangered globally on 23 October 2019; the assessment appeared in the 2020 Red List. The assessment estimated an observed decline of more than 80 percent over three generations (16.5 years), associated with urban habitat change, water pollution and introduced fish. Drainage and conversion erased much of the historic lake habitat, while remaining canals face urban pressure and degraded water quality. This wild crisis is distinct from extensive captive and research colonies; laboratory abundance does not mean Xochimilco has recovered. UNAM researchers and chinamperos have built filtered refuge canals that pair habitat restoration with local agriculture.

Bactrian camel
Camelus bactrianus

The two-humped Bactrian camel is a domestic livestock species of Central and East Asia, valued for transport, milk, meat and fibre. Its scientific name is Camelus bactrianus; the distinct wild camel is Camelus ferus.

Two separated humps distinguish it from the dromedary. Domestic Bactrians are sturdy, shaggy-haired camels, often dark to sandy brown; males tend to be larger. Humps store fat, not water, and the thick winter coat is shed in warmer weather.

Domestic herds occur across Inner, Central and East Asia, notably Mongolia and China. Herders keep them in steppe, semi-desert and desert environments, moving with seasonal forage and temperature; these managed ranges are not a single wild habitat.

It grazes grasses and browses dry, salty or thorny plants. A split upper lip helps it take coarse forage; it regurgitates and rechews food. In snowy winters, Bactrians dig through snow for plants. Hump fat supplies energy when feed is scarce.

Social groups commonly include females, young and a dominant male; excluded males may form bachelor groups. Males display or fight for mates. Calls and scent aid communication. Herders guide managed groups between pastures and use camels for riding or carrying loads.
Spring mating is commonly reported. After about 12–14 months’ gestation, females usually bear one calf; twins are rare. Newborns walk within a day and nurse for roughly one to two years.

Domestic camels convert sparse steppe and desert vegetation into transport, milk, meat and fibre for herding households. Their grazing occurs within managed systems; effects on plants depend on local herd density, mobility and pasture conditions.

Critical-endangerment listings for the “wild Bactrian camel” concern Camelus ferus, not this domestic species. Camelus bactrianus remains livestock; a wildlife extinction-risk category is not a measure of the condition of its domestic herds. Conditions and pressures affecting domestic herds require region-specific assessment.

Baikal seal
Pusa sibirica

The Baikal seal, or nerpa, is a true seal whose entire natural range lies in Lake Baikal, southern Siberia. It is the only mammal native to the lake and the only seal species living exclusively in freshwater.

Adults are about 1.1–1.4 metres long; males are slightly larger at physical maturity. The FAO guide reports adults around 80–90 kilograms. Like other true seals, the Baikal seal has no visible external ear flaps; its foreflippers steer while its hind flippers propel it underwater.
This freshwater seal is endemic to Lake Baikal and its connecting streams. In winter, seals breathe through holes in the ice, while females shelter newborns in snow lairs on the frozen lake.

Baikal seals hunt underwater, taking small endemic golomyanka and sculpins as well as other freshwater fishes; the mix changes with season and location. They also eat amphipods, tiny crustaceans that form dense swarms in some parts of the lake. Video and tag data show seals pursuing these prey at night, when amphipods rise in the water column and fish shift into shallower depths. Behind the canines, its cheek teeth have closely spaced cusps that form a comb-like filter. This lets it expel water while retaining tiny prey, making repeated captures more efficient.

Most seals forage alone and remain spread across the lake in winter, although several may share access to an ice hole. Instrumented seals commonly dived for 10–20 minutes to depths of 50–200 metres; the greatest depth reported in the FAO guide was 300 metres. Baikal seals have been heard vocalizing both above and below water, and reported sound types differ between sexes; recordings remain scarce, so their social function is not settled.

Pups are born in snow lairs on lake ice from mid-February through March. Newborns measure about 64–66 centimetres, weigh 4–4.2 kilograms and have white lanugo, a soft first coat. They stay in the den and generally avoid water for their first two or three weeks. Mating takes place in water, mainly in the first half of April, and pregnancy lasts about 11 months. Lactation lasts around 2.5 months and overlaps with the mating season.

By eating amphipods directly, it draws energy from a lower level of the food chain than when it eats fish that consume those crustaceans. This shorter pathway loses less energy between successive consumers and helps explain how a nutrient-poor lake supports many seals.

Goodman’s IUCN assessment lists Least Concern; it was assessed on 10 July 2015 and published in 2016. Commercial hunting rose in the twentieth century; the population grew after early-century hunting but later declined with harvest and distemper outbreaks. A distemper-related morbillivirus epidemic struck the population in 1987–1988. Pollution, bycatch, illegal hunting and shrinking breeding ice remain concerns. A 2022 field project reported that tourist activity can disturb seals at the Ushkanyi Islands haul-outs.

Banded mongoose
Mungos mungo
The banded mongoose is a small, day-active African carnivore whose dark transverse back bands distinguish it from other mongooses. It lives in mixed social groups that rear their litters communally.

Adults measure about 30–45 cm from head to rump, with a tail of 15–30 cm and a reported mass of 1.5–2.5 kg. The coarse coat ranges from pale to reddish brown, with dark bars starting midway along the back, dark feet and a black tail tip. Each forefoot bears five clawed digits and each hind foot four; rear claws are shorter and blunter, while rounded cheek teeth help crush hard prey.

Across sub-Saharan Africa, banded mongooses occupy forest, savanna, shrubland and grassland. Field studies recorded dens in termite mounds, erosion gullies, aardvark holes and sometimes human structures; most were used briefly, though a few favored dens were reused for weeks.

In a two-year Ugandan study, beetles and millipedes dominated food records, while vertebrate remains occurred in only 12% of droppings. Other observations include termites, grasshoppers, worms, fruit, reptiles, small mammals, birds and eggs; to crack an egg or a snail’s shell, a mongoose may throw it backward between its hind legs against a stone or other hard surface.

A Ugandan field study reported packs of six to 35 adults and subadults; group size varies, and individuals forage for prey while the pack travels together. Frequent close calls help maintain group contact during foraging, when animals often work with their heads lowered to dig. Experimental work found that recruitment calls convey urgency or risk rather than a fixed label for each stimulus. In the Ugandan study population, younger males tended to provide more babysitting than older males, so care is not divided equally among group members.

Females can breed from about one year old and, in the long-studied Ugandan population, several females often give birth together, sometimes on the same day; females there may breed repeatedly through the year. Gestation lasts close to two months, and typical litters contain two to six blind, sparsely furred pups; eyes begin opening at about ten days. Pups leave the den at three to four weeks, then usually form a close escort relationship with an adult that feeds, carries, grooms and protects them until nutritional independence at roughly three months; care received predicts survival to nutritional independence and greater mass at one year in that study population.

In the studied Ugandan population, competition for food and mates across the population increased the probability of encounters between groups. Conflicts were also associated with periods of group growth and with reduced litter and adult survival.

The global IUCN assessment completed on 28 February 2015 and published in 2016 listed the species as Least Concern, citing its broad range, common occurrence, protected-area presence and tolerance of human-modified places; that assessment reported a stable trend. A serious regional exception is documented in northern Botswana: the mongoose-associated bacterium Mycobacterium mungi caused repeated outbreaks and high mortality in troops living near people during 2000–2010. The study did not establish the pathogen’s full host range or transmission to humans, and this local disease record should not be generalized to the species across Africa.

Barn swallow
Hirundo rustica

The Barn Swallow is a small, agile passerine that breeds across much of the Northern Hemisphere and moves south when cold weather reduces flying-insect food. Many European populations cross to Africa for winter. Most North American breeders winter in Central or South America. A small breeding population is established in Argentina, well south of the main Northern Hemisphere range. Its use of barns and other buildings brings it close to people, but it remains a wild aerial hunter.

Adults are about 15–18 cm long and weigh roughly 17–20 g; pointed wings and long outer tail feathers give them a swift, deeply forked silhouette. Plumage varies across geographic forms: European birds are relatively pale below, while North American birds are generally darker underneath. Males usually have longer tail streamers than females.

For breeding, the species needs open airspace rich in flying insects, including meadows, grazed fields, shorelines and wetlands. It commonly attaches a nest to a sheltered beam or ledge in a barn, shed or other outbuilding. Wet mud nearby supplies building material, and shelter helps protect the nest.

Barn Swallows are aerial insectivores: they catch flies, beetles, bees, wasps, ants and moths in flight, often low over grass or water, turning quickly to seize prey. They often select larger individual insects; swallowed grit or tiny shell fragments may help grind food or supply calcium. A farm study linked livestock presence with more large fly and beetle prey in the swallow’s diet.

The swallow’s agile flight lets it skim over water to drink or bathe without landing. Pairs nest alone or in loose colonies, and migrants gather in communal roosts. Its twittering song and short calls help maintain contact.

The pair builds a cup of mud pellets, often mixed with grass and lined with feathers, on a sheltered wall or beam. A typical clutch contains four or five eggs. In Britain, the female usually incubates them for 16–18 days, with occasional help from the male. Chicks hatch altricial, meaning helpless and sparsely feathered, and both parents feed them insects. In Ontario, young fledge at about 19–24 days; parents may continue feeding them for up to a week after they leave the nest.

By feeding on flying insects, the swallow is both predator and prey: diurnal raptors hunt adults, while rats and squirrels may raid nests in Canada. House Sparrows compete for nest sites and can destroy eggs or chicks; nest parasites can also reduce breeding success.

Trends vary by region. Canada’s 2021 COSEWIC assessment classed the species as Special Concern, after a Threatened assessment in 2011; national numbers were broadly stable from 2009 to 2019 following a longer decline. Declining insect prey, severe spring temperature swings, agricultural change and some nest-site losses remain concerns, though causes are not fully understood. In the UK, BTO records a 23% breeding-population fall from 1995 to 2024; it also identifies agricultural intensification and winter survival as possible influences.

Barnacle Goose
Branta leucopsis

The Barnacle Goose is a compact, strongly social Arctic goose whose annual life follows a long migration between northern breeding grounds and milder European wintering areas. Three principal flyway populations breed in northeast Greenland, Svalbard and the Russian Arctic, including Baltic regions; their winter destinations differ, so conservation counts track them separately.

Adults have a black head, neck and breast, sharply set off by a complete creamy-white face; the upper body is blue-grey with fine black bars, while the belly is pale. The short black bill and legs, white tail patch and compact body complete a distinctive pattern. At 58–70 cm long, with a wingspan around 132–145 cm, it is a relatively small goose. Canada Goose is larger and has a black neck with a white chinstrap, not the Barnacle Goose’s full white face.

Arctic breeders use tundra coasts, offshore islets and, in some colonies, ledges on steep cliffs; nesting on islands or heights can reduce access by terrestrial predators. After hatching, families move to tundra, coastal marshes and freshwater margins. During migration and winter, flocks use estuaries, tidal flats, saltmarshes and open grassland, and often graze on agricultural pasture. In northwestern Europe, some descendants of established or escaped birds also breed on temperate islands and lakes.

This is a grazing herbivore: its stubby bill clips grass leaves and shoots close to the ground, and it also takes sedges, mosses, buds and other tundra plants as availability changes. Goslings pick vegetation for themselves soon after hatching rather than being fed by their parents. Like other grazing geese, it processes abundant, fibrous forage rapidly; frequent feeding and cropping young growth help meet the high energy costs of migration and egg production.

Barnacle Geese remain vocal and sociable, gathering into large flocks outside the breeding season and travelling in noisy lines or V-shaped formations. Pairs maintain close bonds, and parents accompany and defend their young within family groups. Their repeated barking calls help keep flock members in contact, especially in flight and at crowded roosts. Seasonal movements connect northern breeding areas with wintering sites in Britain, Ireland, the Netherlands and adjacent coasts.

Pairs nest once each year, usually in a colony. Depending on the population and local predators, a nest may sit on a cliff ledge, a small island or low ground; cliff nesting is not universal. The female usually incubates four to five eggs for about 24–25 days while her mate guards nearby. Downy, precocial goslings leave the nest soon after hatching and feed themselves; both parents guide and protect them. Only cliff-nesting colonies require the famous descent: chicks follow adults down to feeding areas, sometimes by leaping from ledges. They can fly at about 40–45 days and remain with family through their first winter.

On Svalbard, the availability of nutritious plants affects nesting success: females feeding on poorer vegetation spend longer away from their nests, increasing exposure of eggs to predators. Droppings return nutrients to feeding and roosting sites, while seeds may be moved between patches. Eggs and young are vulnerable to Arctic foxes, polar bears, and adults can be taken by raptors. On temperate wintering grounds, concentrated grazing sometimes brings geese into conflict with farmers.

The Barnacle Goose is globally listed as Least Concern in BTO’s species account. AEWA’s 2024 report estimated about 1.4 million birds in the Russia–Netherlands/Germany flyway population in January 2023, following decades of growth and signs of recent stabilization. Protection of breeding and wintering wetlands, coordinated counts and management of crop damage remain important. Arctic habitat change, hunting and disturbance require attention alongside the benefits and pressures created by expanding populations.

Beech marten
Martes foina

The beech marten is a medium-sized mustelid with a long, supple body, short legs and a bushy tail. Its native range spans much of Europe and central Asia east to the Himalaya and north-west China. It uses woodland, rocky slopes and settled landscapes, and in parts of Europe regularly shelters in buildings. The species is also called the stone marten. An introduced population has been reported in southeastern Wisconsin, outside its native range; this isolated record should not be confused with the native American marten, a different species.

Adults generally have sandy to dark brown fur, a cream-white throat and chest patch, rounded ears and a long tail; the head is elongated and angular. The pale bib often forks and may extend down the forelegs. The fur on the underside of the paws is sparse, a useful close-view distinction from the Eurasian pine marten. That relative, Martes martes, usually has a smaller yellowish or cream bib, larger ears and furrier feet. The beech marten’s pinkish-brown nose contrasts with the darker nose of Martes martes. Adults typically measure 45–60 cm head–body, with a 25–30 cm tail, and weigh 1.2–2.3 kg.

Across its range the species occupies deciduous woodland, scrub, forest edges, open rocky ground and farmland. In southern Portugal, radio-tracked martens used structurally complex cork-oak woodland together with riparian strips, orchards and pasture; foraging and resting sites differed by sex and landscape scale. In several central European regions, animals also occupy villages and cities, nesting in attics, barns, garages or wall cavities. Urban tolerance is not universal: the IUCN account reports greater woodland association in Israel. Habitat use therefore reflects local resources and landscape, rather than a simple preference for either forest or people.

The beech marten is an opportunistic omnivore. It takes small mammals, birds and eggs, reptiles, invertebrates and carrion, as well as fruit and other plant material. Stomach analyses in central Greece found animal prey especially prominent in spring, when small vertebrates and arthropods were frequent; fruits and insects became more important in summer and autumn as seasonal foods ripened. The pattern shifted among seasons and individuals, rather than following one fixed menu.

Beech martens forage mainly at night and spend daylight hours in sheltered resting places. They are generally solitary outside breeding; scent marks signal territorial boundaries. In two towns in Luxembourg, radio-tracked animals held stable territories through the year, mostly within the urban boundary; territories of males and females overlapped little with those of the same sex. Urban living did not erase this spacing pattern. Local food and shelter can bring individuals into human structures, while their routine movements still follow territorial boundaries.

Mating occurs in summer, but birth follows the next spring because development pauses after fertilization. A study of more than 100 animals from the Bordeaux region documented about eight months of delayed implantation, ending in late February; implantation is followed by roughly 30 days of active gestation. Litters are born around late March or early April. The young are initially helpless and remain in a den while the mother nurses them. In the Bordeaux study, nursing could continue until mid-May. After weaning, juveniles continue to develop and learn to forage before becoming independent later in the year. The long pause separates mating from the brief period of embryo growth and birth.

In Bussaco National Forest in central Portugal, a study recovered seeds from stone-marten scats and tested their germination, including seeds of native plants and introduced cherry laurel. Gut passage increased and accelerated germination of native elmleaf blackberry, Rubus ulmifolius, but did not measurably affect cherry laurel; preference for that introduced fruit may nonetheless help it spread. Martens also used orchards, woodland edges and buildings in the southern Portuguese landscape studied by radio-tracking, linking their ecology to cultivated and less-modified patches.

Published in 2016 from an assessment dated 3 March 2015, the IUCN classified the species as Least Concern globally, citing its broad range, large population and occurrence in protected areas. Persecution and fur hunting occur locally, but assessors found no evidence of widespread decline from these pressures. Jordan’s 2020 national mammal Red Data Book lists the species as Endangered there and cites habitat degradation and direct killing, illustrating how regional circumstances differ.

American bison
Bison bison

The American bison is a large hoofed ruminant native to North America. Before European settlement, it ranged from northern Mexico to interior Alaska. Two forms are commonly distinguished: plains bison in the south and wood bison farther north.

Its massive head, shoulder hump and short hindquarters create a distinctive profile. Both sexes have short, curved horns. Long hair covers the head, shoulders and forelegs, but the rear coat is shorter. Adults shed much of this winter coat in spring. Plains bison usually have a smaller, rounder hump than wood bison.

Bison use grasslands, prairies, sedge meadows, shrublands and some woods. Historically, herds moved over immense areas. Today, free-ranging and conservation herds occupy fragments of the former range; fences and management often limit movement.
Bison graze year-round, mainly on grasses and sedges, as well as flowering plants and leaves when available. In winter, they sweep snow aside with the head to uncover plants. They need water daily.

Herds vary with sex, age and season: females and young commonly group together, while mature bulls may be solitary or form male groups. Bison alternate grazing, resting and rumination. They move as food and water change, wallow in loose soil, and bulls clash during the summer rut.

Mating occurs mainly from late June to September. After about 285 days, a female usually gives birth to one calf in spring. The reddish calf soon follows the herd, nurses for seven to eight months and is weaned by its first year. Females may breed at two to three years; males often breed later.

Grazing, trampling, wallowing and movement disturb prairie plants and soils, creating varied growing conditions. Seeds caught in the coat travel elsewhere, while dung returns nutrients to soil. These effects create a mosaic of plant communities and small habitats, shaped by landscape and herd management.

The global IUCN Red List assessment, dated 1 September 2016 and published in 2017, classified the species as Near Threatened. It counted wild and conservation herds, not commercial livestock; most American bison are managed for production. The assessment cited few viable populations and many small, isolated herds. It also identified habitat loss and genetic risks, including cattle introgression and hybridization between subspecies.

European bison
Bison bonasus

The European bison, or wisent, is Europe’s largest land mammal. Hunting and habitat loss erased its free-living populations; descendants of a small managed breeding group later founded reintroduced herds.

Adult bulls are larger than cows and have more muscular forequarters, a shoulder hump, and thicker, wider-set horns. Both sexes have short horns, a long-haired head and forebody with a beard, and shorter rear hair; the coat ranges from tawny to dark brown. At Białowieża, adult bulls weigh 440–920 kg and can reach 188 cm at the withers; cows weigh 320–640 kg. Their forequarters are less developed and their horns curve more inward.

Wisent use woodland mosaics with meadows and clearings, as well as forest-steppe and mountain forest–meadow landscapes. In Białowieża, records include mixed woods, alder stands and river meadows. Closed forest alone may limit winter forage, prompting movements into farmland. Historical records also place them in forest-steppe, so they are not strict forest specialists. Reintroduced free-ranging herds were established from 1952.

They ruminate and eat grasses, sedges, herbs and woody plants. DNA metabarcoding in Białowieża found 105 plant taxa during the growing season; woody plants made up 59.4% of detected dietary sequences. Forbs contributed 33.6%. Sample richness rose with food availability, and selection shifted with seasonal resources. These local sequence proportions are not a universal diet ratio or a measure by food mass.

Groups are fluid rather than fixed family units: mixed herds include cows, calves and young, while bulls may gather in small groups or stay alone. Individuals join and leave; bison alternate feeding, resting and rumination. In a 1976–1990 Białowieża study, bulls were solitary in 62% of observations, and bull groups were smaller during the rut than before it.

The rut occurs in late summer and autumn; gestation lasts about 254–277 days, with births usually occurring from May to July. A cow leaves the herd to give birth and returns with her calf after several days. Calves may suckle beyond their first year. Cows usually bear one calf about every second year in free-ranging herds; first birth is generally around age four. Bulls join female-and-young groups during the August–September breeding period and move between them while seeking cows.

Grazing removes plant biomass and can open space for other plants; bison also create small disturbed patches and disperse seeds. An eight-year Danish study found higher vascular-plant richness under grazing in old oak and Norway spruce forest, with no response in closed-canopy beech. Effects were strongest where ground vegetation was dense; bryophytes also increased. The result shows context-dependent habitat engineering, not a universal biodiversity gain.

The species became extinct in the wild in 1927; reintroductions began in the 1950s. IUCN’s global assessment published on 10 December 2020 classified it as Near Threatened. A 2022 conservation plan reported c. 6,800 free-ranging animals, c. 500 semi-free and c. 1,700 in ex-situ facilities by 2020—separate categories. Descendants of only 12 founders retain low genetic diversity, and herds remain fragmented. The estimate covered 47 free-ranging subpopulations in 10 countries. The official pedigree book recorded 12,209 animals on 31 December 2024: 9,762 free-living, 722 semi-free and 1,725 captive. These dated records are not a new assessment of extinction risk.

Black-headed Gull
Chroicocephalus ridibundus

The Black-headed Gull breeds widely across Europe and northern Asia, with a small population on Canada’s east coast. Many birds from colder regions migrate south or west for winter, while populations in mild areas may remain.

Adults are about 34–39 cm long, span 100–110 cm and usually weigh 166–400 g; males average heavier, though sexes overlap. The breeding hood is chocolate brown, not black; in winter the head is white with a dark spot behind each eye, and the red bill and legs, black wingtips and white wing edge remain useful marks.
It breeds and feeds on coastal and inland wetlands, including marshes, reedbeds, lakes, ponds and estuaries. Gravel pits, reservoirs, settling ponds, fields and towns also host birds.

This flexible omnivore eats aquatic and terrestrial insects, earthworms and other invertebrates, as well as fish, rodents, seeds, grain, berries and discarded food. In fields it may stamp the ground with webbed feet to bring worms to the surface. At water margins it takes prey from the surface or dips its head below.
During breeding, adults mob birds that threaten eggs or chicks, but dense flocks may flee falcons attacking adults.

In spring, pairs form through visual displays and calls; courtship includes the male regurgitating food for the female before mating. The pair then defends a small territory within its colony. Both adults build a shallow nest from vegetation, twigs and other plant matter, usually in a marsh, reedbed or island, and sometimes on an artificial raft. A usual clutch contains two or three eggs, incubated by both adults for about 23–26 days. The downy chicks leave the nest soon after hatching but depend on their parents, which guard and feed them by regurgitating food onto the ground for the brood. Young usually fledge at 34–36 days and reach breeding maturity around two years.
In Dutch colonies, gulls sometimes defend Sandwich Tern nests from predators, yet also steal tern fish and eat their eggs and chicks.

The global assessment is Least Concern, although regional trends differ. British coastal breeding populations declined between the 1998–2002 and 2015–2021 censuses, with several pressures involved; avian influenza subsequently caused further mortality in 2022–2023.

Black-legged poison frog
Phyllobates bicolor

This poison frog is native to Colombia’s Pacific-facing Chocó forests, where it walks and hops through damp leaf litter. Its striking yellow or orange body and dark limbs warn predators of defensive skin alkaloids.

Reported adult lengths vary by source, around 32–43 millimetres from snout to vent; females are usually slightly larger. The back and upper limbs are golden yellow to orange, while the legs are mainly black, sometimes spotted blue or gold. Four forelimb fingers and five hind toes have adhesive tips for climbing.

It inhabits humid tropical forests on Colombia’s Pacific slope, from Chocó to western Andean foothills. Records span roughly 400–1,500 metres; it shelters and forages in damp leaf litter near streams.

Adults hunt tiny leaf-litter arthropods, including ants, termites and small beetles, snapping them up with a long, sticky tongue. Tadpoles feed on insect larvae and detritus. Defensive alkaloids in wild frogs are acquired from food rather than manufactured by the frog, although the precise dietary source of batrachotoxin remains unresolved.
By day it moves in short hops, foraging on the forest floor. Males call with trills or buzzes, and rivals may wrestle over calling sites.

Breeding occurs in the rainy season. After courtship, the female lays about 4–30 eggs in a moist sheltered place; fertilization is external, and a parent guards the clutch. At hatching, a parent carries tadpoles on its back to small pools, where they feed and metamorphose before returning to land.

Batrachotoxin is a steroidal alkaloid neurotoxin: it holds voltage-gated sodium channels open, disrupting electrical signals in nerves, muscles and the heart. The frog stores defensive compounds in skin glands; wild frogs carry them, whereas captive-bred frogs generally lack detectable batrachotoxins when their food lacks the relevant alkaloids.

The IUCN Red List assessment published in 2017 classified the species as Endangered. Forest conversion and degradation, including clearing, farming, mining and pollution, threaten its restricted Colombian range.
