Great white shark
Carcharodon carcharias
The great white shark is a large predator of temperate and subtropical seas worldwide. Tagging shows that some individuals travel between distant regions.

Its streamlined body has a pointed snout, triangular dorsal fin and crescent-shaped tail. Dark grey upper skin contrasts sharply with the pale underside. The skeleton is mostly cartilage. Its jaws carry broad, serrated teeth, and replacement rows move forward as teeth are lost. Males mature at roughly 3.5–4.1 metres and females at 4.5–5 metres; estimated maxima are about 5–6 metres, while reports above 7 metres are unverified. In counter-current exchangers, warm and cool blood flow in opposite directions through adjacent vessels, limiting heat loss to cold water and keeping muscles and some organs warmer.

The species uses coastal shelves, islands and open ocean, often where prey are abundant. Pups and juveniles commonly use shallow, warmer nursery areas; larger sharks also visit seal colonies and pelagic waters. Tracking in the eastern North Pacific documented seasonal travel from California toward offshore waters west of Baja California. Tags in southern Africa recorded a return migration between South Africa and Australia. Individuals also dive deeply.

Diet changes with age and differs among individuals. Juveniles eat fish, small sharks, rays and squid; stomach samples from eastern Australia also reveal both bottom-dwelling and open-water prey. Larger sharks take seals and sea lions and sometimes scavenge whale carcasses. At South African seal colonies, some attacks rise rapidly from below and end in a breach; this is a local hunting tactic, not a universal pattern.

White sharks often forage alone, although seasonal prey concentrations bring them together. Biologging at Guadalupe Island recorded brief encounters and a few stronger associations; researchers proposed that these associations may provide information about the location of large prey or their remains, but this remains a hypothesis. Tagged animals differed in depth use and activity, and hunting tactics varied between Guadalupe and South African seal colonies. Ampullae of Lorenzini, sensory organs connected to pores near the snout, detect weak electrical fields at close range.

The great white shark gives birth to live young without a placental connection. Embryos use yolk and lipid-rich uterine fluid, then feed on unfertilized eggs from the mother, a process called oophagy. Litters are reported as two to ten pups, sometimes more, and newborns measure about 1.1–1.65 metres. Gestation may last 18–20 months, but its duration and the multi-year interval between litters remain uncertain. In the Northwest Atlantic, an indirect estimate placed maturity at about 26 years for males and 33 for females; substantial uncertainty remains.

White sharks prey on fishes, rays and marine mammals. Killer whales can kill them, and tagged sharks have left feeding areas during documented encounters. At California’s Farallon Islands, killer-whale visits coincided with a short-term reduction in white-shark attacks on elephant seals. This local observation shows how predator interactions can change pressure on prey, but it does not establish a global effect on shark populations.

The global IUCN assessment, made on 7 November 2018 and published in 2019, lists the species as Vulnerable; its 2022 amendment corrected the distribution map and country list. Regional assessments differ: COSEWIC designated Canada’s Atlantic population Endangered in 2006 and reconfirmed that assessment in 2021. Targeted fishing and accidental bycatch remain important threats; fins, jaws and teeth have also entered trade. Slow growth and few young hinder recovery, despite protections in several countries and international trade controls.

Greater mouse-eared bat
Myotis myotis

The greater mouse-eared bat is one of Europe’s largest bats, a member of the vesper-bat family. Across much of continental Europe, females gather in warm summer maternity roosts, often in large buildings; caves are important in the Mediterranean. At night it searches near the ground for arthropods. Its annual cycle links summer roosts, autumn mating, winter hibernation and the short season when females raise young.

Adults measure about 65–80 mm from head to body, weigh roughly 24–40 g and have a wingspan of 365–450 mm. The back is brown or sandy-brown, the underside pale; the bare face and long ears are pinkish. Its elongated muzzle and prominent tragus help with identification. The related lesser mouse-eared bat (Myotis blythii) can look very similar; field separation is improved by combining several measurements rather than relying on one trait. It has broad wings and flies slowly, close to the ground.

Day roosts and feeding grounds differ. In Central Europe, maternity colonies often occupy warm, spacious, draught-free roofs of churches or historic buildings; southern colonies also use caves. Winter quarters include caves, tunnels, mines and similar cavities, and bats show fidelity to hibernation sites. Foraging commonly favours mature deciduous or mixed woodland with an open floor, where ground prey is accessible, as well as woodland edges, pastures and recently cut grass. A Bavarian tracking study found a local preference for deciduous forest, not a universal rule.

This bat often gleans ground-active prey. It flies low, listens for arthropods rustling in leaf litter, then lands briefly to seize them. It continues echolocating as it approaches prey but can lower call strength; echoes from prey can be masked by the forest floor, making passive listening useful. Carabid beetles were the main prey by volume in one Swiss Alpine study, while bush-crickets dominated the diet of M. blythii. Other studies report seasonal changes and locally different prey mixes, so one colony cannot define the species’ diet.

After dusk, females from maternity colonies disperse to individual feeding grounds. After hibernation, males usually roost alone while females gather in maternity colonies. Experiments show that background noise can reduce use of feeding areas: bats avoided noisy compartments, especially when playback resembled vegetation movement. Such results show how noise may mask prey sounds, though a laboratory choice test does not measure wild population effects. At six roosts surveyed over two years, males showed fidelity to display spots; females visited from mid-August to mid-September, and repeated copulations were observed. Seasonal movements connect summer roosts with winter quarters.

Mating occurs from late summer into autumn. Females can retain sperm through hibernation, and fertilization follows after winter, when pregnancy begins. Females gather in maternity colonies and usually produce one pup annually, generally from late May to early July. At five German roosts monitored during 2005–2015, births began between 17 May and 14 June, showing local variation. The young practise flying at about three to four weeks. In that German study, warmer springs correlated with earlier births; this does not establish identical timing across the range.

By taking ground-active arthropods, the greater mouse-eared bat uses prey that many aerial-hawking bats reach less readily. Its diet can include predatory ground beetles as well as other insects, but composition changes with season and place. Reliance on rustling sounds links foraging to acoustic conditions: experiments demonstrate interference by noise, a plausible way for noisy infrastructure to degrade a feeding patch. Its life therefore depends on both secure roosts and extensive, accessible feeding habitat; these needs connect building and cave protection with woodland management.

The Convention on Migratory Species (CMS) species account consulted on 11 October 2026 lists the global IUCN category as Least Concern. A British mammal review published by Natural England in 2018 classed it as Critically Endangered in Great Britain and England; at that time, it knew one male and cautioned that summer roost searches were not exhaustive. These geographic and dated assessments describe different situations. EUROBATS identifies cave tourism, building renovation, habitat fragmentation and pesticides as threats. Protection therefore includes secure maternity roofs, quiet hibernation sites and connected feeding habitat.

Green sea turtle
Chelonia mydas

The green sea turtle is a marine reptile of tropical and subtropical waters in the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian oceans, and the Mediterranean. It is the largest hard-shelled sea turtle, moving through open-ocean juvenile habitat, coastal feeding grounds and sandy nesting beaches as it grows. Adults breathe air and migrate between feeding and breeding areas. The name “green” refers to the colour of some body fat, not the shell.

The smooth, oval carapace is usually brown, olive or mottled, above a pale plastron; hatchlings are dark above and pale below. A small rounded head, one pair of scales between the eyes and four pairs of costal scutes distinguish it from other hard-shelled sea turtles. Broad foreflippers provide propulsion, while hind flippers steer and help females dig nests. A typical adult has a straight carapace length near one metre and weighs about 150 kilograms, though sizes vary among populations. Mature males have longer tails and larger foreflipper claws than females.

Adults and larger juveniles use shallow bays, lagoons and reef-fringed shores, especially where seagrass or algae are abundant. Hatchlings swim offshore and spend several years in open water, often among floating seaweed, before many settle into coastal feeding habitat; the timing varies among populations.

Diet changes with age: hatchlings and small oceanic juveniles take both animal and plant matter, while many older turtles graze algae and seagrass. Adults crop leaves with a keratin-covered beak and are predominantly herbivorous, though local menus vary. Microbes in the caecum and colon ferment fibrous plants, helping extract nutrients from bulky, low-energy food.

In a St Croix study, juvenile green turtles usually foraged alone, though groups of up to three were seen. Biologgers on free-ranging juveniles in the Lesser Antilles recorded underwater rumbles during rest and grunts near other turtles; these sounds may serve social or warning roles, but their meanings remain untested. Experiments show that green turtles can use magnetic cues as a map for open-sea navigation.

Females mature late, often around 25–35 years, and adults return to breeding areas every few years. A female lays several clutches, commonly about two weeks apart, in sand chambers dug with her hind flippers; clutch size varies around a regional average near 100 eggs. Eggs incubate for roughly two months. Warmer nests tend to produce more females. Hatchlings emerge together and crawl toward the sea, where exhaustion and predators make their first journey dangerous.

As a large herbivore, the green turtle links coastal plant production to marine food webs. Grazing trims seagrass and can create short, repeatedly cropped patches, sometimes encouraging fresh growth. Results depend on local plants and turtle density: a Great Barrier Reef experiment found an intense grazing patch at one site. Work in Lakshadweep documented seagrass decline under concentrated grazing, showing that turtle feeding can also damage habitat. Grazing can shape coastal habitats locally; turtles depend on their sustained productivity.

The IUCN Red List now classifies the global species as Least Concern in 2025, replacing its 2004 global Endangered assessment. Regional populations remain uneven: the Central South Pacific is Endangered, the East Pacific and North Indian Ocean subpopulations are Vulnerable, and the Mediterranean Near Threatened. Overharvest of eggs, nesting females and feeding turtles, bycatch and habitat degradation have long reduced populations. Today, coastal development, vessel strikes, debris and disease remain pressures; hotter sand can skew hatchling sex ratios, while storms threaten nests. At southern Gulf of Mexico nesting sites, long-term protection and monitoring accompanied rising green turtle nest counts.

Grey seal
Halichoerus grypus
The grey seal is a large North Atlantic mammal that hunts at sea and returns ashore to rest and breed. Its name means “hook-nosed sea pig,” describing the male’s arched muzzle.

As a true seal, it has no external ear flaps and cannot turn its hind flippers forward to walk; on land it moves in a caterpillar-like undulation. Adult females commonly reach about 2.0–2.3 metres and 150–200 kilograms, while large males can exceed 2.3 metres and 300 kilograms. Females are usually lighter silver-grey or brown with dark spots; males tend to be darker, with a longer muzzle and pale patches. A thick blubber layer insulates the body and stores energy.

It ranges along temperate and subarctic North Atlantic coasts, especially off Canada and north-western Europe. It rests and breeds on islands, reefs, sandbanks, rocky beaches and, in some regions, seasonal ice. The Baltic population is distinct from the eastern North Atlantic group.

It catches fish near the seabed and in open water, especially sandeels, cod-family fish and flatfish, but also squid, octopus and some crustaceans. The local menu shifts with season and prey availability; adults may eat several kilograms daily, depending on body size and the energy content of their prey.

The foreflippers steer while the hind flippers propel the seal underwater. The species has been recorded diving to about 475 metres and remaining submerged for nearly an hour; these are upper reported capacities, not every hunt. At Sable Island, playback experiments showed that mothers distinguished their own pup’s call; at Isle of May, playback tests found no detectable discrimination, revealing variation between populations.

After mating, a dormant embryo delays uterine implantation for about three months, timing birth for the following breeding season. Births fall in autumn in much of the eastern Atlantic, winter in the west and late winter in the Baltic. A female usually gives birth to one white-coated pup and nurses it for about two to three weeks on energy-rich milk. On studied Atlantic breeding grounds, mothers fast during lactation and use stored reserves; after weaning they return to sea. Females often return to familiar colonies, where dominant males may mate with several females. The pup sheds its lanugo near weaning and remains ashore while it matures before entering the sea without further maternal care. At Isle of May, pups can fast ashore for several weeks after weaning; timing varies among colonies.

Grey seals alternate feeding trips with visits ashore to rest, moult and breed, sometimes travelling far offshore before returning to familiar areas. Their fish consumption links them to marine food webs and fisheries. Some North Sea porpoise carcasses show injuries judged consistent with grey seal predation, although its frequency remains uncertain.

In the Baltic, hunting and pollution had sharply reduced grey seal numbers by the 1970s; the monitored population has since increased over several decades. HELCOM’s regional 2024 Red List assessment classed the population as Least Concern, but cites coastal development, fishing-gear entanglement and contaminants; warming could shift more pupping from ice onto land, where pup survival is lower, potentially affecting population growth. In U.S. waters, the species is protected under the Marine Mammal Protection Act, although vessel strikes and disturbance remain local concerns. HELCOM’s 2024 account also reports Least Concern for global IUCN status.

Greylag Goose
Anser anser

The Greylag Goose is a large, social waterfowl native across much of Europe and temperate Asia, where it uses wetlands for breeding and open grasslands or farmland for feeding. Adults are about 76–89 cm long, with a 147–180 cm wingspan and a usual mass of roughly 2.9–3.7 kg. These are wild-species measurements: released or feral domestic geese may be larger, paler, or otherwise unlike wild birds.

Its bulky body, thick neck and large head carry a mottled grey-brown plumage, paler breast and belly, and a white tail with a dark band; dark bars or spots on the belly vary between individuals. Pink legs and a broad bill distinguish its silhouette, while the bill colour follows geography: western European birds are usually orange-billed, eastern birds pink-billed, with intermediate birds in central Europe. In flight, large pale patches on the upperwing and a contrasting grey-and-dark underwing help identify it; the bill pattern also separates it from Taiga Bean-Goose, whose bill has dark areas and an orange band.

Breeding pairs select lakes, marshes and other wetlands with quiet nesting cover, often reedbeds or small islands that make nests less accessible to terrestrial predators. They feed in nearby meadows and wet grassland, then use larger wetlands as resting and roosting places. Outside breeding, they also graze on stubble or crops before returning to safe water; wetlands and open feeding areas therefore complement each other.

The Greylag is predominantly herbivorous. Its broad bill clips grasses and cereal leaves. It also digs out roots. In water, it reaches submerged plants by tipping forward. Seeds and spilled grain become important where fields are available, and the balance changes with season and locality. Its muscular gizzard helps grind fibrous plant food after it is swallowed. It may also take small aquatic animals, but plants dominate its diet.

Outside nesting, families and other Greylags gather into large, noisy flocks. Honking contact calls keep birds in touch; call patterns can identify individuals and reveal social relationships. Many northern populations migrate south or west for winter, while some western and introduced populations are resident, so routes vary by population. During the annual wing moult, flight feathers are replaced together, leaving the goose unable to fly for several weeks.

Greylags are monogamous and breed in spring. British records give a typical clutch of five to seven eggs; the female incubates alone for 27–28 days. The male helps guard the goslings after hatching. The goslings hatch down-covered and precocial: once dry, they leave the nest, walk and swim, and pick up food themselves under parental protection. They fledge at about 50–60 days and commonly do not breed until around three years old.

Greylags carry intact seeds in droppings between aquatic and agricultural habitats, linking plant communities across the landscape. In a long-term Dutch reedbed study, repeated grazing during the geese’s flightless moult changed reed growth and increased the movement of nitrogen and phosphorus from standing plants; this is a documented local effect, not a universal result for every marsh. Their appetite for crops can bring local conflict with farmers where flocks grow. Eggs and goslings are vulnerable to predators.

The global IUCN assessment published in 2018, based on an assessment dated 9 August 2018, classifies the Greylag Goose as Least Concern and reports an increasing overall population trend. This global result reflects the species’ very large range and population; it does not describe every local group. The same assessment identifies hunting, lead poisoning from spent shot, wetland drainage and degradation, crop conflict and disturbance or alteration of nesting habitat among pressures. In Britain, native Scottish birds coexist with re-established and naturalized populations elsewhere, so management and conflict are strongly regional. European domestic geese descend mainly from Greylags, whereas most traditional Chinese domestic geese descend from the distinct Swan Goose, Anser cygnoides; feral birds can blur the boundary between wild and managed flocks.

Harbour porpoise
Phocoena phocoena

A small toothed whale of northern temperate and subarctic seas, the harbour porpoise ranges across coastal and shelf waters of the North Atlantic and North Pacific, with separate regional forms in the Black Sea. Populations differ in distribution and prey, so local evidence matters when describing this widespread species.

The compact adult has a rounded head without a long beak, dark grey back, paler flanks and light underside. Its low triangular dorsal fin sits near mid-back; small pointed pectoral flippers and flattened, spade-shaped teeth distinguish its form. Females are generally larger; throat markings vary.

It mainly inhabits cold-temperate and subarctic coastal and shelf waters, including bays, estuaries and fjords. The University of British Columbia reports typical depths to about 150 m, though deeper sightings occur. In Europe it is widespread around the North Sea and British Isles, but patchier in the Baltic and Iberian Atlantic.

Its diet varies by place, season and year. It takes small fish from both the water column and seabed; herring, capelin, sandeels, whiting or cod dominate in different regions. Squid and other invertebrates supplement the diet. Porpoises in one locality often rely chiefly on a few fish species and swallow prey whole.

Usually alone or in small groups, harbour porpoises surface in a low rolling motion and rarely approach moving boats. Echolocation clicks guide navigation and prey detection; rapid click bursts help focus on targets. Seasonal shifts occur in some areas, but coordinated long-distance migration is not generally evident.

Maturity is usually reached at three to four years. Following summer mating, gestation lasts about 10–11 months and usually yields one calf. Birth season varies: May–July in the Bay of Fundy and Scottish waters, June–August in the German North Sea and Baltic. Calves begin solid food around five months and nurse about eight or nine months.

Feeding on small pelagic and bottom-associated fish connects prey communities to this coastal marine predator. Killer whales and large sharks prey on porpoises; fatal attacks by bottlenose dolphins are also documented. Its use of productive coastal grounds overlaps with fisheries and vessel traffic, exposing it to bycatch and underwater noise.

The 2020 IUCN global assessment classified the species as Least Concern, while identifying the Baltic subpopulation as Critically Endangered. Black Sea populations are assessed separately. A UK assessment published in 2026 rated status Unfavourable-inadequate nationally and Unfavourable-bad in the Celtic and Irish Seas unit for 2019–24. Gillnet bycatch, noise, pollution and prey depletion are pressures.

Harbour seal
Phoca vitulina

The harbour seal, also called the common seal, is a phocid pinniped distributed around northern temperate and Arctic coasts of the Atlantic and Pacific. It uses both marine and estuarine waters, and some populations enter rivers or freshwater lakes. Its rounded head, short muzzle and spotted coat vary in colour and pattern across individuals and regions.

Adults have a compact, spindle-shaped body, short fur, a rounded head and no external ear flaps. The coat ranges from pale grey to brown or nearly black, usually with contrasting spots; the underside is often lighter. Long hind flippers provide underwater propulsion. In this true seal, the pelvic structure prevents the hind flippers from rotating beneath the body, so it cannot walk on land like a sea lion: it moves by flexing and undulating its body. Sensitive whiskers, or vibrissae, detect water movements and help locate prey when vision is limited.

The species occupies coastal waters across the northern hemisphere, from temperate shores to Arctic regions. Estuaries, bays, tidal channels and river mouths provide access to feeding grounds as well as sheltered haul-out sites. Seals rest on beaches, rocks, reefs and, in glacial fjords, floating ice. A haul-out is a resting place rather than a feeding habitat: seals return to water to forage and may range far beyond the nearby shore. Site use and travel distances differ among animals and populations.

Harbour seals eat fish as well as squid, crustaceans and other available aquatic prey. Fish commonly include schooling and bottom-associated species, but the menu changes by season and place with prey availability; no single fish dominates throughout the range. Seals pursue prey underwater, using dives of different depths and durations. Before submerging, they take in oxygen at the surface; oxygen carried in blood supports aerobic activity underwater, and these stores develop rapidly in pups. Their vibrissae can sense the trails left by moving fish, an additional way to follow prey in dim or turbid water. This flexible feeding helps them exploit estuarine and coastal food webs.

Much of the seal’s day alternates between foraging at sea and resting ashore or on ice. Individuals often gather at haul-outs, especially during the annual moult, when they shed and regrow their coat over several weeks and spend more time out of the water. These groups are not tightly coordinated colonies: seals may rest close together while maintaining individual space. Mothers and pups can form temporary nursery groups. At sea, tracking studies show substantial variation in how far seals travel and where they forage.

Birth timing varies geographically, generally falling in spring or summer. After mating, development pauses before the embryo implants in the uterus; this delayed implantation shifts active gestation so that birth matches a favourable season. Females give birth to a single pup, usually on shore or ice. The pup can swim soon after birth and nurses for roughly four to six weeks while its mother also makes feeding trips. In the Wadden Sea, long-term observations documented an earlier pupping season, illustrating that timing can shift within a population.

Harbour seals are predators in coastal food webs, and their effects depend on which prey and other predators occur locally. In the Strait of Georgia, an ecosystem model linked seal predation on hake with an indirect benefit to herring, because hake also prey on herring. The model illustrates why a seal’s consumption of fish does not by itself establish competition with fisheries. Diet records and tracking also show that foraging areas and prey differ among regions, connecting nearby coasts, estuaries and offshore waters.

The IUCN global assessment published in 2016, based on an assessment dated 4 January 2016, classified the species as Least Concern, while noting that trends were unknown for several subspecies and that local declines occurred. This global category does not describe every population. The freshwater Lacs des Loups Marins population in Québec’s Ungava region is the distinct subspecies P. v. mellonae, assessed separately as Endangered by IUCN in 2016 and considered susceptible to designation as threatened or vulnerable by Québec. Regional pressures include entanglement, disturbance at haul-outs, habitat change and contaminants; their importance varies by location.

European hedgehog
Erinaceus europaeus

The European hedgehog is a ground-dwelling insectivore native to much of Europe; people introduced it to New Zealand. Short legs and a pointed snout suit foraging in low cover. Mostly active after dark, it hibernates when cold weather reduces prey. Its spiny back protects it when curled. The IUCN’s 2024 assessment classifies it Near Threatened.

The adult has a pointed snout, small eyes and short limbs. Brown-and-cream keratin spines cover its crown and back; face, limbs and belly bear fur. A broad muscle sheet under the skin draws head and limbs inward while smaller muscles raise the spines, enclosing vulnerable surfaces in a defensive ball.

The species uses pasture margins, hedgerows, scrub, woodland edges, parks and gardens. It benefits where cover, prey and nesting material occur together; large exposed fields offer fewer refuges. By day it rests in nests and makes a sturdier winter shelter from dry leaves, supported by nearby vegetation or other objects. The nest insulates and protects it during hibernation. Use of gardens and farmland depends on local cover and food, so habitat use varies among populations.

Food consists mainly of ground invertebrates: slugs, snails, earthworms, beetles and other insects. DNA analysis of faeces from 193 hedgehogs admitted to rescue centres in northern Belgium detected slugs and snails in 92% of samples, earthworms and beetles in 54% each. These frequencies describe that sample, not a universal diet. The study also detected occasional vertebrate prey and human-provided foods. The hedgehog is opportunistic, but invertebrates remain its characteristic natural food.

Radio-tracking in Switzerland found a mostly nocturnal rhythm, with strong activity early in the night and marked variation among individuals. Smell and hearing help locate prey; the mobile snout probes litter and soil. Adults generally forage alone and do not defend fixed territories. Hibernation lowers body temperature and metabolism, conserving energy during winter food shortages. Animals may arouse and change nests; timing and duration vary with weather, region and body condition.

Breeding begins as activity resumes after winter. A male may follow and circle a female before mating; the pair does not remain together and he provides no routine care. After about five weeks of gestation, the female gives birth in a sheltered nest, usually to three to six young; a second litter is possible. Newborns are blind, and their first spines emerge from beneath swollen skin soon after birth. The mother nurses the litter; young become mobile and independent over the following weeks.

Hedgehogs eat soil and litter invertebrates and are prey for badgers, foxes and large owls; spines deter some predators but do not ensure safety. Their movements connect feeding and nesting areas, and hedgerows can guide travel. Radio-tracking in two English urban sites found roads and verges little used and documented crossings. Roads can therefore kill hedgehogs and impede movement, depending on traffic and landscape. Ticks and fleas also use them as hosts.

The IUCN’s 2024 publication assigns Near Threatened (NT) globally and in the EU27, from an assessment dated 18 February 2023; the trend is decreasing. Declines in over half of range countries and reductions near or above 30% per decade across extensive areas informed the category. This replaces the 2016 and 2008 global Least Concern assessments. Monitoring remains uneven, so regional populations may differ.

Hermann\'s tortoise
Testudo hermanni

Hermann\'s tortoise is a land-dwelling tortoise native to Mediterranean and nearby parts of southeastern Europe, from northeastern Spain to the Balkans. The current specialist checklist recognizes western Testudo hermanni hermanni and eastern Testudo hermanni boettgeri as subspecies.

The domed, oval shell is usually yellow to yellow-orange with dark marks, and its plastron, the shell\'s underside, often has two black bands whose pattern varies by region. A horny claw at the tail tip and a supracaudal scale above the tail that is almost always divided help identify it. Unlike Testudo graeca, it lacks prominent spurs on the inner thighs; unlike Testudo marginata, its rear shell edge does not flare. In the Var, females can reach 20–25 centimetres in shell length. Males are smaller, with a longer, thicker tail and a slightly concave plastron. Across western populations, adult females average about 15–18 centimetres and males 13–15 centimetres in straight carapace length; Balkan adults are generally larger.

Hermann\'s tortoise uses a patchwork of Mediterranean vegetation, from coastal lowlands to inland hills. At a central Italian site, tortoises selected small patches where bare ground lay beside dense plant cover and several favored plant species.

It crops leaves, flowers and other low-growing plants as it forages on foot. Wild diets are chiefly plant material, especially soft annual plants, and the menu changes with season and local growth. A central Italian study of the western subspecies found mostly legume leaves and grasses in spring, then flowers and unripe butcher\'s-broom fruit in autumn.

This tortoise is mostly active by day, but its schedule changes with temperature. It basks in the morning, then moves between feeding grounds and cover. In hot Mediterranean summers, activity often pauses during the hottest hours and resumes toward evening; winter brings a prolonged inactive period in a sheltered place. Adults generally live alone and meet to mate. Courtship also uses high-pitched calls and scent cues.

Mating begins after winter dormancy and can continue through the active season. Females dig nests in soil and lay hard-shelled eggs, usually in late spring or early summer; clutch size and frequency vary among populations. In the Var, incubation averages about one hundred days, and hatchlings usually emerge in early September after late-summer rain. Incubation temperature influences hatchling sex. After laying, the female leaves the nest; the young develop without parental care. In the Var, maturity averages about eleven years.

As a herbivore, it crops leaves, flowers and seasonal fruit. Eggs and young tortoises are prey for mammals and birds, while the hard shell protects older individuals from many attacks. In some studied areas, nest predators destroy many eggs before hatchlings can join the population.

The global IUCN Red List assessment was dated 5 May 2024 and classified Testudo hermanni as Vulnerable with a decreasing population trend; its corrected version was published in 2025. Former western populations have disappeared from parts of their range, including Roussillon, and France now retains populations in Corsica and the Var. The 2015 French assessment classified the species as Vulnerable and the Var population as Endangered. Urban development, roads, intensive land use, wildfire and illegal collection for the pet trade are documented threats. France\'s action plans for the Var covered 2009–2014 and 2018–2027, with work on habitat and populations.

Hippopotamus
Hippopotamus amphibius

This large African mammal links freshwater and grassland in its daily life. It rests in rivers, lakes or pools by day, then usually leaves after dusk to graze. This routine shapes its anatomy, feeding and social life.

Its barrel-shaped body has sparse hair, thick purple-grey skin and short, strong legs. High-set eyes, ears and nostrils let it remain submerged; nostrils close underwater. Its broad mouth bears prominent incisors and long canine tusks, especially developed in males.

It ranges across sub-Saharan Africa where permanent freshwater and grazing ground remain available. Hippos rest in rivers, lakes and pools, then feed on nearby grassland. During dry periods they may crowd around shrinking water, while suitable grazing can lie farther inland.

Grass is its main food. At dusk, hippos follow familiar routes from water and graze for several hours, mainly on grasses, sometimes reeds or other plants. They feed mostly on land; when forage near the bank is scarce, they travel farther before returning.

Hippos rest in water during much of the hot day, often in groups, and become active at night. In shallow water they push off or walk along the bottom. Dominant males defend stretches of water and mark boundaries by scattering dung with the tail; crowding can intensify disputes.

After a gestation of about eleven months, a female usually gives birth to one calf. Birth occurs on land or in water; the newborn can swim and nurse underwater, closing its nostrils to suckle. The mother may isolate before birth and cares for the calf. Breeding can occur year-round, though seasonal peaks are reported in some populations.

Dung and urine carry nutrients from grassland into water. In Kenya’s Mara River, research linked hippo inputs to aquatic food webs; experiments also showed heavy waste loading in hippo pools can deplete oxygen and contribute to fish kills. These measured effects depend on local density and river conditions.

The IUCN assessment published in 2017 and dated 2016 classified the species as Vulnerable, estimating 115,000–130,000 animals globally and a stable trend at that time. It identified habitat loss and unregulated hunting as major threats. These are historical assessment figures, not a current census.

Western honey bee
Apis mellifera

The western honey bee is a social insect whose colony functions through cooperation among thousands of females and a smaller number of males. Its natural range spans Africa, Europe and western Asia, while people have transported managed colonies widely for honey and crop pollination. Wild colonies still nest independently in some regions, so the species cannot be described only as a domesticated hive animal.

Adults have a hairy thorax, a banded abdomen and two pairs of wings joined by tiny hooks in flight. Worker females are usually about 10–15 millimetres long, drones about 15–17 millimetres, and egg-laying queens roughly 18–20 millimetres; these are indicative caste ranges, not fixed limits. A worker’s hind-leg pollen basket, or corbicula, and its branched body hairs help carry pollen, while the male’s very large eyes aid aerial mate-searching.

Colonies need repeated access to flowering plants, water and a protected nesting cavity; hollow trees are natural nest sites, and buildings or managed hives can provide alternatives. The species uses meadows, open woodland, gardens and agricultural landscapes, and may persist in drier or wetter settings where forage and shelter remain available.

Foragers use a long proboscis to drink floral nectar, carrying it in a crop separate from the digestive midgut; pollen is packed into hind-leg baskets and supplies protein, lipids and micronutrients. Nectar fuels adult flight, while digested pollen supplies nurse bees with nutrients used by their head glands to produce larval food. Nestmates receive incoming nectar, add glandular enzymes, pass it among workers and fan air over it as water evaporates, turning the sugary liquid into stored honey. Pollen mixed with nectar and salivary secretions becomes bee bread in comb cells, and stored honey fuels the colony when flowers are scarce.

A colony is eusocial: queens reproduce, workers normally do not, and drones mate with queens from other colonies. Worker jobs commonly shift with age from cleaning cells and feeding brood to building wax comb, guarding entrances and foraging, although workers can change tasks when the colony loses bees or brood. Pheromones and food-sharing coordinate the colony’s tasks. Workers fan air or vibrate flight muscles to hold the brood nest near 34 degrees Celsius. Returning foragers may perform a waggle dance: its angle relative to vertical signals direction relative to the sun, and the waggle-run duration roughly indicates distance.

Usually, unfertilized eggs develop as haploid males, with one chromosome set, and fertilized eggs as diploid females, with two sets; rarely, a fertilized egg carrying two identical variants of the sex-determining gene csd develops as a diploid male, which workers generally destroy early. Larval nutrition helps determine whether a female becomes a worker or queen. Workers rear queens in enlarged cells, feeding them royal jelly throughout development; worker larvae receive nurse-produced brood food that changes with age and includes honey- and pollen-derived nutrients. After emerging, a virgin queen takes orientation flights and mates in flight with several drones at congregation areas, storing sperm for later egg fertilization; drones die after successful mating. Egg-to-adult development usually takes about 16 days for queens, 21 for workers and 24 for drones, though temperature affects timing. In a seasonal colony, swarming is colony-level reproduction: the old queen and many workers leave to establish a nest elsewhere while a successor queen develops.

When workers visit flowers for nectar and pollen, grains stick to their hairy bodies and can reach stigmas on later visits, making the bee an important pollinator of wild plants and crops. Wild insects can improve crop fruit set even where honey bees visit flowers, so managed colonies do not replace diverse pollinator communities. Where managed colonies are dense and forage is limited, honey bees can compete with wild bees for nectar and pollen; studies find variable outcomes, and many have measured visitation or resource overlap rather than lasting population effects. Shared pathogens are another possible route of impact, so ecological effects depend on local colony density, resources and species.

Conservation assessments distinguish self-sustaining wild colonies from human-managed hives. In 2025, IUCN classified wild colonies in the 27 European Union member states as Endangered, based on estimated decline and evidence of threats. The wider pan-European status remains Data Deficient because distribution, survival and trend data are sparse; the 2014 European assessment was also Data Deficient. Threats cited for wild honey bees include parasites, pests, predators, pathogens, pesticides and hybridization. Across European wild pollinators, IUCN also identifies habitat loss, intensive farming, fragmentation, nitrogen deposition and pesticides as pressures.

Eurasian hoopoe
Upupa epops

The Eurasian hoopoe is a distinctive bird of open country across Europe, Asia and Africa. Its cinnamon body, striped wings and long crest stand out; its long bill and ground-foraging habits help it find invertebrates in short vegetation and loose soil.

An adult has a cinnamon-orange head and body, a long, slender, slightly down-curved bill, and a fan-shaped crest tipped black and white. Broad black-and-white bars cross the wings and tail, conspicuous in flight. The sexes look alike.

Across its broad range, the hoopoe uses semi-open pasture, orchards, farmland, heath and open woodland. It walks and probes for food, nesting in cavities in trees, walls or banks. Bare ground or short grass helps it reach prey; dense cover limits access to feeding sites.

It eats insects and other invertebrates, including beetles, larvae and crickets, found at or beneath the soil surface. It probes loose earth with its bill, then opens it to seize prey. In one Swiss population, mole-cricket availability was linked with territory use and breeding output.

Hoopoes are often seen alone or in pairs, walking over open ground and probing methodically. The song consists of a short series of hollow, repeated notes. Many populations migrate; some birds stay year-round, while others travel between breeding areas and warmer winter quarters.

The species nests in enclosed cavities; the female incubates as the male brings food. British records report seven to eight eggs, 15–16 days of incubation and fledging at 26–29 days. These regional figures vary. Chicks hatch downy and helpless; both parents feed them.

Hoopoes host bacteria in the preen gland. During nesting, secretions from females and chicks become dark and odorous; experiments linked symbiotic bacteria to antimicrobial compounds. These may protect eggs and nestlings, although researchers continue to examine how the relationship works.

BirdLife International’s global IUCN assessment of 14 August 2020 lists Least Concern but reports a decreasing population trend. This category can conceal local pressures: the University of Bern records a past decline in Valais and conservation work to maintain suitable feeding and nesting habitat.

Domestic horse
Equus caballus

The domestic horse is a single-toed grazing mammal shaped by human breeding. Ancient genomes trace most living domestic horses to a western Eurasian steppe lineage that spread about 4,200 years ago. Its expansion replaced many local horse populations across Eurasia. Earlier horse management did not produce most living domestic lineages. People keep horses worldwide for varied roles.

Horses have a long head, mobile ears, maned neck, deep body, and long limbs with one hoof each. Breed variation spans compact ponies to tall draft horses, with different coats and proportions. Adult males are stallions, females mares, young horses foals.
People keep horses in pastures, paddocks, and stables across the inhabited continents. Their surroundings depend on local land use and husbandry; domestic horses have no single natural range.
Horses graze grasses and fibrous plants. Symbiotic microbes in the cecum ferment plant cellulose, enabling hindgut digestion without a ruminant’s multi-chambered stomach.

Horses are social: free-ranging mares and offspring form stable family bands, while young or unattached males may gather separately. Domestic herds also form preferred bonds. Horses communicate through senses, posture, and calls, and often graze or rest together.

Mares generally cycle in long-day seasons. Pregnancy averages about 340 days, or eleven months, with variation. Usually one foal is born; it soon stands, follows its mother, and nurses as she protects it.

Grazing removes plants and can change habitat. At springs in Nevada’s Great Basin, plots accessible to feral horses had less plant cover and species richness than horse exclosures. In high-elevation meadows, protected vegetation was taller than vegetation grazed by horses and cattle. These local results depend on habitat and grazing pressure.

Domestic horses are maintained through breeding, not as a wild population. Breeds vary in size, build, coat, and inherited traits selected for different uses and conditions. Preserving distinct breeds maintains domestic diversity; a wild equid’s conservation status does not describe domestic horses.

House Martin
Delichon urbicum
This small swallow breeds across Europe, North Africa and temperate Asia, then migrates to sub-Saharan Africa following seasonal supplies of flying insects.

Adults average about 13 cm long, with a 26–29 cm wingspan; the sexes look alike. Blue-black upperparts, white rump and belly, and a shallowly forked tail mark the species. Unlike the barn swallow, it has no red throat or long tail streamers; juveniles are duller.

It hunts over open country, meadows, farmland and water, where flying insects are accessible. It nests on cliffs or, commonly, outside buildings and bridges beneath sheltered overhangs. British surveys in 2016–17 found lower breeding success on PVC than on brick, concrete or wood, with more nest collapses: the supporting surface matters as well as available mud.
It captures small insects and spiders in flight. Flies and aphids are common breeding-season prey; flying ants also contribute on African wintering grounds.
They often forage in loose groups above water and nest socially in colonies. Soft twittering maintains contact, while sharper alarm calls alert nearby birds to danger.

After courtship, both partners build or repair a closed mud nest under an eave, leaving a small entrance; grasses and hair soften its lining. The female lays usually four or five eggs, incubated by the pair for about two weeks. Helpless hatchlings stay in the nest for roughly three to four weeks, then parents feed them for about another week. Mud mixed with saliva dries into a durable cement, allowing nests to be reused in successive years. Two broods in a season are usual in Britain.
It eats flying insects, is prey for the Eurasian hobby, and its reused mud nests can harbour fleas and mites.

The LPO reports a 26% decline in European breeding numbers from 1980 to 2019; pesticides, poor weather, scarce mud and nest destruction are local pressures. This regional trend differs from the global IUCN assessment: dated 1 October 2016 and amended in 2017, it classed the species as Least Concern.

House mouse
Mus musculus

The house mouse, Mus musculus, is a small rodent whose global spread followed human food storage and transport. Its ancestral range lay in Asia, and it now occurs on most continents and many islands. Some populations live in buildings and farms; others forage outdoors. A flexible diet and rapid breeding when conditions permit help it exploit varied settings. But populations differ: mice in food-rich buildings often remain close to nests, while outdoor populations tend to disperse farther. On islands where people introduced them, they can become damaging invaders.

An adult measures about 65–95 millimetres from nose to rump; its tail is usually nearly as long, and mass is about 12–30 grams. Large rounded ears, dark eyes and a nearly bare tail marked by rings of scales help identify it; its proportions and tail distinguish it from short-tailed voles. Fine whiskers read air currents and nearby surfaces. Incisors grow continuously: hard enamel coats the front, while softer dentine behind wears faster, preserving a sharp cutting bevel. Molars grind food.

The species occupies buildings, barns, granaries, cultivated fields, hedgerows and wooded margins. A mouse may spend summer in a field and move into a barn or house as autumn cools. Inside, cracks, wall cavities, stored goods and debris offer shelter beside food; outside, burrows and rock crevices conceal nests. They line nests with shredded fibres. Human settlements let them persist in places too cold or dry for independent survival. Ships and later cargo carried populations to remote islands.

The mouse is an opportunistic omnivore. Wild foods include seeds, grains, green plants, roots and insects; near people it takes stored food and scraps. Switching among foods helps it persist when one resource dwindles. Mice feed in frequent small bouts: UC Agriculture and Natural Resources reports up to one fifth of body mass per day and roughly 200 small meals nightly. Moist foods supply water, but dry diets and heat increase drinking.

Mice are often active at night. Smell, hearing and whiskers help them navigate; scent cues signal social and reproductive information, and males can produce ultrasonic courtship songs. Social structure changes with density and setting. In commensal colonies, a dominant male may defend a territory containing females and young; family members repel outsiders. In wild populations, territories are less distinct and ranges may overlap. A long-term study of free-living mice in a Swiss barn found patterned social contacts, while also showing how ordinary movement could generate some apparent group structure. Young males often leave after conflict; females more often remain nearby.

Where food and shelter remain available, mice can breed throughout the year; outdoor breeding is often seasonal. Pregnancy lasts about 19–21 days, and a litter usually has five or six pups. Newborns are blind and hairless; fur grows by about day ten, eyes open near two weeks, and weaning occurs around three weeks. Young become sexually mature at about five to seven weeks, although wild populations vary with season and conditions. In some wild populations, females share nests and nurse pups communally. Young females are more likely than males to remain near their mother\'s territory; adult aggression often drives young males away.

Mice eat seeds and invertebrates and are prey for owls, hawks, snakes, foxes, weasels and cats. At high density they can consume grain that would otherwise feed other animals. On some remote islands, introduced mice also attack seabird eggs and chicks. In 2021 on Gough Island, researchers found wounded breeding Tristan Albatrosses; one female was later found dead beside her nest after a mouse-inflicted wound. In 2023 on Marion Island, two wounded adult Wandering Albatrosses and eight carcasses were found. The cause of those Marion deaths remained undetermined, although two fresh carcasses bore wounds consistent with mouse attacks. Such effects are local, not typical of every population.

The Mammal Diversity Database, consulted in October 2026, reports the IUCN global category as Least Concern, consistent with the species’ broad distribution. That global category does not describe every local impact. Introduced mice can threaten native wildlife on islands. Around people, control addresses food contamination, property damage and pathogens; rodenticides can also harm non-target animals. Management priorities therefore vary: the species remains globally widespread, while some island ecosystems face pressure from introduced populations.

Humpback whale
Megaptera novaeangliae

The humpback whale is a baleen whale found in all major oceans. Most populations migrate between high-latitude feeding grounds and warmer breeding areas, but the Arabian Sea population remains in its region year-round. Males sing patterned songs, and South Pacific research documents song themes spreading socially between populations.

Adults have a stocky dark-grey body, a broad flattened head and a small dorsal fin behind the midpoint; the fin varies in shape. Females average about 15 metres and are slightly longer than males in NOAA’s Pacific Marine Environmental Laboratory account. The pectoral fins reach roughly one-third of body length; fleshy tubercles on the head and lower jaw bear sensory hairs. Researchers identify individuals by the distinctive black-and-white pattern beneath each broad fluke.

Migratory populations typically feed in cold, productive high-latitude waters in summer and move to tropical or subtropical breeding grounds in winter. Some whales travel up to 8,000 kilometres between feeding and breeding grounds; routes differ among populations and hemispheres. Southern populations commonly breed from July to October and feed near Antarctica from November to March; northern populations follow the opposite seasonal cycle. Arabian Sea whales are resident rather than migratory, using warm regional waters that also provide feeding opportunities through seasonal upwelling.

Prey varies geographically: Southern Hemisphere whales mainly take Antarctic krill, while northern populations eat small schooling fish including herring, anchovies and sand lance. During a lunge, a whale engulfs prey-rich water; expandable throat grooves let the mouth and ventral pouch distend. It then expels water through fringed baleen plates that retain prey. In Southeast Alaska, solitary tagged whales formed bubble curtains around krill layers before lunging through the concentrated prey. This detailed bubble-net mechanism is documented at that Alaskan feeding site and does not establish a universal tactic.

Breeding groups are fluid: a female may travel with a calf and a principal male escort, while other males join and jostle for close position. Off eastern Australia, observed males used both escorting and singing tactics; whether song attracts females or mediates competition remains debated. In Hawaiian breeding-area recordings, social “wops” and “grumbles” varied with group context and were quieter when a nearby singing whale could hear them. South Pacific recordings show song themes spreading between populations and some singers combining old and newly introduced material during rapid song change.

Mating and birth occur mainly in warm lower-latitude waters during each hemisphere’s winter; gestation lasts about 11 to 11.5 months. A pregnant female feeds on temperate or polar grounds to build reserves before returning to give birth; she may reach breeding areas before other whales. Females usually have one calf every two or three years, and mother-calf pairs often use shallow, sheltered water. Calves nurse for about 10 to 11 months; compiled estimates place their length near 4.3 metres at birth and 8.8 metres at weaning. In Exmouth Gulf, resting lactating females had respiration rates about half those of adults on feeding grounds, consistent with rest conserving maternal energy.

Baleen whales release nitrogen, phosphorus and iron near the surface in waste, and these nutrients can support phytoplankton growth. A recent model including humpbacks among several whale species estimated variable regional and seasonal effects of whale nutrient recycling on primary production. The model does not isolate a global contribution attributable to humpbacks alone.

NOAA reports that commercial whaling greatly reduced all humpback populations and depleted most by more than 95 percent before the commercial-whaling moratorium. An IWC assessment found strong overall North Pacific recovery from the low level around 1966, with a peak in 2014 and regional declines linked to the 2014–2016 marine heatwave. The CSG’s 2025-2 summary lists the species globally as Least Concern but the Arabian Sea and Oceania subpopulations as Endangered. The global Least Concern assessment was published in November 2018; the separate Arabian Sea assessment is dated 2008. Current pressures include entanglement in fishing gear and debris, vessel strikes and disturbance, underwater noise, and climate-related changes to prey; their effects vary by region. NOAA notes that entanglement can impair feeding or cause injury and death, while prey shifts may worsen nutritional condition and affect reproduction.

Greater one-horned rhinoceros
Rhinoceros unicornis

This Asian herbivore is native to the northern Indian subcontinent. Wild populations persist in scattered sites in India and Nepal, especially river floodplains. Its distribution reflects the link between grazing, abundant grass, water and seasonal wetlands.

Adults bear one dark nasal horn of compacted keratin, not bone. Thick grey-brown skin folds at the neck, shoulder and hindquarters, with raised bumps on the shoulders and upper legs. Its flexible upper lip gathers food; young rhinos develop adult folds as they mature.

It favours low alluvial grasslands beside large rivers, with marshes, reed beds, pools and woodland. Flooding renews the plains, producing patches of tall grass and wet ground. Rhinos bathe and wallow, may move higher as floods rise, and also use dry grassland and forest edges.

Grasses, including tall riverine growth, form most of its diet. It also eats aquatic plants, leaves, shoots, twigs and fruit, varying its menu with season and vegetation. Its flexible upper lip gathers plants; it sometimes feeds partly submerged.

Adults are usually solitary, though females stay with calves and animals may gather at grazing sites or wallows. Males hold loosely defended ranges and mark with dung and urine. Activity often peaks in cooler hours. Bathing and wallowing help with heat and biting insects; rhinos also rub against vegetation.

After about 15–16 months, a female gives birth to one calf. Breeding has no fixed annual season, and births are years apart. The calf soon walks and nurses; weaning takes about 12–18 months. Maternal care continues as it learns to forage and becomes independent.

This large herbivore changes plant cover through grazing, trampling and paths. Dung returns seeds and nutrients to floodplain soil, and other wildlife uses its muddy wallows. These effects vary with local conditions.

The IUCN’s 2019 Red List assessment classified it as Vulnerable, estimating 2,100–2,200 mature animals in 11 subpopulations and noting habitat decline. This dated assessment is not a current census. The International Rhino Foundation later reported about 4,075 wild animals after recovery under protection in India and Nepal. Poaching, floodplain habitat loss and fragmentation, and conflict near crowded reserves remain concerns.

Jaguar
Panthera onca

The jaguar is the largest cat native to the Americas and the only living member of its genus there. Its range stretches from Mexico through Central America into South America, with its strongest continuous populations centered on the Amazon basin.

A jaguar has a compact, muscular body, broad head, short limbs and a tawny to reddish coat. Dark rosettes usually contain smaller central spots; their arrangement differs across the two flanks. Some individuals are melanistic, so rosettes remain faintly visible on black fur.

It favors dense lowland forest, wetlands and river margins, where cover and water are close, but also occupies scrub, savanna and some dry woodland. In the southwestern United States and northwestern Mexico, it uses wooded and riparian corridors rather than rainforest alone.

This obligate carnivore takes prey ranging from reptiles and fish to large mammals. Peccaries, deer, capybaras, tapirs, caimans and turtles feature in regional diets; livestock may be taken where natural prey has declined. Its strong jaws help dispatch armored reptiles, including by biting through shells.

Jaguars generally live and hunt alone, and scent or scratch marks help signal territorial use. Activity is mainly nocturnal, though individuals may move at any hour as conditions change. Hunting relies on concealment, a short rush and a forceful pounce rather than prolonged pursuit.

Breeding can occur throughout the year across much of the range, although seasonality appears at its northern and southern edges. After roughly 100 days of gestation, a female gives birth to one to four cubs, usually two, in a sheltered den and raises them alone.

As a large predator, the jaguar consumes many animals and can influence prey populations in the ecosystems it occupies. It also depends on connected territories, freshwater and adequate prey. Forest fragmentation can therefore disrupt both its movements and access to food or mates.

Habitat conversion and fragmentation, prey depletion, illegal trade and retaliatory killing all pressure jaguar populations. Livestock losses can bring conflict where ranches overlap with jaguar habitat. Protecting connected landscapes, wild prey and practical coexistence measures addresses several linked pressures across the species’ range.

Common kingfisher
Alcedo atthis

The Common kingfisher is a small hunter of waterways, often watching fish from a low branch before plunging into the water. It ranges across Europe, North Africa and much of Asia. A European synthesis of ringing records found movement most marked in northern populations, while most adults and juveniles were sedentary; winter dispersal varies by region and age. Its piping call can reveal the bird before its bright colours do.

Adults are typically 16–17 cm long. The compact body carries a long dark bill, blue-green upperparts and orange underparts. The blue is structural: a spongy keratin-and-air layer in the feather barbs, branches along its shaft, coherently scatters light, rather than relying on blue pigment. Both sexes look alike at a distance, but the female’s lower bill is orange-red with a dark tip, whereas the male’s bill is almost entirely black. British ringing samples average 39 g for adults and 36 g for juveniles.

It uses slow rivers, streams, canals, lakes and marshes where fish can be watched from a perch and caught in shallow water. Clear water can make prey easier to see, but field studies also find kingfishers in small wetlands and ponds away from the nest, so a riverbank alone does not define its feeding habitat. Open, steep earth or sand banks provide places to excavate a nesting tunnel. Bank reinforcement, channel straightening and intensive river works remove nesting faces and can sever feeding reaches and habitat corridors.

Small fish make up most of the diet, although aquatic insect larvae and crustaceans are also taken. It watches from a perch, then dives after a fish; surface refraction shifts the prey’s apparent position. Experiments with this species found more attacks and higher capture success in shallow tanks, consistent with prey being more accessible there. After a catch, it beats the fish against its perch to stun it, swallows it head-first, and later regurgitates indigestible bones in a pellet. A study on Italy’s River Ticino found fish in pellets collected at resting sites from March to October 2019, documenting diet outside nesting but not in winter.

Outside courtship and nesting, adults usually forage alone and defend stretches of water that supply dependable fish and perches. A rival may be chased or confronted in a prolonged display, and fights can become physical. Courtship includes the male presenting fish to the female, linking food delivery with pair formation.

The pair excavates a tunnel in an earth or sand bank, usually ending in a bare chamber. In Britain, five to seven eggs are typical. Both adults incubate for about 20 days, and the naked, dependent chicks remain in the nest for roughly 23–26 days. Hampshire nest observations found that fish delivered grew larger as nestlings developed. In observations from Chiplun, Maharashtra, both parents fed chicks, and fledglings continued begging near the nest for about a week. In Britain, one or two broods are usual and three are recorded in favourable seasons.

The kingfisher catches small fish and aquatic invertebrates, while its eggs and nestlings can be preyed upon by snakes and other ground-dwelling animals. In the River Ticino, pellet analysis found mainly common native fish and fewer introduced fish than expected from their availability, showing how this local predator selects prey.

Cold snaps can freeze fishing waters and cause heavy mortality. Pollution, sediment and river engineering can reduce prey visibility or remove nesting banks. North Rhine-Westphalia’s state nature conservation agency identifies bank reinforcement, channel modification, contaminated runoff and disturbance at nest sites as local pressures. BirdLife’s 2024 global IUCN record classifies the species as Least Concern. In the 2021 European assessment, published by the EU in 2022, it is also Least Concern, though the trend remains downward at a slower rate than in 2015, when it was Vulnerable. These dated assessments use different geographic scales and do not establish that every regional population is secure.

Koala
Phascolarctos cinereus

The koala is an Australian marsupial whose range follows eucalypt forests and woodlands across Queensland, New South Wales, Victoria and a small part of South Australia. Its distribution is broad but patchy: suitable food trees, soils and local conditions determine where animals can persist. It is the sole living member of the family Phascolarctidae and spends most of its life in trees.

Adults have a large rounded head, conspicuous furry ears, a broad black nose and dense grey to brown fur, usually paler on the chest, inner limbs and rump. Their strong limbs and curved claws grip trunks; two opposable digits on each forepaw help secure a hold while climbing. Males tend to be larger and have a prominent chest scent gland, while females have a pouch opening towards the rear. Size and coat thickness vary geographically, with northern animals generally smaller and lighter than southern ones.

Koalas occupy open forests and woodlands from tropical Queensland to temperate southern Australia, including some fragmented and urban landscapes. Habitat quality depends especially on the local mixture and abundance of food trees; fertile soils and watercourses often support higher densities. Koalas also use non-food trees for resting and shelter, including during extreme weather. Because preferred tree species differ by region and season, suitable habitat is a network of feeding and refuge trees rather than simply any stand of eucalypts.

Leaves of selected Eucalyptus, Corymbia and related trees make up almost all the diet; a koala may eat roughly half a kilogram of foliage daily, although intake varies. It does not choose every tree of a favoured species: leaf water and nutrients matter, as do defensive chemicals such as terpenes and phenolic compounds. The koala’s ridged molars crush leaves, and its liver processes some absorbed toxins. In the hindgut, an enlarged caecum and proximal colon retain fluids, microbes and fine particles for extended fermentation, while less digestible coarse material passes more quickly. This slow, selective processing extracts nutrients from fibrous leaves but yields little energy, so activity is economical and rest is prolonged. Free-ranging females have been observed increasing foliage intake during peak lactation, with digestive adjustments that preserve nutrient extraction.

Koalas are mainly solitary, but neighbouring home ranges often overlap and allow encounters. They rest for much of the day, commonly wedged in a tree fork, and feed or move more often at night and around dawn and dusk. Ground travel between trees exposes them to danger, so connected tree cover matters. Males advertise during the breeding season with deep bellows and scent marks from the chest gland; interactions and movement increase as animals seek mates or compete. These signals help coordinate contact across a dispersed population rather than forming stable social groups.

After a gestation of about 35 days, a female usually gives birth to one very small, hairless joey. It crawls unaided to the rear-opening pouch and attaches to a teat, where it continues developing for around six months. At first emergence it begins tasting the mother’s soft faecal pap, which transfers maternal gut microbes that contribute to foliage digestion. The young then rides on her back and continues nursing while learning to feed; weaning is usually complete near its first birthday. It may remain within its mother’s range before dispersing, often around two to three years old. Timing of births and breeding varies with region and conditions.

The koala’s close dependence on a short list of tree species ties its distribution to the composition and condition of forest. It uses several tree types for shelter as well as food, and moves among them to forage, rest and meet other koalas. Fragmentation can therefore separate feeding patches and make ground crossings more frequent. Drought, heat and fire can reduce foliage quality or availability, while disease, dogs and vehicles add direct mortality; effects differ among regions and populations.

The koala’s conservation situation varies geographically. Under Australia’s EPBC Act, the combined populations of Queensland, New South Wales and the Australian Capital Territory were listed as Endangered on 12 February 2022. Queensland also changed its state category to Endangered on 8 April 2022, and New South Wales did so on 20 May 2022. The 2022 national recovery plan reports the whole species as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List, while Victoria and South Australia are outside that federal endangered listing. Habitat loss and fragmentation, climate-related heat and drought, disease, vehicle strikes and dog attacks are interacting pressures. The recovery plan therefore prioritizes connected habitat and coordinated action across jurisdictions; local population trends and legal categories should not be generalized to the entire range.

Least weasel
Mustela nivalis

The least weasel has a very slender, elongated trunk, short limbs and a short tail, a form that lets it follow rodents into narrow burrows. Its high surface-to-volume ratio and inability to curl into a compact ball increase heat loss. Its native range spans much of Europe, northern Asia and northern North America, with introductions to some islands.

In Britain, adult males usually measure 19.4–21.7 cm in body length, with a 4.2–5.2 cm tail, and weigh 106–131 g; females measure 17.3–18.3 cm, with a 3.4–4.3 cm tail, and weigh 55–69 g. Adult body size also varies geographically. The British coat is reddish brown above and cream below, with an irregular boundary; its short tail lacks the stoat’s black tip. Some northern populations turn white in winter, unlike Britain’s. In northeastern Poland, observations from 1997 and 2003–07 associated fewer snow-cover days with a smaller share of white winter coats. In a separate 2015–16 experiment, predators detected coat models more often when their colour mismatched the background; snow-cover percentage did not significantly predict detection.

Across its Holarctic range, it uses grassland, meadows, farmland, woodland edges, scrub, steppe, wetlands and some alpine or coastal habitats. It favors ground cover and prey-rich patches for ambushes, and shelters in abandoned rodent nests or burrows, often using several resting sites rather than digging a den.

In a Polish forest, five radio-tracked males attacked bank voles and yellow-necked mice above and below ground. Of 60 observed attacks, success was 23% on voles and 60% on mice, so tunnel access did not guarantee a catch. On English farmland, voles made up 16% of the diet in low-vole years and 54% at peak abundance, while birds became the main alternative when voles were scarce. Smaller weasels consumed more food relative to body mass; captive trials also found assimilation varied with diet and temperature, so they do not define a wild daily ration.

An English woodland study found resident male ranges varied in size and shifted with prey distribution; males generally ranged farther than females. Usually solitary, least weasels mark den sites with scent. Their small bodies need frequent feeding, and surplus prey may be cached near shelters. Measurements of free-ranging males in Poland found higher thermoregulatory costs in cold weather and daily activity adjusted with temperature, body mass, habitat and season.

From 18 breeding females and three immature young sampled in Poland, the author inferred a season from April mating to the last young leaving in October, cautioning that the sample was small. Unlike stoats, least weasels do not delay implantation: total gestation lasts about 34–37 days from mating, including roughly 25 days after implantation. A five-year captive study recorded 65 litters, averaging 5.1 kits among 53 litters of known size; this is not a universal wild average. Newborns weigh about 1–1.7 g and are naked, blind and deaf; ears open at 21–28 days and eyes at 26–30 days. The female alone nurses for about 32 days; weaning may continue to 42–56 days. In captivity, young can kill prey at about 47 days; they disperse and become independent at about nine to ten weeks.

On 25 km² of southern English farmland, vole density peaked at fourteen times its low-year level in a four-year cycle; weasel numbers lagged and females failed to breed in the trough, documenting a local predator response without showing that weasels caused the vole cycle. In Białowieża Forest, winter estimates attributed 11–21% of rodent predation to weasels, compared with 56–71% to tawny owls and 10–15% to pine martens.

The global IUCN assessment dated 2 May 2015 and amended in 2019 lists the species as Least Concern, citing its broad range, presumed large population and tolerance of some habitat change. In Britain, gamekeepers historically trapped weasels as supposed gamebird enemies; the Mammal Society says they probably killed few chicks and that trapping likely had no long-term effect because populations recover and recolonise.

Leopard
Panthera pardus

The leopard is a powerful cat native to Africa and Asia. It occupies a broad range of environments, from tropical forest to desert and mountains. Its flexible hunting and climbing abilities help it persist where other large cats may not.

Adults have a long body, short muscular legs, broad paws and a long tail. Their coats range from pale gold to ochre, with dark rosettes and smaller solid spots. Some are melanistic; their markings remain visible in suitable light.

Leopards use rainforest, woodland, savanna, scrub, rocky slopes and desert where cover and prey are available. They also occur in some human-used landscapes. Himalayan records reach about 5,200 metres, an exceptional local record rather than a typical habitat.

This carnivore hunts prey from small mammals and birds to larger ungulates. Its menu depends on locally available animals: a Gabon study found forest ungulates important, while research in Tanzania recorded substantial primate consumption. Leopards may also take livestock near farms.

Leopards generally live alone, except when females travel with cubs or adults meet to mate. Activity varies: many studied savanna populations are mainly nocturnal, while some in Gabonese rainforest were largely active by day. Scent marks, calls and scratches signal presence.

After about three months of pregnancy, a female gives birth in a concealed den, commonly to two or three cubs. They remain hidden, then follow her and learn to hunt. Independence is gradual; reported ages vary among populations, from about one year to two years.

The leopard consumes different prey in different habitats, so no single species defines its diet everywhere. It may carry a kill into a tree, making it less accessible to competitors. When wild prey is scarce, livestock may enter its diet and cause conflict with people.

The IUCN SSC Cat Specialist Group’s account, citing Red List version 2024-2, classifies leopards as Vulnerable and reports an 11% contraction of extant range during 2016–2023. It identifies habitat loss, prey depletion, illegal killing and trade, retaliation, and poorly managed trophy hunting as pressures.

Lingcod
Ophiodon elongatus

The lingcod is a large northeastern Pacific predator in the greenling family Hexagrammidae, not the cod family Gadidae. It ranges from the Gulf of Alaska to Baja California and may live for more than twenty years.

Its elongated body tapers toward the tail and is mottled grey, brown, green or blue, often with copper spots. A broad, unscaled head and large mouth hold many sharp teeth. Canadian records place maturity near 45 centimetres in males and 61–75 centimetres in females. Some have blue-green flesh that loses colour when cooked; its cause remains unknown.

Adults occupy coastal rocky reefs and other complex bottom habitats, with crevices that provide shelter. Adhesive eggs stay in shallow crevices, and larvae drift near the surface. Juveniles settle on nearshore sand among eelgrass or kelp, then move toward deeper reefs as they grow.

Adults seize prey with a sudden lunge, eating bottom fish—including smaller lingcod—as well as octopuses, squid and crabs. Larvae feed on drifting zooplankton such as krill and tiny crustaceans; juveniles switch to small fish.
Lingcod remain near familiar reefs; males defend nesting territories in late autumn while females visit spawning grounds seasonally. Sharks, marine mammals and larger lingcod prey on them.

Males mature near age two and females near three. In winter and spring, females lay adhesive eggs in rocky crevices; males fertilize and guard them for eight to ten weeks. The eggs hatch into drifting larvae that eat plankton, then settle in coastal nurseries and later feed on fish.
Rockfish, sculpins, greenlings and sea stars consume unguarded eggs. Young lingcod enter coastal food webs after feeding on surface plankton.

Commercial and recreational fisheries target lingcod; bottom trawls can disturb habitat and catch other groundfish. NOAA reports both U.S. Pacific stocks were not overfished in 2021 assessments and were not subject to overfishing in 2024. Seasonal closures and limits protect spawning fish.
