Lion
Panthera leo

Wild lions now survive in fragmented parts of sub-Saharan Africa and in one Asian population in western India. They use settings from savanna and scrub to dry woodland, while prey and human pressures vary between regions. In India, lions move through the wider Gir landscape, where protected forest meets farms and settlements.

The lion has a muscular, deep-chested body, a short tawny coat, pale underparts and a long tail tipped with a dark tuft; cubs often have fading spots. Adult males usually grow a mane whose length and shade vary with age and individual; females generally lack one. African reference adults average 180 kilograms and 1.20 metres at the shoulder for males, and 130 kilograms and 1.05 metres for females; individuals vary. Asiatic lions often have shorter manes and a more visible abdominal fold. Retractile claws grip prey; long canines kill and cheek teeth slice meat.

Lions occupy savannas, grasslands, scrub, open woodland and dry forests, provided that cover, prey and relatively undisturbed den sites are available. Gir combines dry deciduous forest, thorn scrub, grassland and river corridors within a cultivated regional landscape. Asiatic lions may rest in dense vegetation by day and range more widely at night, sometimes near farms and settlements. A comparison across ten habitats found that seasonal food scarcity, rather than overall prey abundance alone, was linked to larger home ranges.

Lions are opportunistic carnivores, but medium and large hoofed mammals usually supply most of their food. They stalk close before a short rush, then use jaws and forelimbs to bring prey down. Group hunts may divide roles, but observations show that participation varies and some lions hang back when prey is easier to catch. In Gir, chital, sambar, nilgai and wild pigs are documented prey; livestock made up a larger share of recorded kills in peripheral areas than inside the protected landscape.

In many African populations, a pride is a flexible, fission-fusion group built around related females and their young. Males may hold territory in coalitions, while females often stay in their birth group and young males disperse; local patterns vary. Pride members split into smaller parties and reunite to rest, care for cubs, mate or defend territory. Both sexes roar and growl to communicate. Roars maintain contact with pride members and advertise territorial boundaries; lions can use the number of callers they hear to assess the strength of rivals. At Gir, female groups and male coalitions commonly use separate ranges, meeting mainly to mate or at large kills.

Females breed in different seasons; gestation lasts about 110 days and litters usually contain one to four cubs. A mother gives birth in a secluded thicket, hiding the cubs for their first weeks and returning to nurse them. Cubs eat meat from about three months and are weaned near six months, yet Gir young may depend on the natal group for food until two or three years old. Females may first breed at about three and a half years; males often mate only after securing territory. A takeover by unfamiliar males can put cubs at risk; mothers may hide or defend them, and outcomes vary with age and local conditions.

Food scarcity can enlarge territories and reduce prides: a comparison of ten habitats linked lean-season prey availability with group size and cub survival. Lions consume large herbivores, but also compete with other carnivores over carcasses, scavenging and sometimes losing kills to rivals. In Gir, the balance between wild prey and livestock shifts with season and location, linking prey access to local feeding patterns.

The IUCN global assessment, made on 1 February 2023 and published in 2024, lists lions as Vulnerable and the trend as decreasing. It inferred a 36 percent range reduction over three generations, with habitat loss, prey depletion and conflict-related killing among the pressures. African populations are fragmented; Gujarat’s protection and habitat management have supported a recovery, but India’s lions remain concentrated in one regional population. The government reported 891 Asiatic lions in its 2025 count on 10 August 2026.

Lowland paca
Cuniculus paca

The lowland paca is a large, mostly nocturnal rodent of tropical America, from eastern Mexico through Central America and much of South America. It belongs to Cuniculidae, the paca family; the agoutis are separate rodents in genus Dasyprocta, despite the similar common name. Its close relative, the mountain paca, is a distinct species associated with higher Andean forests.

Adults commonly weigh about 6–12 kilograms and measure roughly 60–82 centimetres from head to body; males tend to be a little larger. A compact, nearly tailless body, short sturdy legs, blunt head and long whiskers suit this ground-dwelling animal. Its coarse reddish- to dark-brown back bears several lengthwise rows of pale spots, above a lighter belly. The mountain paca is generally smaller and more thickly furred. The agouti is a separate rodent, not another paca.

In the Lacandon rainforest, pacas also use secondary woodland and riparian cover. It favors stream and river banks, which provide den sites and quick access to water as an escape route. A daytime refuge may be a self-dug burrow or a cavity among roots, rocks or an old burrow; several exits can connect to forest paths. In the Lacandon Forest, used cavities lay under roots or inside fallen logs in riparian or secondary vegetation, generally within 100 metres of water.

Fallen fruit is the main food, supplemented by seeds, tender leaves, stems and roots; the exact menu follows local fruiting seasons. A French Guianan stomach-content comparison found that fruit dominated the paca diet, with more seasonal variation than in smaller terrestrial rodents. In the Lacandon Forest of southern Mexico, cameras confirmed fruit at 31 of 57 monitored feeding sites, with fruits from 20 tree species recorded. Only 40 percent of the tree species eaten were shared between preserved and transformed sites, evidence that local pacas use a flexible menu.

By day the paca rests; around dusk it follows familiar trails to feed. Adults are often encountered alone, though some accounts describe territorial pairs using separate burrows. Alarmed pacas may flee into water, stamp, grind their teeth or give a low rumble. Expanded cheek arches and hollows in the upper jaw form a bony chamber proposed to amplify that call, but this acoustic function remains uncertain.

In tropical populations, breeding may occur throughout the year, while some subtropical populations have a seasonal cycle. After roughly 97–118 days of gestation in the wild, a female usually gives birth to one well-developed young; twins are reported but less typical. The young are well developed at birth: their eyes are open and their movements already coordinated, rather than remaining helpless in a nest. They start sampling solid food at about three weeks and are usually weaned within six to twelve weeks; this early development helps a young paca move to shelter and escape danger.

By feeding on fallen fruit, pacas can disperse seeds and support fruit-tree regeneration. Their abandoned burrows provide shelters that other animals may use. Jaguars, ocelots and other predators hunt pacas, which may compete with agoutis and other forest mammals for fruit.

Globally, IUCN lists the paca as Least Concern. The same system reports a Near Threatened Argentine assessment by SAREM in 2025 and a Vulnerable national assessment published in 2021. The paca is among the most heavily hunted Neotropical mammals for food and sport; researchers warn that modest reproductive output may not offset intense hunting. A slow life history, with first parturition only after several months, makes recovery vulnerable to sustained hunting pressure, even where the species remains widespread overall.

Eurasian magpie
Pica pica
The Eurasian magpie is a familiar corvid of Europe and much of northern and central Asia, recognizable by its black-and-white pattern and exceptionally long tail.

An adult is about 46–50 cm long and usually weighs 185–268 grams. More than half the bird’s length is tail, creating a striking silhouette in flight and on the ground. The head, back, and breast are black, with white belly, shoulder patches, and large white wing panels; juveniles are duller and have a shorter tail. In strong light, the dark wing and tail feathers flash blue and green: layers of hollow melanosomes in the feather barbules reflect light selectively, producing structural iridescence. A harsh, rattling chatter is its characteristic call.

Magpies use farmland, villages, gardens, parks, open woodland, and the edges of towns. Trees and hedges provide nesting sites. They generally avoid dense forest, extensive wetlands, and treeless country, so the meeting of cover and open feeding ground matters more than any single habitat type.

This opportunistic omnivore searches mostly while walking or hopping over the ground, pausing to inspect likely prey before picking it up with its bill. Beetles and other invertebrates are important, alongside seeds, fruit, scraps, carrion, and occasionally eggs or nestlings; vertebrate food is usually a small share overall. A study of urban Manchester birds found a varied diet dominated by surface-dwelling invertebrates, with plant foods especially important in winter. Magpies also hide surplus food in small caches and retrieve it later, using nearby visual landmarks and other cues; some buried acorns are left behind and can germinate.

Pairs usually defend a breeding territory, while young or nonbreeding birds may gather in family groups or communal roosts. Their harsh alarm chatter warns other magpies when cats and other predators are nearby. Magpies can store and relocate food, and experiments show that they use local cues to recover caches. The familiar tale that they are compelled to steal shiny trinkets is unsupported: captive and free-living birds in one experiment showed no unconditional preference for shiny objects and often hesitated around unfamiliar items. A 2008 mirror-mark experiment was interpreted as evidence of self-recognition. A larger 2020 replication did not confirm that result, so the test does not establish a universal capacity for self-awareness.

A pair builds a domed stick nest with a side entrance, usually in a tree; both sexes gather material, with the male bringing most and the female doing most construction. The female lays a typical clutch of five or six eggs and incubates them for about 20 days, while her mate supplies food. Chicks hatch naked and helpless, and both parents feed them. They usually fledge at about 26–31 days, then receive food from the adults for several more weeks. One brood is usual each year, and British records indicate that breeding commonly begins at about two years old.

By taking eggs and nestlings, magpies can affect particular nests, especially when dependent fledglings increase the food demands of territorial adults. In a UK farmland study, artificial nests faced greater magpie predation inside breeding territories late in the season, but wider research has not found a simple national link between corvid increases and songbird declines. Their ecological role also includes seed dispersal: in western Mediterranean farmland, magpies carry and bury holm-oak acorns, and some caches produce seedlings. The balance between predation and seed movement therefore depends on local prey, habitat, and plant communities.

The latest global IUCN assessment, published in 2024, classifies the Eurasian Magpie as Least Concern. That category does not rule out declines in particular local populations. In Britain, the BTO reports a 104% increase in the monitored population index between 1967 and 2024, alongside a 6.4% expansion in breeding distribution. Magpies have also been culled in British game management; a 2022 review documents this history and notes that control policies differ among UK nations. Evidence does not support treating magpies as a general cause of songbird decline; habitat change and food availability also shape those populations.

Mahi-mahi
Coryphaena hippurus
The mahi-mahi, or common dolphinfish, is a fast-growing, open-ocean fish found in tropical and warm temperate seas worldwide. Despite its English name, it is a fish, not a dolphin.

Its laterally flattened, streamlined body carries a single dorsal fin that runs from above the head almost to the deeply forked tail. The back is metallic blue-green, the sides flash gold and silver with dark spots, and these vivid colours fade quickly after death. Adult males develop a high, squared forehead, while females have a more rounded head. The related pompano dolphinfish, Coryphaena equiselis, is deeper-bodied and has a trapezoid-shaped tooth patch on the tongue; C. hippurus has an oval patch.

It lives near the surface of offshore tropical, subtropical and warm temperate waters across the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific oceans, entering the Mediterranean occasionally. Floating seaweed rafts and other drifting objects offer shelter and concentrated feeding grounds, especially for smaller fish. Adults commonly reach about one metre; rare specimens approach 2.1 metres.

A daytime predator, the mahi-mahi pursues small pelagic fish such as flying fish and juvenile tuna, as well as squid, crabs and other drifting invertebrates. Its fast swimming and broad prey menu let it exploit abundant food around floating weed and in open water.

Young fish commonly school, whereas older individuals are often solitary; large males tend to range in open water, while females and smaller males often gather near floating objects. Its changing colour pattern is striking in life but fades rapidly when the fish is landed.

Both sexes can mature within their first year, at about four to five months in Atlantic populations. Females release eggs into the water repeatedly during the warm spawning season; in the Atlantic, spawning occurs beneath floating Sargassum mats.

Mahi-mahi transfer energy from small fish and drifting invertebrates to larger predators, including tuna, marlin, sailfish, swordfish and marine mammals. Floating algae serve as juvenile shelter and feeding habitat, linking this open-water predator to drifting surface communities.
Its global conservation status is Least Concern. Fishing pressure and longline bycatch of turtles or marine mammals are concerns; Atlantic stock assessments remain incomplete in several U.S. regions.

Mallard
Anas platyrhynchos

The Mallard is a widespread Northern Hemisphere duck of wetlands, farms and city ponds. Its success comes from a flexible diet, broad tolerance of shallow waters and the ability of many populations to remain near open water through winter. In North America, adults typically measure 50–65 cm long with an 82–95 cm wingspan; the sexes are similar in size, usually weighing 0.9–1.4 kg. Those measurements describe the species, while regional populations and individual condition cause variation.

The adult male is unmistakable in breeding plumage: an iridescent green head, narrow white neck ring, chestnut breast, grey body and curled black tail feathers. The female is mottled brown, with a dark eye-line and orange-and-black bill; her patterned plumage blends into nesting cover. Both sexes show a blue-violet speculum bordered by white, visible when the wing opens. After breeding, the male moults into a dull, female-like eclipse plumage while replacing his flight feathers, leaving him temporarily flightless; a later moult restores bright colours.

Mallards favour shallow, sheltered water: marshes, ponds, small lakes, estuaries and flooded fields provide feeding areas and nearby cover. They also graze on land, including stubble fields, and readily use artificial ponds and urban parks. Nests are usually on dry ground in grass or other dense vegetation, often some distance from water; after hatching, the female leads the brood from the nest to water. This combination of wet feeding habitat and undisturbed nesting cover matters more than any single plant community. In the Prairie Pothole Region of North America, small seasonal wetlands are especially important breeding and brood-rearing sites.

A broad, flattened bill fringed with comb-like lamellae lets the Mallard strain edible particles from water and mud. It usually feeds by dabbling at the surface or tipping forward to reach submerged plants and invertebrates, rather than pursuing prey underwater. Water and food move through the bill; the lamellae retain particles as water and fine debris drain away. Seeds, aquatic vegetation, insects, worms, snails and crustaceans all occur in the diet, whose balance changes with season and local supply. On land, it takes grain and other plant foods, then returns to water to rinse and separate indigestible material from a food bolus.

Outside nesting, Mallards gather in flocks and feed or rest together, while pairs form well before eggs are laid. Courtship uses head bobs, calls and chases; females give the loud quack, males a quieter rasp. Many northern birds migrate south as wetlands freeze, but movements vary: some populations are resident, and others mix residents with seasonal visitors.

Pairs commonly form in autumn or winter, months before breeding, and are generally seasonal rather than lifelong. The female makes a shallow, grass-lined ground nest, adds down from her breast, and lays a clutch usually numbering about 11–14 eggs in British records. She alone incubates for roughly 27–28 days; the male leaves to join other males. Ducklings hatch covered in down, leave the nest soon after hatching and swim and feed themselves under the female’s guidance. They are precocial, but remain vulnerable to predators and depend on their mother for protection and access to suitable feeding wetlands. They typically fledge at 50–60 days. Mallards generally reach reproductive maturity at about one year.

Feeding on aquatic vegetation, seeds, invertebrates and crops makes Mallards consumers of plant production and small animal prey across wetlands and farmland. Their broad bill and opportunistic diet overlap with those of other dabbling ducks; prey size and the amount of detritus can alter how much food each species filters from the same water. Aquatic invertebrates are especially important to growing ducklings, and field experiments in North American prairie wetlands linked greater invertebrate abundance with faster early growth. Eggs and young are prey for mammals, birds, reptiles and fish, so dense cover and productive brood wetlands affect survival. Mallards also hybridize with related ducks; releases of farm-reared Mallards have introduced domestic ancestry into some wild populations, documented in Europe and North America.

BirdLife International’s global IUCN assessment dated 5 June 2025 lists the Mallard as Least Concern, while recording a decreasing population trend. That global category reflects the species’ enormous range and population; it does not mean every regional population is stable. North American monitoring and management have long tracked breeding numbers, habitat conditions and harvest, while wetland availability remains important to nesting and brood survival. A separate, well-documented pressure comes from releasing farm-reared birds: genomic studies identify ongoing domestic introgression in parts of Europe and North America. The species is also the ancestor of most domestic duck breeds, so feral and farm-origin birds can complicate local conservation of closely related wild ducks.

Moon jellyfish
Aurelia aurita

Aurelia aurita is a translucent scyphozoan, or true jellyfish, whose familiar saucer-shaped medusa is only one part of its life cycle. Once treated as cosmopolitan, the species was later separated from many similar Aurelia; A. aurita is now reported mainly from the northeastern Atlantic, with introduced populations in northeastern US and Argentina, though natural arrival in the US remains possible.
A typical adult bell is about 25–40 cm across. Four horseshoe-shaped gonads show through it, above four oral arms and fine marginal tentacles; the clear body may have a faint blue or pink tint.
The medusa lives in pelagic water; its polyp is benthic and attaches to a hard surface, often under shelter in shallow brackish sites.

Tentacles and bell mucus intercept zooplankton, including copepods and small larvae. Cnidocytes are stinging cells containing nematocysts, tiny capsules that fire venomous harpoons when prey touches a tentacle. The same contact-triggered discharge can stun predators, so these cells serve defense as well as feeding. Cilia carry captured food along the oral arms to the mouth and gastrovascular cavity for digestion.
Bell pulses propel the medusa briefly, while currents carry it farther. Medusae may gather to breed; attached polyps bud asexually.

Adults have separate sexes; males release sperm, and fertilized eggs develop in brood pockets on female oral arms. The ciliated planula swims briefly before settling and becoming a small attached polyp, or scyphistoma. The polyp may bud, then strobilate: constrictions segment it and release disc-shaped ephyrae. Ephyrae develop into adult medusae. Seasonal temperature affects strobilation timing.
Podocysts, protective resting cysts produced by polyps, help them endure food shortages and resist nudibranch predation during the benthic stage.
Periodic local blooms can strand jellies on beaches or clog coastal seawater intakes, creating a local infrastructure problem rather than evidence of a global population decline.

Moose
Alces alces

The moose is the largest living deer, inhabiting northern forests of North America and Eurasia, from Alaska and Canada to Scandinavia, Russia, northern China and Mongolia. In British English it is often called elk.

A shoulder hump, heavy body, long legs and drooping muzzle define its shape. Only males grow annual antlers: broad palms are common in North America, narrower forms occur in Eurasia. Coat colour ranges from brown to nearly black. Long legs cross deep snow; nostrils close underwater, aiding submerged feeding.

Moose favour northern woodland, young forest, wetlands and shores. In Alaska they use river corridors, timberline plateaus and burns where willow, birch and aspen regrow. Lakes and marshes offer food and cover. Seasonal movements link feeding, calving, rutting and wintering areas.

Food varies with season and supply. In summer it eats leaves, herbs and shallow-water plants; spring also brings grazing. Woody shoots, especially willow, birch and aspen, matter more in autumn and winter. Its long muzzle and closable nostrils help crop submerged plants.

Moose are usually solitary; cows stay with calves, and adults meet more during the autumn rut. Males push antlers against rivals; winners may mate with several females. Seasonal movements vary locally. Daily activity centres on feeding, resting and rumination.

In Alaska, mating peaks in late September and early October. After about 230 days, females calve in spring, usually producing one calf; twins occur in favourable conditions. Calves grow quickly, nurse through summer and are usually weaned in autumn, remaining with their mother into the next year.

Browsing shrubs, saplings and aquatic plants affects forest regeneration. At unusually high density in Forillon, Parks Canada documents major vegetation changes. That local case shows how abundant moose can shape plant communities; effects vary with population and habitat.

The global IUCN assessment (last assessed 27 September 2015; published 2016) classed moose as Least Concern, with an increasing overall trend. It cited habitat alteration as a major human threat. This dated assessment is not a current survey of regional populations.

Mugger crocodile
Crocodylus palustris

The mugger, or marsh crocodile, is a broad-snouted crocodilian native to South Asia and eastern Iran. It occupies freshwater rivers, lakes, marshes and ponds, including reservoirs and irrigation waters. This adaptable predator persists in both protected wetlands and human-altered waterways.

Males usually stay below 3.5 m; females average 2.5–3 m, though exceptional individuals approach 5 m. The mugger has the broadest snout in Crocodylus. Adults are grey-brown; young have lighter colouring and dark bands. Its muscular tail drives swimming, and sturdy limbs support movement on land. Crocodilians can also lift the body into a high walk, though fast gaits are poorly documented for this species. Hatchlings measure about 25–27 cm.

Muggers inhabit freshwater rivers, lakes, marshes and ponds, often using deeper pools with sandy banks and dense riverside cover. They also occupy reservoirs, irrigation canals and aquaculture ponds; some enter brackish lagoons. This flexibility allows use of human-made waters, but can bring crocodiles near fishing and farming communities.

Muggers are opportunistic carnivores whose diet changes with size. Young take insects, crustaceans and small fish; adults eat fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals. Deer and buffalo are occasional large prey, not a routine meal for every crocodile. Local feeding reflects available prey and body size; individuals have also been seen corralling fish.

As ectotherms, muggers warm by basking and cool by entering water or shade. Individuals dig bank burrows that buffer harsh heat and cold; underground temperatures change more slowly than surface air. During prolonged hot, dry spells, a mugger may aestivate—remain inactive in its burrow—then travel overland when seeking permanent water. Such treks can cross roads and railways.

Females lay 10–30 eggs in a hole nest, often in sandy bank soil; some nests sit beside or inside burrows. Dry-season laying varies geographically. Eggs incubate for about 55–75 days. Temperature affects sex: controlled experiments yielded all females at 28–31 °C and all males at 32.5 °C, with both sexes at intermediate temperatures. The female guards the nest and may help hatchlings emerge and carry them to water; field observations document such care, but its duration and effect on survival remain uncertain. Captive double clutches have not been documented in the wild.

As a generalist predator, the mugger links aquatic and terrestrial prey in wetland food webs; its eggs and young are also eaten by other animals. In the Chambal River, a 2024 study found increasing mugger numbers and occupancy in a sanctuary established for gharial recovery. Researchers flagged possible competition with this more habitat-specialised crocodilian as a local management concern, not a proven species-wide effect.

The global IUCN assessment dated 30 June 2009 and published in 2013 classified the mugger as Vulnerable (A2cd). The IUCN Crocodile Specialist Group estimated over 20,000 adults in its 2025 action plan. Habitat loss, fishing nets, egg collection, persecution and transport deaths remain documented threats. A 2008–2010 survey near Vadodara documented crocodile rescues and relocation after human encounters, illustrating the need for local coexistence measures.

Murray cod
Maccullochella peelii

The Murray cod is a large freshwater predator endemic to eastern Australia. Unlike true cod, it belongs to Percichthyidae, alongside the related trout cod and eastern freshwater cod. It is Australia’s largest freshwater fish.

Its robust, elongated body carries a broad, flattened head, small eyes and a wide mouth with fine teeth; the snout profile is concave. Adults commonly measure under 70 cm, while exceptional historical fish reached about 1.8 m and 113.5 kg. Olive-green flanks bear darker marbling and fade to a pale belly. Rounded fins frame a long dorsal fin with a notch between spiny and soft parts. The mouth reaches behind the eyes; the lower jaw may protrude. Maximum lifespan estimates range from 75 to 114 years.

Deep pools, boulders, undercut banks and submerged fallen timber provide ambush cover and shelter. The fish is most characteristic of lowland rivers, though it also occurs in some upland reaches. Its native range spans the Murray–Darling Basin in Queensland, New South Wales, Victoria and South Australia, excluding the coldest upper reaches.

Adults take crayfish, freshwater shrimp and fish, including introduced carp and redfin when available; molluscs and occasionally small animals from the water’s edge broaden the menu. It hunts by ambush from cover.
Territorial, it favors deep pools beside logs, boulders or overhanging banks. By day it shelters; at night it may hunt shallows or the surface.

Maturity usually comes at about five years, though growth and location alter the timing. In spring, pairs court and choose hard surfaces, often submerged logs or rocks. The female lays eggs on this submerged surface; the male fertilises them externally. The male guards and fans the eggs until free-swimming larvae hatch. The larvae drift away, use their yolk reserves, then feed on tiny invertebrates as they develop.
A top predator, it eats native fish, crustaceans and introduced carp in the same river food webs.

Overfishing sharply reduced stocks from the nineteenth century; dams, altered flows, cold releases and snag removal still damage habitat and recruitment. The species is listed as Vulnerable under Australia’s EPBC Act; this national conservation status is distinct from local fishing regulations.

Muskrat
Ondatra zibethicus

The muskrat is a medium-sized rodent of fresh and brackish wetlands, with an insulating coat and aquatic adaptations for foraging among emergent plants and retreating to shelters with underwater entrances. Native to North America, it has also established introduced populations across parts of Europe and Asia.

Adults have a head-and-body length of about 23–33 cm, a tail 18–30 cm, and a mass of roughly 0.7–1.9 kg; size varies among populations. The tail is nearly naked, scaly and compressed from side to side, about as long as the head and body. Stiff hairs fringe the toes, and the hind toes are partly webbed; small ears sit almost hidden in dense brown fur. Unlike the much larger beaver, it has a narrow, laterally flattened tail; nutria are far heavier and have a rounded tail with conspicuous pale whiskers.

Muskrats use marshes, ponds, lakes, streams, drainage canals and estuarine wetlands where water and food remain available. Dense stands of cattails, bulrushes, sedges or reeds provide both edible shoots and cover, while open water lets them travel between feeding and resting sites. In Texas, shallow marshes with stable water around 15–60 cm supported especially favorable conditions; that local range should not be treated as a universal requirement. Houses of cut marsh vegetation rise above water, whereas animals along rivers and canals may excavate bank burrows with underwater entrances.

The diet consists mostly of aquatic plants, especially roots, rhizomes and lower stems of cattails, sedges, bulrushes and water lilies. Strong incisors cut this vegetation, and lips that close behind the incisors allow the animal to gnaw while submerged without taking water into its mouth. It often carries plant pieces to a feeding platform or shelter to eat. Animal food is occasional rather than the norm: documented items include crayfish, mussels, frogs, fish and small turtles, particularly when plant food is scarce. A large, compartmentalized cecum retains fibrous food for microbial fermentation, helping process its plant-heavy diet.

Muskrats are active throughout the day but often become most active from mid-afternoon into dusk. Family members may share a lodge, but crowding and breeding-season competition can cause aggression; scent from musk glands and squeaks or squeals provide communication. In winter, animals in icy regions dig for submerged roots and may build a protective feeding shelter over a hole in the ice.

The breeding season shifts with latitude; in Indiana, most litters arrive in May and June, and females may produce two to four litters per year. After about 28–30 days of gestation, a female gives birth in a grass- or cattail-lined nest, commonly to around six kits. They are born blind and helpless, begin swimming at roughly ten days, and can eat green plants at about three weeks. The mother nurses them until weaning at three to four weeks; young may remain with her longer, especially in the final litter of the season. A two-season field study found that male care varied with mating strategy, and juvenile survival in that study did not depend on the amount of paternal care.

Muskrats are prey for mink, otters, foxes, coyotes, owls, hawks and other wetland predators, linking plant production to higher trophic levels. Their grazing and the vegetation they pile into lodges or feeding platforms can open dense marsh stands into a mosaic of channels, grazed patches and emergent cover. This effect depends on local density and plant growth: heavy grazing can strip vegetation or weaken banks, while moderate activity creates structural variety. Lodges can also be used by other wetland animals as nesting or resting sites.

The global IUCN assessment completed on 20 August 2016 classified the species as Least Concern, citing its broad range and lack of major global threats; this is not a current census of every population. A 42-year analysis of harvest records from 37 U.S. states found evidence of decline from 1970 to 2012 after accounting for pelt prices, with a steeper trend in the Southeast; harvest data remain an indirect measure. The European Union’s consolidated regulation of 7 August 2025 still lists the muskrat as an invasive alien species of Union concern. It was added to that list by Commission Implementing Regulation 2017/1263 in 2017. Burrowing can damage dikes and banks, and intense grazing can alter wetlands, so European management addresses local ecological and infrastructure impacts.

Mute Swan
Cygnus olor
The Mute Swan is a large Eurasian waterfowl of lakes, slow rivers, marshes and sheltered coasts, feeding and nesting close to water.

Adults are white, with black legs, a bright orange bill and a black knob at its base; typical birds measure 127–152 cm long, with a wingspan of 208–238 cm. Males are generally larger than females, although the sexes look alike. Young cygnets are downy and pale grey, with dark bills and legs; older juveniles may show brown-grey feathers as their plumage gradually turns white during the first year. The orange bill and black knob distinguish this species from the Whooper Swan (Cygnus cygnus) and Tundra Swan (Cygnus columbianus), whose bills lack that knob. Both sexes bear the fleshy black knob; it is usually larger in males and varies seasonally, peaking near hatching in one monitored population, so size alone cannot reliably determine sex.
It uses freshwater and brackish wetlands, including ponds, lakes, estuaries and sheltered bays, nesting on islands or vegetated banks near water.

Aquatic vegetation is the main food, though Mute Swans also take animal prey such as snails, insects and small aquatic animals. They skim plants from the surface, tip forward to reach submerged growth and rake the bottom with their feet to uncover tubers. In the eastern Gulf of Finland, one study found a seasonal shift from stranded filamentous algae in late winter to new plant growth during egg laying and incubation.

In one Midlands study, 85% of paired breeders retained the same mate from year to year if both survived. During nesting, pairs defend nest territories with raised-wing displays and arched necks. Though called mute, the swan is not silent: it hisses and snorts when disturbed and gives muffled calls during territorial encounters. After breeding, adults shed all their flight feathers at once and cannot fly for roughly six to eight weeks.

Pairs build a large nest from reeds and other plants; males choose the site and begin the platform, while females shape the cup. British records give a typical clutch of four to seven eggs, usually incubated by the female for about 34–44 days. Newly hatched cygnets can move around the nest, feed and enter the water once their down dries. British records report a typical fledging duration of 120–150 days.

Grazing submerged vegetation can change the biomass and structure of shallow plant beds, although effects vary with local conditions. In an Illinois experiment, swan access was associated with lower below-ground plant biomass, while above-ground biomass did not differ detectably. In Chesapeake Bay, introduced Mute Swans (Cygnus olor) remain year-round, unlike Tundra Swans (Cygnus columbianus), which migrate there for winter. Across Europe, populations are generally resident, although cold weather can displace birds locally.

BirdLife International’s 2016 global IUCN Red List assessment classified the Mute Swan as Least Concern. The species is native across much of Eurasia and introduced in North America. Locally dense introduced flocks can compete with native waterbirds and affect aquatic vegetation. In Britain, population recovery followed severe declines associated with lead poisoning from swallowed fishing weights and shot; restrictions on lead weights and improved protection helped recovery.

Mainland clouded leopard
Neofelis nebulosa

The mainland clouded leopard is a medium-sized Asian cat in the genus Neofelis. Genetic and morphological evidence distinguishes it from the Sunda clouded leopard, N. diardi, native to Sumatra and Borneo. Neofelis nebulosa ranges across parts of South and Southeast Asia. Its long tail and cloud-shaped coat are distinctive, but its secretive habits leave much of its biology poorly documented.

Adults have sturdy short legs, broad paws and longer hind legs. Dark-edged, pale-centred blotches mark a yellowish, grey or brown coat; the tail is banded. Nearly as long as the head and body, it helps balance the cat on branches. The skull has exceptionally long upper canines for a living cat. This anatomy alone does not imply unusually large prey: accounts describe a nape bite when it subdues larger animals.

Its range includes Nepal, India, southern China and the Indochinese Peninsula. It is strongly associated with dense evergreen and tropical forests, although secondary and logged forests are also used. Camera-trap surveys in Peninsular Malaysia found local differences in habitat use, including associations with elevation and distance from water; these relationships are not universal habitat requirements.

It takes vertebrate prey on trees and on the ground. Records include macaques, gibbons, muntjacs, pigs, porcupines, pangolins, squirrels and birds. Diet evidence is patchy and varies by site; no comprehensive range-wide study exists. Long canines and climbing ability do not show that arboreal prey dominate. In southern Thailand, muntjacs occupied less disturbed core forest more often, where clouded leopard density was also higher; this local association does not establish cause.

Broad gripping footpads and specialized ankle bones allow varied climbing positions, including descending a trunk headfirst. Direct observations are rare, so one radio-tracking study provides a useful, geographically limited view of movement. In Thailand’s Phu Khieo Wildlife Sanctuary, four cats were tracked for one to 17 months. Their annual ranges measured 22.9–45.1 km², daily travel averaged 1,932 m, and they were active during 58% of recorded diel readings. The small sample cannot establish a universal daily schedule or social pattern.

Most developmental measurements come from captive animals. Smithsonian records report 85–93 days of gestation and one to five cubs, usually two or three. Eyes open around 10–14 days, weaning occurs around 90–100 days, and sexual maturity is reached at about two years. These records do not establish wild reproductive-season or survival averages.

Its role in local food webs is poorly measured. At Khlong Saeng–Khao Sok, Thailand, camera traps recorded at least 27 individuals over 5,242 trap-days. Estimated density was higher in a less accessible forest core than at a more heavily hunted edge. Muntjac occupancy was also higher in the core. These site-specific findings suggest that access, hunting and prey communities may relate to local abundance, but do not establish a universal pattern.

The IUCN Cat Specialist Group cites the 2021 global assessment as Vulnerable. Forest fragmentation, prey depletion, killing and capture for trade threaten the species. Stronghold habitat declined between 2000 and 2018, while population estimates remain uncertain. Conservation priorities include connected forests, reduced snaring and better field surveys.

Nile crocodile
Crocodylus niloticus

The Nile crocodile is a large African crocodilian of rivers, lakes, swamps and estuaries, with a modern range centred in eastern and southern Africa and Madagascar. The Red List’s current taxonomic scope separates it from Crocodylus suchus, the West and Central African species once included in many broad Nile crocodile accounts. It waits at the water’s edge with only its eyes and nostrils exposed, then lunges when prey comes within reach. Fish and other aquatic animals connect its hunting to the food webs of African wetlands.

Its muscular tail supplies the main thrust in water, while strong limbs support movement on land. An Okavango account describes typical adults around 3.5 m long, with males able to reach 5 m. Exceptional males may approach 6 m, an exceptional value rather than a representative adult size. The pointed crocodile muzzle differs from an alligator’s broader one, and its fourth lower tooth remains visible when the jaws close. Eyes, ears and nostrils sit high on the head, and nostrils can close underwater.

The species uses slow and still waters, including rivers, lakes, seasonal swamps, reservoirs and coastal estuaries. It also occurs in desert oasis pools and, in Madagascar, underground streams. Around the Nile, its northernmost modern population is localized at Lake Nasser in Egypt. Older accounts include western populations now assigned to C. suchus.

Its diet changes as it grows. Young juveniles take insects and invertebrates, later adding frogs, crabs, snails, small fish, birds and rodents. Adults eat fish, reptiles, birds and mammals; local prey availability shapes the menu. Large land animals are occasional prey, not the routine food of every large crocodile. It ambushes from water or shore; a crocodile may roll to tear large prey apart.

As an ectotherm, it adjusts body temperature by moving between sunlit banks, shade and water. It often basks by day and spends much of the night in or near water, with activity shifting by weather and season. When submerged, it can expose only its eyes, ears and nostrils and close its nostrils underwater. Nile crocodiles tolerate one another at basking sites, but large males may defend shoreline stretches. Hatchling calls draw adults to the nest and help keep young together.

In local dry seasons, females dig sandy hole nests near permanent water and lay around 40–60 eggs. Incubation commonly lasts about 80–90 days, although temperature changes its duration. Egg temperature also influences sex: one Zimbabwe study produced only females at constant 31 °C or below, while the threshold for males varied among clutches above that range. The female guards the nest and responds to calls from hatching young, uncovering them and carrying hatchlings in her mouth to water. Hatchlings measure about 28 cm and stay guarded in groups for up to three months before dispersing.

In the Okavango Delta, studies describe crocodiles taking fish, recycling nutrients and maintaining wet refuges during drought. Eggs and young also feed other animals: fish, herons, storks, monitor lizards and mammals can prey on them, while larger crocodiles may eat juveniles. These relationships vary by site, water level and life stage, making the crocodile both predator and prey in a changing wetland community.

The global IUCN assessment completed on 30 April 2017 and published in 2019 listed the species as Least Concern, estimating 50,000–70,000 mature individuals. The assessment reports that hunting depleted populations in many countries from the 1940s through the 1960s, while legal protection and CITES trade controls supported recovery in many areas. Habitat conversion, pollution, uncontrolled harvest and conflict killings remain regional pressures; local declines and die-offs are documented within the wider range. Some commercial skins come from ranching or captive breeding, while local harvest still needs careful management in the wild.

Northern gannet
Morus bassanus

The northern gannet is a large seabird of the North Atlantic, breeding on offshore islands and cliffs from northeastern North America to western Europe. It spends much of the year at sea, returning to crowded colonies to nest.

Adults are about 85–100 cm long, with a wingspan of roughly 165–180 cm. The sexes look alike: the body is white, the long narrow wings have black tips, and the head and neck are buff-yellow in breeding plumage. Young birds are dark brown and acquire more white feathers over several years.

Breeding colonies occupy steep sea cliffs, rocky islands and other isolated coastal sites, where many nests fit close together. At sea, gannets range widely over productive shelf waters and follow moving shoals; after breeding, many migrate south within the Atlantic or into the western Mediterranean.

It eats mainly schooling fish, including mackerel, herring and sandeels, as well as squid. From a glide or steep flight it folds its wings and plunges bill-first, often striking at high speed; it can also pursue prey below the surface. Its eyes are protected by a translucent third eyelid, and air spaces beneath the skin cushion the impact. It swallows captured fish underwater or at the surface.

Gannets forage singly or in loose groups, and several birds may dive where fish are driven toward the surface by predators or boats. At colonies, close neighbors defend small nest spaces with upright postures, bill-pointing and harsh calls. Pairs greet with raised bills and mutual display; their repeated calls help maintain contact in the noisy crowd.

Pairs usually return to the same colony and may remain together across years. They build a mound of seaweed, grass and other material, then lay a single egg. Both parents incubate it between their webbed feet for about 42–46 days. The chick hatches helpless and is fed regurgitated fish by both adults; it grows for roughly 84–97 days before its first flight, then leaves the colony and must find food at sea. Breeding generally begins at around five years.

Northern gannets consume schooling pelagic fish and squid, linking their feeding to stocks also sought by commercial fisheries. They can be caught accidentally in fishing nets, so fishing activity affects both their food supply and survival.

The species is globally classified as Least Concern, a status that describes extinction risk across its full range and does not mean every colony is secure. Past egg collection and hunting reduced some colonies, while fishing pressure, bycatch, pollution and changing food supplies remain concerns. Highly pathogenic avian influenza caused severe recent losses: in 2022, at least 11,000 gannet deaths were recorded in Scotland and 5,000 at Grassholm, Wales.

Okapi
Okapia johnstoni

The okapi is a forest-dwelling giraffid native to the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Its short neck and compact body contrast with the tall giraffe, its closest living relative. Pale bands on the hindquarters and legs do not make it a relative of zebras.

Adults have a sturdy body, sloping back, short neck and upright ears. The torso is dark brown to reddish; cream-white bands cross the rump and upper legs. Males bear two short, skin-covered ossicones; females lack them. Both sexes use a long dark tongue to grasp leaves and ruminate.

Its known range is northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, including Ituri. It inhabits dense tropical forest. The IUCN assessment records it from about 450 to 1,500 metres elevation. The Okapi Wildlife Reserve protects a major part of Ituri forest.

This browser eats leaves, buds and shoots from shrubs and low branches, as well as fruit and fungi. The Okapi Conservation Project reports leaves from over one hundred plant and tree species in its diet. Foods vary by place and season. Okapis also eat clay or soil, probably for minerals, though its nutritional role is uncertain.

Okapis are usually solitary; females stay with calves. Adults may use overlapping areas, while males can exclude other males. Foot glands leave scent traces; males also mark with urine. Calls include coughs, bleats and whistles. Very low calls have been linked to mother–calf communication, though their function remains uncertain.

Gestation lasts about fourteen to sixteen months; births are usually single. Calves resemble adults and stand soon after birth. A mother may leave a calf hidden while feeding, then return to nurse. Young sample solid food within weeks. Maturity near three years is reported mainly from managed animals.

Okapis browse forest vegetation and are prey for leopards. Conservation programmes use this distinctive animal as an emblem for protecting the Ituri forest, benefiting other species sharing its habitat.

The 2015 IUCN assessment classified the okapi as Endangered, estimating a decline over 50% across three generations. This is the assessment date, not a new 2026 measurement. Pressures include poaching, forest loss and degradation, and insecurity. The Ituri reserve and local conservation programs support protection.

Orca
Orcinus orca

The orca, or killer whale, is the largest member of the dolphin family. It occurs in every ocean, from polar waters to the tropics. Its species-wide range contains distinct populations whose diets, calls and social traditions vary considerably.

A robust, streamlined body carries sharply contrasting black and white markings, including pale oval eye patches and a grey saddle behind the dorsal fin. The rounded head has no distinct beak; a tall fin, especially in adult males, helps identify the species.

Orcas inhabit coastal seas, continental shelves and open ocean across all major ocean basins. They are most abundant in colder regions but also occur in tropical and subtropical waters. Some communities range widely offshore; others use coastal corridors, and ranges can overlap.

Food choice differs among populations and is often shaped by learned hunting traditions. In the northeast Pacific, resident communities mainly take fish, including salmon; Bigg’s whales hunt marine mammals, while offshore whales eat fish and sharks. Elsewhere, prey includes herring, rays, seals or penguins.

Many orcas maintain long-lasting, often maternally related social groups. Clicks, whistles and pulsed calls coordinate activity and keep groups in contact; call repertoires can be learned and shared within communities. Some populations cooperate during hunts, but group size and social structure vary.

Females mature at roughly 10–13 years and carry a single calf for about 15–18 months. A calf nurses for at least a year and remains close to its mother for two years or longer. Births occur throughout the year; intervals differ among populations.

As a predator, an orca can influence prey abundance and behaviour, depending on local food webs and hunting traditions. It also transfers energy and nutrients through the marine food web. Persistent pollutants accumulate in its blubber over a long life.

Risk is uneven: some local populations face depleted prey, fishing-gear entanglement, vessel disturbance and underwater noise, while contaminants can affect health and reproduction. The IUCN’s 2017 global assessment classed the species Data Deficient, reflecting limited population-wide information, not proof that every population is secure.

Common ostrich
Struthio camelus
The common ostrich is the largest living bird, a flightless inhabitant of Africa’s open landscapes. Its long stride is carried by a two-toed foot whose large inner toe bears most of its weight.

Adult males are larger on average: the Paris Muséum gives females as 1.75–1.90 metres tall and 90–110 kilograms, and males as 2.10–2.75 metres and 100–150 kilograms. Males have black plumage with white wing and tail feathers; females are grey-brown. Each foot has two toes, a large clawed inner toe and a smaller outer toe. Pressure recordings show that the main toe bears most of the load, while the mobile outer toe helps balance the foot during walking and running. In laboratory trials, two adult females ran at 3–6 m/s; the study did not test a maximum speed.
It uses open savannas, grasslands and dry scrub, including places with sparse or short vegetation. Sparse plants leave open sightlines. The species occurs across much of Africa.

Leaves, roots, flowers and seeds make up much of the diet; ostriches also take insects and other small animals. Food is swallowed whole. In adult domesticated birds, a study describes pebbles grinding food in the muscular gizzard and microbial fermentation in the caeca and colon. These digestive observations come from managed birds; wild food choices vary with local and seasonal plant growth.

Ostriches are social ground-dwellers. Groups loosen outside breeding and become more organized around territorial males during courtship; reported flock sizes vary with place and season. Males court with bows, wing movements and conspicuous feathers, accompanied by calls. Although flightless, it uses its wings while running to help change direction, and fans them in hot weather to help keep cool.

Breeding arrangements vary among populations. In East Africa, several hens laid in one shallow scrape; a field report describes communal nests holding 30–40 eggs of about 1.5 kilograms each. Genetic work in Nairobi found multiple mothers and fathers among eggs in the same nest. A dominant hen and territorial male guard and incubate; the female’s pale plumage blends by day and the male’s dark plumage by night. San Diego Zoo gives 42–46 days for incubation. Chicks leave within days, follow adults and are sheltered from sun, rain and predators. Their patterned down is replaced as adult feathers develop; the zoo account says they near adult size at about six months. Adult size precedes sexual maturity, which the Smithsonian account places around three to four years.

Ostriches move nomadically as rainfall changes the availability of fresh plant food. A South African field guide reports that breeding and laying precede rains, so chicks hatch as forage becomes available. In northern Tanzania, surveys of the Masai population found local ostrich densities correlated with those of nine of ten large ungulate species, although their site-specific population trends were not closely correlated. Ostriches themselves are prey for large carnivores, including lions, cheetahs, leopards and hyenas.

BirdLife International’s 2025 global IUCN assessment lists the common ostrich as Least Concern, with a decreasing population trend. This global category does not describe the condition of every regional population. Northern Sahel transects repeated in 1971–73 and 2004 documented severe regional declines and identified hunting, overgrazing and woodland degradation among local pressures. Historic feather hunting and egg collection also affected ostriches, while habitat loss remains a concern.

European pine marten
Martes martes
Native across much of Europe and western Eurasia, the European pine marten varies greatly in abundance and local range. It climbs and forages extensively on the forest floor.

Adults have rich brown fur, a yellow to orange bib on the throat and chest, pale-edged ears and a long, bushy tail. The bib’s colour and outline vary among populations and individuals. Males average larger than females; European samples report adult masses of about 0.8–2.4 kilograms for males and 0.6–1.5 kilograms for females, with ranges varying among studies. The beech marten usually has a white bib that forks toward the forelegs and a pale nose; the pine marten usually has a yellowish bib and dark nose.

The species uses coniferous, deciduous and mixed forests; mature stands are valuable where they provide canopy cover and cavities in old trees or standing deadwood. These structures offer cover and secure resting or breeding sites. In an Irish landscape with few tree cavities, monitored martens also denned in caves, rock crevices, stone walls and wood debris, while avoiding most immature plantations.

The pine marten is an opportunistic omnivore: small mammals, birds and eggs, carrion, invertebrates and fruit all feature in its diet. In Northern Ireland, scat analyses found animal foods prominent in spring and summer and berries important in autumn; birds and small mammals became more important when fruit was scarce. In Galloway, no carrion was detected in denning females’ scats; birds, small mammals and anurans were important, unlike some carrion-containing mixed-sex spring diets reported elsewhere in Scotland.

Pine martens are usually solitary outside mating and mostly nocturnal, though activity varies with season. Scent marks, including conspicuously placed scats, signal occupancy along routes; Spanish observations found marking concentrated at exposed sites and crossroads, especially in May and July. British studies found larger home ranges in males than females, with estimates varying among habitats and food conditions.

Mating in July–August is followed by about seven months of delayed implantation. Implantation in late winter is followed by 30–35 days of development; births occur in late March or April. Females usually have one litter of one to five kits each year. Born blind, deaf and toothless, kits open their eyes at 34–38 days, eat solids from 36–45 days and are weaned at about six weeks. Young emerge at 7–8 weeks; dispersal may start at 12–16 weeks, though some overwinter in their natal territory and leave the following spring. Females use protected dens during the early weeks.

After eating fleshy fruits, pine martens can carry seeds away from parent shrubs in their scats. In a temperate-forest experiment, marked seed mimics embedded in fruit were recovered up to 1,233 metres from feeding stations, a study maximum rather than a typical distance. In the Irish midlands, surveys recorded grey-squirrel decline alongside red-squirrel return where martens recovered. Later analyses across Britain and Ireland found regional associations between marten exposure, lower grey-squirrel occupancy and higher red-squirrel occupancy. In an Irish feeder-camera study, red squirrels became more vigilant and fed less after a marten visit; this short-lived response is a possible mechanism, not proof of the population pattern. These patterns do not show that martens eliminate grey squirrels everywhere or always benefit red squirrels.

The IUCN Red List classified the species as Least Concern globally in an assessment dated 3 March 2015 and published in 2016, citing its wide range and large population despite past declines. This global category does not describe every national population: the Mammal Society lists Great Britain as Least Concern, while martens remain scarce in parts of England and Wales amid habitat fragmentation and persecution. Across Great Britain, the amended Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 protects the species, with schedule coverage varying by jurisdiction. Ireland separately lists the pine marten under its Wildlife Act 1976.

Platypus
Ornithorhynchus anatinus

The platypus is a semi-aquatic Australian mammal and a monotreme: a mammal that lays eggs. Its streamlined, furred body, broad tail and sensitive bill suit a life of searching freshwater beds for food and resting in bank burrows. Females produce milk for their young despite having no nipples. The species occurs naturally in eastern Australia, including Tasmania, in varied freshwater habitats.

Adults have dense waterproof fur, usually dark brown above and lighter below, a flattened bill and a broad tail. The tail stores fat and helps steer. Webbed forefeet provide propulsion; their webs fold back around the claws on land. Hind feet are less webbed and help steer underwater. Males have a sharp hind-ankle spur connected to a venom gland; females lack this functional apparatus. Southern animals tend to be larger than northern ones.

The species ranges through eastern Australia, from tropical Queensland to Tasmania and the Australian Alps. It uses rivers, streams, lakes and farm dams, but needs freshwater for feeding and earthen banks for burrows. Root-stabilised banks offer resting and nesting sites; shaded pools, riffles and gravel or cobble beds support aquatic invertebrates. Platypuses sometimes cross land between water bodies, making catchment connectivity relevant to habitat use.

It hunts small animals, especially bottom-dwelling insect larvae, worms, crustaceans and molluscs. Underwater it closes its eyes, ears and nostrils, locating prey with bill receptors that detect water movement and weak electrical fields from prey muscles. Sweeping its head from side to side helps it orient in murky water. It stores small prey in cheek pouches and grinds food at the surface with horny pads rather than teeth.

Adults are mostly solitary and generally occupy separate resting burrows, although several may use one stretch of water. Activity often peaks from dusk through the night. Forelimbs power swimming, while hind limbs and tail steer; on land, the splayed limbs make walking less efficient. Repeated dives separated by brief surface pauses allow long foraging periods. Grooming maintains the insulating coat needed during extended time in water.

Breeding is seasonal and earlier in northern populations. The female lays one to three soft-shelled eggs in a long bank burrow, which she plugs with soil. Embryos develop partly before laying; external incubation lasts about a week to ten days. Hatchlings are tiny and dependent. The mother secretes milk onto abdominal skin, and young lap it from her fur because she has no nipples. They feed on milk in the burrow and commonly emerge after three to four months, with timing varying by region.

As predators of bottom-dwelling invertebrates, platypuses are part of stream food webs. An Australian field experiment found that their feeding affected invertebrate communities differently in flowing streams and still-water habitats, so ecosystem effects depend on setting. Their reliance on aquatic prey ties them to productive waterways, while bank burrows depend on stable margins. Movement overland may connect catchments, although barriers and dry periods can interrupt dispersal.

A 2022 Australian government report cites the IUCN global category as Near Threatened; this reports a dated assessment record, not a new population estimate. The same report said the platypus was not then listed as nationally threatened under federal or New South Wales law, while relaying a 2020 UNSW review that recommended Vulnerable status. It names threats including bank clearing, altered flows, pollution, fishing by-catch, disease, drought, fire and floods. Victoria listed the species as Vulnerable in 2021. These categories refer to different dates and geographic scales.

Polar bear
Ursus maritimus

The polar bear is a marine mammal whose life follows Arctic sea ice, the platform from which it reaches seals. Its fur, fat, smell, and broad paws suit cold water and ice, but it hunts most effectively from sea ice. Seasonal ice loss changes both access to food and the distances bears must travel.

Adult males commonly weigh about 270–545 kg and measure roughly 2.4–3 m from nose to tail; adult females are smaller, commonly about 180–320 kg. These are broad wild adult ranges: age, region, season, and fat reserves change an individual’s mass. The long neck and narrow head help distinguish the species, while the coat’s translucent hairs scatter visible light so the dense fur appears cream or white. Beneath the fur lie dark skin and a thick layer of subcutaneous fat; the hairs do not channel sunlight to the skin like fibre-optic cables. Dense underfur and guard hairs trap still air, while blubber adds insulation in water. Broad paws spread weight on weak ice and paddle during swimming; partial webbing increases paddle efficiency. Small, round ears and a short tail reduce exposed surfaces. A keen sense of smell helps locate seals, while the muzzle and claws help seize prey.

Its range circles the Arctic, from Alaska and Canada to Greenland, Svalbard, and Russia; movements vary with coastlines and ice. Productive sea ice over continental shelves gives bears access to seals resting or raising pups. Some follow seasonal ice toward shore at breakup, while others remain farther north; an ashore summer is not universal. Many land maternity dens are excavated in snow, but in Western and Southern Hudson Bay some females begin in frozen peat or earth before extending the den into accumulating snow. In some other regions, pregnant bears also den on stable sea ice.

Ringed seals are staple prey; bearded seals also matter, depending on local availability. A bear may wait by a breathing hole, detect a seal by smell, and seize it as it surfaces, or stalk one resting on ice. Bears often eat blubber and skin first, leaving remains for foxes, ravens, gulls, and other bears. They digest and store these lipids efficiently as fat, which fuels movement, warmth, reproduction, and fasting. On land they may eat birds, eggs, plants, fish, carrion, or refuse; most terrestrial foods are scattered or relatively low in energy and generally cannot replace seal hunting. Rich marine-mammal carcasses, such as whale or walrus remains, can nevertheless be locally important. Bears can enter a facultative fasting state even while actively searching for food: stored lipids supply energy while protein is spared. The duration and energetic cost of fasting vary among bears.

Adults are usually solitary outside mating and family groups; females use large home ranges whose size varies with local land and sea ice. Regional movements may follow freeze-up and breakup, while elsewhere bears remain on ice in summer. In spring, males follow tracks and scent trails left by females’ feet. Experiments show that bears can distinguish scent donors by sex and reproductive condition, so trails carry more than a simple signal of presence. When seals are unavailable, some rest while others search for land foods; either strategy spends stored energy and can still bring weight loss.

Mating occurs on sea ice in spring. After fertilization, the embryo pauses and usually implants in autumn only if the female has built adequate reserves; this is delayed implantation. The interval from mating to birth is about 195–265 days, but active fetal development lasts only two to three months. Only pregnant females enter maternity dens, often in October or November, and births occur from November to early January depending on latitude. The mother fasts while giving birth and nursing; this winter dormancy is not species-wide hibernation. Litters contain one to three cubs, usually twins; newborns are blind and weigh about 0.5 kg. They grow quickly on fat-rich milk and stay with their mother for about 2.5–3 years, learning to hunt and swim.

As the Arctic’s largest terrestrial predator, the polar bear links sea ice to marine food webs: ice algae support small consumers, then fish and seals, which feed bears. Seal remains feed Arctic foxes, gulls, and ravens, extending each kill’s benefit to other species. Seasonal fat storage links prey abundance with survival and cub production, carrying effects of ice change through the ecosystem.

The IUCN Polar Bear Specialist Group’s global assessment, published in 2015, classified the polar bear as Vulnerable. It identified climate-driven sea-ice loss as the leading long-term threat because ice provides access to seals. Longer open-water seasons can force some bears ashore, lengthen fasting, and affect condition, reproduction, or survival; effects differ by region and period. In Canada, COSEWIC assessed the species as Special Concern in 2018; individual management-unit trends are separate from the global Red List and may be uncertain or dated. In 1973, the five range states signed an agreement for coordinated protection and management of feeding, denning, and migration habitat.

Powderblue surgeonfish
Acanthurus leucosternon

The powderblue surgeonfish is a reef-dwelling member of the surgeonfish family, Acanthuridae, native to the tropical Indian Ocean. Its blue body, dark head and white chest make it distinctive. It grazes on algae growing on reefs and may feed alone or join other fish. The species is best known from shallow reefs, where feeding grounds and territorial behaviour are tied to patches of algal growth.

Its deep body is flattened from side to side. A broad white band crosses the chest from the pectoral-fin bases, and a narrow pale line outlines the lower face. The dorsal fin is yellow with a pale edge and dark submarginal line; the tail base and paired spines are yellow. A pale crescent marks the dark tail fin. Each side of the tail base bears a sharp spine that folds into a groove and can be raised when the fish bends its tail. The Andaman Sea account reports specimens up to 23 cm. FishBase lists a maximum total length of 54 cm.

It ranges through the tropical Indian Ocean, from eastern Africa to the Andaman Sea and Indonesia, reaching Bali; records include Cocos (Keeling) and Christmas islands. It occupies shallow coastal and island reefs, especially reef flats and upper outer slopes, generally down to about 25 metres. These sunlit surfaces support the benthic algae it eats, although feeding grounds vary among reef zones.

Adults are herbivores that crop benthic algae, including short microalgal turf on hard reef surfaces. At Aldabra, researchers observed adults defending permanent feeding territories containing these algal mats. FishBase also records feeding on scattered algae and small growths in crevices. Each jaw bears a row of incisor-like teeth. High-speed recordings show the fish grasping algae, then pulling them free by rotating its head and closed jaws downward. An articulation within the lower jaw enables this movement without turning the whole body sideways. This may help feeding in strong currents, although that ecological advantage remains an interpretation of the mechanics.

Individuals forage alone or gather in feeding groups. At Aldabra, adults defended permanent algal territories against other fishes, protecting access to food. The study describes territorial defence within and between species among surgeonfishes.

The sexes are separate, and observations describe paired spawning during the breeding period. FishBase describes the species as monogamous. At Aldabra, the study documented pairs among permanently territorial surgeonfishes and no parental care in its study group. Eggs and sperm are released into open water for external fertilization. Surgeonfish yolk-sac larvae float near the surface, then swim and feed after the yolk is absorbed. They pass through a pelagic acronurus stage before reef settlement.

By cropping attached algae, this fish uses food produced on reef surfaces and participates in grazing those patches. Herbivorous reef fishes can limit algae that impede coral recruitment, although the strength of this effect varies among species. At Aldabra, adults defended small turf plots against competitors, dividing access to algal resources. Territories focus grazing on defended patches. Feeding aggregations bring several fish to shared food areas.

The IUCN Red List account lists the species as Least Concern, assessed on 3 May 2010 and published in 2012. On the Kenyan coast, people harvest it for subsistence and commercial fisheries. This species is also collected for the aquarium trade. Along Kenya’s southern coast, a fishery study found 27% of sampled Acanthurus leucosternon below estimated maturity length; beach seines caught the largest share of immature fish (64%). Its exploitation estimate was below the sustainable-yield threshold, unlike that of sympatric Acanthurus triostegus. Reef Life Survey recorded it at 27% of surveyed sites, averaging six fish per transect where present.

Puma
Puma concolor

The puma, also called cougar or mountain lion, is a large cat native to the Americas. Usually solitary, it ranges from western Canada through much of South America. Its presence across varied landscapes makes it one of the continent’s most widely distributed native mammals.

Adults have a tawny, grey-brown or reddish coat, usually paler underneath, with a small head, rounded ears, powerful hindquarters and a long, thick tail. Adults lack spots; kittens are spotted, and their markings fade as they grow.

Pumas occupy forests, scrub, grasslands, deserts and wetlands, from lowlands to mountains. They use places with prey and cover, including dense vegetation, rocky crevices and caves. Habitat use varies locally: Florida panthers, for example, use swamp forest and wooded hammocks.

This carnivore takes locally available prey. Deer are important across much of North America; elk, moose, wild pigs, guanacos, hares and smaller mammals may also be eaten. Pumas stalk and ambush prey, then cover large carcasses to return for later meals.

Adults generally live alone, except during mating and while females raise young. Home ranges can overlap; a male’s range may encompass several females. Scent marks, scraped ground and scratched logs signal occupancy. Pumas may be active by day or night, often around dusk and dawn.

Pumas breed year-round, though some populations have seasonal peaks. After about three months, a female gives birth to one to six kittens in a den. Spotted at birth, they eat meat at six weeks and stay with her for about a year.

As a large predator, the puma hunts herbivores and can affect where prey feed and move. Its effects depend on local conditions and interactions with other predators. Yellowstone research examines cougars alongside wolves, bears and elk; carcasses also provide food for scavengers.

The IUCN assessment published in 2015 classified the species as Least Concern, while noting uncertainty and suspected declines in parts of Central and South America. Habitat loss, fragmentation, persecution, hunting and depleted prey threaten some populations. Connected habitat and reduced conflict are conservation priorities.

European rabbit
Oryctolagus cuniculus

The European rabbit is a burrowing lagomorph native to the Iberian Peninsula and parts of southwestern Europe. Human transport and escape from domestication have spread it far beyond that range, so the same species can be a threatened native animal in one landscape and an invasive grazer in another. It is also the wild ancestor of domestic rabbits.

A wild adult is usually 38–50 cm long and weighs 1.5–2.5 kg. Its compact body, short ears and strong hind legs support quick dashes between feeding ground and cover. The grey-brown coat is paler underneath; the white underside of its short tail flashes as it bounds away. Compared with a hare, it has shorter ears and legs and relies on underground refuge. Its young are helpless at birth, unlike furred, mobile leverets.

In its native range the rabbit favours open, short-grass ground near dense cover, especially where soft soil allows digging. Scrub, grassland, woodland edges and some farms or urban spaces provide food and shelter, though ploughing can destroy burrows. A warren’s linked entrances and chambers offer escape routes and protected places to rest or nest. Where soil is unsuitable, rabbits use surface cover such as dense vegetation.

The rabbit selectively eats grasses, tender shoots, leaves and buds, sometimes roots or bark. Because plant fibre is difficult to digest, microbes ferment fine particles in its enlarged caecum while coarse particles pass quickly through the gut. The rabbit periodically re-ingests soft, nutrient-rich caecotrophs, allowing their contents another passage through the small intestine. These differ from ordinary firm, dry pellets, which carry much of the indigestible fibre and are not recycled.

European rabbits are unusually social for a leporid. Where food and soil permit, groups share warrens and defend a territory. Several females and males may live together; dominance shapes access to space and mates, with conflict clearest between males. Rabbits feed mainly at dusk and night, then retreat underground by day. Scent marks signal occupancy, while a hind-foot thump warns nearby animals of danger. Group boundaries and a familiar warren provide security.

Wild breeding is seasonal and responds to food and local conditions. After mating-triggered ovulation, gestation lasts about 30 days and litters commonly contain five or six young. A doe digs a nursery burrow and lines its nest with dry plants and fur. Kittens are born naked and blind, unlike furred, open-eyed hare leverets. The mother returns briefly to nurse, then leaves the nest concealed. Young leave the nest and are weaned at about four weeks; first-year mortality can be high from predation, weather and disease.

In Mediterranean Iberia, rabbits are key prey for many predators, including the Iberian lynx and Spanish imperial eagle. Their grazing changes plant cover, while burrows shelter other animals and communal latrines concentrate nutrients that affect plant growth. Rabbits therefore act as ecosystem engineers, with effects that depend on density and habitat. Their role in native food webs can become damaging when dense introduced populations overgraze and compete with local wildlife.

The latest global IUCN assessment located was published in 2019 from an assessment dated 15 August 2018. It classified rabbits as Endangered across their native range in Spain, Portugal and southern France. Myxomatosis, rabbit haemorrhagic disease and habitat degradation drove declines; GI.2/RHDV2 added pressure after reaching Iberia in 2011–12. A 2025 study of hunting records from about 6,000 central-Spain estates found declines in most areas without emergency crop-damage control during 2009–22, but trends differed where rabbits damage crops. In Australia, feral rabbits are widespread and harm native vegetation and threatened species. Conservation priorities therefore differ between the native range and introduced populations.
