Common raccoon dog
Nyctereutes procyonoides

The common raccoon dog is a stocky member of the dog family, native to mainland East Asia. Its adaptable habits let it use woodland, wetlands, open country and some human-modified landscapes. Its dark facial mask gives the head a raccoon-like appearance, but its build and ancestry are canid. The species has also established far beyond its original Asian range after people released it for fur production in Europe.

Despite its name and dark eye mask, it is a canid, not a raccoon. Adults average about 56 cm in head-and-body length and roughly 4.5 kg, with local seasonal variation. A broad head, short legs and dense, shaggy coat give the animal a low, rounded outline; the dark mask contrasts with paler cheek fur. The tail is short and bushy, about 18 cm in one specialist account, and lacks the bold rings of a true raccoon. Winter fur grows longer and thicker, while moulting restores a shorter coat for warmer months. These dimensions describe wild adult reference samples, not a maximum: body mass changes substantially before and during winter rest.

In its native range it occurs from China and Mongolia through Korea and the Russian Far East to northern Vietnam. Woodland edges, river valleys, scrub and wet ground offer cover beside varied feeding sites. Breeding adults use a den to raise their young.

This opportunistic omnivore shifts between plant foods and animal prey as local supplies change, and it also scavenges carrion. Estonian stomach samples illustrate the seasonal shift: autumn diets contained more amphibians and invertebrates, while winter samples held more small mammals, carrion and human-associated foods. Cereals and fruits at supplementary feeding sites, especially those for wild boar, supplied plant foods in that study.

Raccoon dogs often form a breeding pair whose members use overlapping ranges and cooperate around the den. Field tracking in Germany found males guarding nursing pups while females made longer foraging trips. They are mainly active at night and around twilight, although local conditions and human disturbance can alter when they move. In southern Finland, tracked animals usually stayed in dens during midwinter but sometimes wandered even in the coldest months. In cold northern winters, individuals can enter long but intermittent bouts of reduced activity, rather than one uniform, deep hibernation.

In southern Finland, mating peaks in March; gestation lasts about 60–62 days, births are concentrated in May, and the mean litter at birth is about nine. Litter size and the proportion of females breeding vary with age, food and local conditions. Pups remain in a den for about six weeks, then begin travelling with their parents. Juveniles in Finland usually begin dispersing in August, with most leaving the natal range by September or October.

In northern European wetlands, its predation can affect frogs and nesting waterbirds, although broad population effects remain difficult to establish. Local studies have found amphibians and bird eggs among its foods, so vulnerable island or shoreline breeding sites may face concentrated pressure. It also scavenges carcasses and competes with other medium-sized carnivores for this winter resource, though studies reviewed in Europe found little evidence of severe competition with foxes or badgers. In its introduced range, it can carry parasites and pathogens, making disease transmission an ecological and veterinary concern alongside predation.

The global IUCN assessment, last assessed on 1 March 2016 and published in 2016, classified the raccoon dog taxon then recognized as Nyctereutes procyonoides as Least Concern with a stable trend; at that time it included Japanese populations now recognized separately by the Mammal Diversity Database. This historic category is not a new assessment of the current mainland species. Fur-farming releases in the former Soviet Union began a European expansion that continues to shape management. Between 1929 and 1955, about 9,100 animals were released in European Russia, and descendants spread into northern, eastern and central Europe. Its listing as an invasive alien species of Union concern applies from 2 February 2019. The current Union-list framework requires prevention or management measures. The main concerns are predation at sensitive local breeding sites and the spread of parasites and disease; evidence for continent-wide declines in native birds remains limited.

Keel-billed toucan
Ramphastos sulfuratus

The keel-billed toucan is a resident canopy bird of humid forests, ranging from southern Mexico through Central America to northwestern South America. Its large, multicoloured bill gives it the alternate name rainbow-billed toucan. In a pasture-dominated landscape in Mexico, tracked birds selected forest remnants while also using several wooded and agricultural habitats.

Adults are about 50 cm long. The body is black with a yellow throat and chest, white rump, red undertail feathers, blue eye skin and blue feet. The sexes look alike, though males may be slightly larger. The oversized green bill has orange, red and blue accents and can approach a third of body length. A species sheet describes a lightweight honeycomb-like core under a keratin covering; direct mechanical tests used the related toco toucan. Two toes point forward and two back to grip branches.

The species occupies humid tropical forest, mainly in the middle and upper canopy. It also visits edges, secondary growth and trees retained in pasture or cropland. In Los Tuxtlas, Mexico, six birds followed for 349 hours preferred forest remnants at both landscape and local scales. Their activities were similar among habitat types, suggesting some altered patches still supplied resources. This regional result does not mean open land replaces intact forest across the range.

Fruit is the staple, including figs and palm fruits. A toucan can pluck fruit from branches too slender to support its body, swallow it whole, then regurgitate or pass seeds away from the parent tree. It also eats insects and small vertebrates; eggs and nestlings are recorded prey. One published observation documents a keel-billed toucan taking vertebrate carrion, an unusual opportunistic food rather than evidence of a regular habit.

Keel-billed toucans move between fruiting trees, often in small flocks; older accounts report groups of six to twelve. They hop along branches and fly between trees with rapid wingbeats followed by a glide. In one Mexican study, foraging and perching each occupied about 35–40% of observed time, while calling and social interactions each took 10% or less. They also roost in tree cavities; group composition and year-round social bonds remain poorly documented.

The toucan nests in a natural tree hollow or an old cavity made by another bird. Species accounts report two to four eggs, incubated by both parents, who also feed the helpless chicks. They hatch after about 16–20 days and remain in the cavity while growing; fledging is reported around eight to nine weeks. These timings come from limited, partly older natural-history sources and may vary locally.

Fruit feeding carries seeds between feeding and resting sites. A Panamanian study of Virola surinamensis found heavier weevil attack beneath and near parent trees; dispersal beyond 20 metres by large birds, including keel-billed toucans, appeared more favorable for seedling survival. Gut passage has different effects in different plants. In an experiment with captive keel-billed toucans, Ficus insipida seeds recovered from droppings did not germinate significantly better than uneaten controls. Seed transport and enhanced germination are therefore distinct processes.

BirdLife International’s global IUCN assessment, dated 18 March 2021, lists the species as Near Threatened with a decreasing trend. It estimates 50,000–499,999 mature birds and links decline to habitat loss, degradation, hunting and trapping. Earlier assessments through 2016 listed Least Concern; that category is no longer current.

Common raven
Corvus corax

The Common Raven is a large member of the crow family, occupying much of the Northern Hemisphere. Its success comes from a flexible way of life: it can hunt, scavenge, eat plant matter, and exploit food made available by people.

An adult measures about 58–69 cm from bill to tail, with a wingspan of roughly 120–150 cm and a mass of about 0.7–1.6 kg; body dimensions vary geographically. It is entirely black, with a heavy bill, thick neck, shaggy throat feathers, and a long, wedge-shaped tail. In comparison, a Carrion Crow is smaller and has a squarer tail, a slimmer bill, and a less shaggy throat; size and silhouette together are more useful than colour, which is black in both. Young ravens look browner and duller than adults. The raven\'s broad, pointed wings support slow flaps, soaring, and agile rolls or steep dives. Its deep, rough croak carries far, and the species also makes a varied set of softer calls; vocal sounds serve contact, alarm, and territorial contexts.

Across its range, the raven uses tundra, mountains, coasts, forests, open country, farmland, and some settlements. It needs suitable ledges, trees, or structures for nesting and enough food nearby; consequently, local abundance depends on landscape and resources rather than a single preferred habitat.

The raven is an opportunistic omnivore. It takes carrion, small mammals, birds and their eggs or nestlings, fish, insects and other invertebrates, as well as grains, fruit, buds, and human food waste. Small prey may be swallowed whole, while hairs, feathers, bones, and other poorly digested remains can be brought back up in compact pellets. It hides surplus food in caches, particularly when a large carcass or other temporary bounty is available, and may move or conceal a cache when competitors are nearby.

Breeding adults usually live as territorial pairs and may remain paired year-round; they defend the nest area and key food patches. Outside these territories, young birds and nonbreeders often gather, and several ravens may converge on a carcass, rubbish tip, or seabird colony. Its characteristic call is a harsh, resonant croak; during courtship, ravens perform tumbling aerial displays. In captive studies, ravens have adjusted cache placement after observing competitors. In one controlled experiment, they guarded caches in response to a rival’s sounds when a peephole allowed that bird to see the caching area; this suggests sensitivity to visual access, without establishing human-like thought.

A pair generally establishes and defends a territory before nesting. It builds a bulky stick platform in a tree, on a cliff, or on a human-made structure, then lines the cup with softer material. The female usually incubates a clutch of three to seven eggs for about 20–25 days, while the male often brings food. Chicks hatch helpless, with closed eyes and sparse down; both parents feed them. They leave the nest after roughly four to seven weeks, though fledging does not mean immediate independence. Ravens commonly raise one brood in a year, and young birds may not breed until two to four years old.

At carcasses, ravens feed alongside other scavengers; in some seabird colonies, groups take eggs and chicks, so their effects on prey are strongly local. The species is thus both a consumer of carrion and a predator whose impact can matter for vulnerable nesting birds.

The 2021 European Red List assessment classified the breeding population as Least Concern and increasing; this regional assessment is not a guarantee that every local population is secure. In Britain, raven numbers fell historically and the range contracted westward; as persecution eased from the mid-twentieth century, populations recovered and expanded again. The return has renewed conflicts with livestock interests and conservation managers where ravens take vulnerable young or eggs. The British Trust for Ornithology reports licensed control in Scotland and concern that illegal killing may still affect some local populations.

Red deer
Cervus elaphus

The red deer is a large hoofed ruminant native to Europe, the Atlas Mountains, Anatolia, the Caucasus and northwestern Iran. Current classifications distinguish it from the wapiti and Central Asian red deer. Introduced populations occur elsewhere, including New Zealand.

Adults have a reddish-brown summer coat, greyer or darker in winter; it is not spotted. Stags are generally larger and darker than hinds and have a pale rump. Males grow branching antlers, shed annually and regrow them beneath velvet, which they rub off when growth ends. Point count does not reliably show age.

It uses deciduous and coniferous woods, edges, scrub, grasslands and moorland, feeding in open areas with cover nearby. Habitat use varies regionally. Introduced deer released in New Zealand since 1851 now occupy forest and tussock country on the main islands.

This flexible herbivore grazes grasses and herbs and browses leaves, shoots and shrubs. Spring growth, winter bark and ferns, and other foods vary with season and location. As a ruminant, it regurgitates and rechews plant matter; diets differ between woodland and open habitats.

Hinds often associate with calves and younger deer; mature stags tend to keep apart outside breeding season. In autumn, males roar, scent-mark and display. Rivals may walk parallel, then clash with locked antlers; successful stags gather temporary harems. The sexes usually separate again after the rut.

In Europe, the rut usually occurs in autumn, though timing varies with latitude and hemisphere. After about eight months, a hind generally bears one calf in late spring or early summer. Its reddish coat has pale spots that fade within months. At first it hides in vegetation while its mother feeds nearby.

Grazing and browsing change vegetation, depending on deer density and habitat. In Swiss subalpine grasslands, seeds in red deer dung showed that deer disperse plants between feeding and resting areas. This can shape local plant communities, though effects vary by site.

The global IUCN assessment, last assessed on 12 October 2015 and published in 2018, classified red deer as Least Concern because of its wide range and presumed large populations. This dated assessment is not a new count; it also noted regional contractions and likely declines. In introduced New Zealand populations, deer can damage native plants and forest regeneration, prompting control. Taxonomic limits in Asia have changed since that assessment.

Red fox
Vulpes vulpes

The red fox is an adaptable canid native across much of the Northern Hemisphere, from Arctic regions to North Africa, Central America and Asia. It occupies wild, farmed and urban landscapes, while local abundance and habits depend on food, cover and human pressures.

Its familiar coat is rusty red above, pale underneath, with dark lower legs and a bushy tail often tipped white. Colour is variable: individuals may be pale, dark or cross-patterned. The pointed muzzle, upright ears and slender build remain useful features across these forms.

Red foxes use forests, scrub, grasslands, deserts, mountains, farmland and city edges; they often benefit from a patchwork of cover and open feeding ground. In Australia they were introduced for hunting in the nineteenth century and spread widely, though distribution remains uneven.

It is an opportunistic feeder, taking small mammals such as rodents and rabbits when available, as well as birds, invertebrates, reptiles, fruit and carrion. Proportions shift with season and place. Urban foxes may use discarded food, while Australian foxes consume introduced and native prey.

Foxes often forage alone around dusk or at night, but schedules vary with disturbance and food. They cache surplus food in small buried stores. A pair may share a territory; some populations form family groups where related nonbreeders help provision or guard young.

Breeding is seasonal, with timing shifting across the species’ range. After about seven to eight weeks of pregnancy, a vixen gives birth in a den. Cubs are born blind, leave after several weeks and are gradually weaned; litter size and helper care vary among populations.

As predator and scavenger, the fox consumes many kinds of animal matter and sometimes fruit, but its effects depend on local food webs. In Australia, government reviews link introduced fox predation to declines in several native ground-dwelling mammals and birds; other pressures can also contribute.

The global IUCN assessment published in 2021 retained Least Concern, based on the assessment dated 2016 and the species’ broad range. This category does not describe every local population. In Australia, introduced foxes are managed as invasive predators because of risks to native wildlife.

Red junglefowl
Gallus gallus

The red junglefowl is a wild galliform bird of the pheasant family, native to South and Southeast Asia and the principal wild ancestor of the domestic chicken. Whole-genome comparisons support an early contribution from the Southeast Asian subspecies Gallus gallus spadiceus, followed by gene flow among chicken populations and other junglefowl; domestication was not a simple, isolated event. Some regional chicken genomes also carry introgressed DNA from grey junglefowl (Gallus sonneratii), with lesser or rarer signals from Ceylon junglefowl (Gallus lafayettii) and green junglefowl (Gallus varius); these findings do not displace red junglefowl as the main ancestor.

The wild adult male has a bright red comb and wattles, orange-gold neck feathers, a dark iridescent body, and long curved feathers over the tail; total length can reach about 70 centimetres including that tail. Females are smaller-looking and mottled brown, with a short tail and camouflage suited to nesting on the ground. A study of the Thai subspecies Gallus gallus spadiceus found breeding males with long golden neck hackles, unlike the shorter black feathers outside the breeding period. A wild-type outline alone cannot establish genetic purity, because domestic ancestry may be invisible in appearance. Domestic chickens have also been selected for rapid growth, so breed size and body form are not reliable norms for wild birds.

Its native range spans the Indian subcontinent and much of mainland and island Southeast Asia, with regional subspecies occupying different areas. It uses old and secondary forest, mangroves, and forest edges, often feeding in a clearing or plantation beside cover.

This opportunistic omnivore takes seeds, fruits, and small invertebrates, including ants, beetles, and termites; the mix changes with local and seasonal availability. It scratches through soil and leaf litter with its feet before pecking at food, often visiting open ground in the early morning and evening. Its digestive tract includes a crop and muscular gizzard; the gizzard mechanically breaks down ingested food.

Wary and mostly terrestrial, red junglefowl can fly strongly when alarmed and commonly roost in trees at night. Field observations describe small, changing groups: a male may accompany one or several females, while solitary males and females are also seen. Males crow repeatedly, often before dawn, and crowing helps reveal their presence; calls and displays also communicate between birds, though social patterns vary with place and season.

Breeding schedules differ by region: a two-year study of the subspecies Gallus gallus spadiceus in Malaysian agricultural landscapes recorded nests year-round, with a local peak in December. Nests averaged about four eggs, and captive incubation lasted roughly 19.5 days, close to three weeks. In Hainan, field researchers observed only females tending the brood, while accounts from southern Yunnan report both sexes incubating eggs; parental roles vary among the populations studied. Chicks hatch covered in down and leave the nest soon; a natural-history account places full feathering at about four to five weeks and sexual maturity near five months, somewhat later in females.

Field observations and local reports from Thailand and Malaysia identify wild cats and birds of prey among predators of adult junglefowl. In Hainan, nest monitoring found predation to be a major cause of breeding failure, with coucals and rodents recorded at experimental nests and reptiles proposed as other potential predators.

BirdLife International’s global IUCN assessment published in 2024 classifies the species as Least Concern, a global risk category that does not guarantee the security of each local population. An Indian Wildlife Institute of India project reported a fragmented distribution and growing pressures in several states, and found ten domestic-chicken hybrids among 220 birds sampled at captive centres. A 2023 genome comparison found domestic ancestry of about 20–50 percent in the modern wild populations sampled, relative to museum birds collected roughly a century earlier, with strong variation among individuals and places; habitat change and contact with free-ranging poultry remain local concerns.

Red kangaroo
Osphranter rufus

The red kangaroo is a large grazing marsupial of mainland Australia’s arid and semi-arid interior. It uses open plains, grasslands and shrublands. Its fortunes follow irregular rain: fresh growth can support breeding and population increases, while prolonged drought reduces forage and may lower numbers.

The largest living marsupial, it shows striking sexual dimorphism. Males may reach 1.4 m head-and-body length and 92 kg; females about 1.1 m and 39 kg. Males are often rusty red and females blue-grey, though shades vary. Both have pale undersides and black-and-white cheek markings, including a light stripe from mouth towards ear. Fast travel uses powerful hindlimb bounds; a long muscular tail swings with the legs and helps reduce trunk pitch. During each bound, ankle extensor tendons stretch under load and recoil, returning stored elastic energy. This reduces the muscle work needed to repeat the movement; oxygen use on level ground changes little across hopping speeds, though uphill travel costs more.

Across mainland Australia’s dry interior, it inhabits open plains, grassland, shrubland and savanna woodland. Scattered trees and shrubs offer shade from intense heat. In hot conditions, blood flow rises in superficial vessels of the forelegs; licking spreads moisture there, which evaporates and carries heat away. Radio-tracking in Western Australia found adult females’ core ranges stable and compact, with grazing and shelter together; males used larger areas. Drought increased adult dispersal, and journeys to water were prominent. Local distribution thus reflects vegetation and changing forage as well as water access.

It mainly grazes grasses. A 12-year study in southern Australian arid shrubland found more forbs in wet seasons and more shrub browsing in dry conditions; grasses still formed almost 90% of sampled food in severe drought. Microbes ferment fibrous plants in its enlarged forestomach, making nutrients available. Experiments with red kangaroos found methane yield varied with food intake. Green herbage supplies some water, but drought reduces both forage and moisture.

Groups are small and temporary rather than fixed family units: one field study in northwestern New South Wales recorded a mean of 2.2 animals, with size and membership changing frequently. Radio-tracking found adult females relatively sedentary with stable ranges, while subadult males dispersed widely; drought increased adult movements. Male ranges were larger and could include the core areas of several females. In an arid-pasture study, grazing peaked between dusk and dawn, when animals spent over 60% of their time grazing.

Breeding can occur year-round, with more births in spring and summer, and responds to food and rainfall. After about 33 days, one very underdeveloped young crawls into the pouch and attaches to a teat. A female may mate again soon after birth. If the pouch young still suckles, the new embryo can pause at the blastocyst stage; this embryonic diapause delays development until the older joey permanently leaves the pouch. The joey exits permanently at about eight months but may continue suckling for months.

The red kangaroo is prey for predators such as dingoes and shares arid rangelands with livestock. In a long-term southern Australian study, dietary overlap with sheep increased in drought, when both relied heavily on grasses; potential competition grew as pasture deteriorated. An analysis of 1978–2002 aerial counts across four South Australian areas modelled population growth against rainfall, harvest, kangaroo density and domestic herbivore density. The best model found a positive statistical association with livestock density, which the authors proposed could reflect resource availability beyond rainfall. These findings describe regional pastoral systems, not a universal effect of livestock.

The Mammal Diversity Database reported the IUCN global category as Least Concern when consulted in October 2026, reflecting the species’ broad Australian range and large population. This status coexists with marked local fluctuations: drought can reduce forage and survival, while favourable rain can support population growth. Management figures are regional. A New South Wales government report dated 17 December 2025 set commercial quotas for 2026 and gave 2025 estimates for monitored zones; these guide harvest in that state rather than estimate the global population.

Red squirrel
Sciurus vulgaris

The Eurasian red squirrel is a small tree-dwelling rodent widespread across Europe and northern Asia. Curved claws and powerful hind limbs aid climbing and leaping; its long bushy tail helps balance and thermoregulation. It feeds mainly on plant foods that change with forest and season. Usually foraging alone, individuals may share winter nests. Autumn scatter-hoarding stores food and sometimes disperses seeds. The species remains widespread globally, despite sharp regional declines in parts of Britain and Italy.

This slender squirrel has prominent eyes, a long bushy tail and, in winter, often tufted ears. Its coat ranges from bright red or chestnut to brown, greyish or nearly black, commonly with a pale underside; the name does not describe every animal. In a Hokkaido subspecies, specimens had lighter winter coats and more pronounced seasonal colour shifts, but appearance also varies geographically. The North American eastern grey squirrel, Sciurus carolinensis, is a different species; colour alone cannot distinguish them because red squirrels may also be grey or dark.

Red squirrels inhabit boreal conifer forests, mixed and broad-leaved woods, wooded parks and some fragmented landscapes. Local food and tree structure shape their use of habitat: conifer seeds may be dependable, while deciduous woods supply seasonal nuts, buds and fruit. In one northern Greek mixed forest, four adults used the canopy extensively, especially small branches and terminal twigs. This study illustrates how connected crowns provide feeding and escape routes, not a universal habitat preference. Squirrels build twig nests high in trees and line them with softer material; they may also use cavities.

Seeds and nuts are staple foods, but the menu shifts with season and habitat. Cones and seeds may dominate in conifer forest; buds, shoots and flowers become important at other times, supplemented by berries, fungi and deciduous seeds. Incisors strip cone scales and open hard seed coverings. Some animal matter is also eaten, though plants predominate. Rather than one larder, squirrels bury food in many separate caches. In a Japanese Korean-pine forest, researchers documented red squirrels carrying cones and burying seed clusters; those observations describe that population and tree system.

Curved claws grip bark, letting squirrels climb trunks and move onto slender branches. In northern Greece, clawed climbing aided vertical travel and retreat to trees after ground feeding; quadrupedal movement and sitting helped squirrels use terminal twigs and handle food. Jumps cross gaps between crowns. The long tail helps balance and thermoregulation, while hind limbs support climbing and leaps. Red squirrels forage mostly alone rather than in stable troops. Their home ranges overlap, and familiar individuals may tolerate one another or share nests during cold periods. Space use shifts with food and breeding conditions.

Breeding timing varies with latitude, food and condition. Gestation lasts about 38–39 days. When a female is receptive, several males may follow and compete; mating does not establish a lasting pair bond, and males provide no routine care. The female raises the litter in a nest and may move young if disturbed. Newborns are blind and sparsely furred; eyes open at about a month, and young begin leaving the nest at roughly 40–45 days. They sample solid food before weaning at around 8–10 weeks, remaining under maternal care during early life. Litter size and breeding frequency vary, so regional averages are not fixed outputs for the species.

Scatter-hoarding links squirrel feeding with forest regeneration. In Hokkaido, Japan, red squirrels carried Korean-pine cones from source trees and buried seeds in small clusters. One study found seedlings as far as 600 m from parent trees; another recorded them up to 1.8 km from the nearest source. These are separate site-specific observations, not a typical distance. Squirrels recover some caches; seeds left in suitable microsites may germinate. This interaction is documented for Korean pine in parts of East Asia, not every tree or squirrel population. Caches also provide food when fresh resources are scarce.

The 2023 IUCN global assessment classifies the species as Least Concern because of its broad Eurasian range; this does not mean all populations are secure. In Britain, introduced eastern grey squirrels compete with red squirrels and can carry squirrelpox virus, which causes severe disease and mortality in reds. English surveillance from 1993–2005 found cases in areas where seropositive greys also occurred, supporting a reservoir link in that setting. Grey squirrels and squirrelpox are not a universal Eurasian threat. Habitat fragmentation, forestry and other local pressures also matter, so conservation needs depend on region.

Red-tailed green ratsnake
Gonyosoma oxycephalum

This large colubrid snake ranges across Southeast Asia, from the Andaman Islands to the Philippines and Indonesian archipelagos. Records include Myanmar, Thailand, Vietnam, Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia and the Philippines. Its common name reflects the frequent green body and rusty-red tail, though brown and other colour forms occur.

Adults generally measure 1.6–2.3 metres. Singapore’s National Parks Board lists the species at 2.4 metres. The body is laterally compressed, with broad smooth belly scales for gripping branches, a dark eye stripe and often green colouring with a rusty tail.
It inhabits tropical forests, including mangroves, lowland woods and forest edges, and may also occur in plantations or gardens. Fully arboreal, it moves through the branches above the ground.
Its prey includes birds and eggs, lizards, bats and small mammals. It hunts in trees, sometimes hanging from a branch to seize prey moving through the canopy, including bats in flight.
Diurnal and arboreal, it moves through branches above the ground. When threatened, it can inflate its body and strike defensively.

Mating occurs in trees, and the female lays eggs in a sheltered place. In one captive case, a fertile clutch of four eggs was incubated at 30°C; hatchlings emerged over days 87–89. The three young first shed 10–14 days after hatching, then accepted pinkie mice; all fed regularly within a month. The same report noted a second fertile clutch after the female had been kept apart from a male, suggesting stored sperm.
As a tree-dwelling predator, it feeds on animals that use the canopy, including birds, bats and lizards, as well as small mammals.

The IUCN assessment published in 2012 classified the species as Least Concern. Singapore’s National Parks Board records it in Bukit Timah and Central Catchment forest reserves, a local occurrence within its much wider range.

European robin
Erithacus rubecula

The European robin is a small, upright songbird of Europe, western Asia and parts of North Africa, where its range spans woodland, scrub and settled landscapes. It is the robin of European gardens, a member of the Old World flycatcher family, Muscicapidae. The similarly orange-breasted American robin is a different species, Turdus migratorius, in the thrush family; the shared English name reflects appearance, not close relationship. Many robins stay near their breeding range, while birds from colder northern and eastern populations move south or west for winter.

Adults of both sexes look alike: a bright orange-red face and breast form a bib against a grey-blue border, brown upperparts and a pale belly. At about 14 centimetres long, adults weigh roughly 14–25 grams across published reference ranges; it has a short, fine bill and long legs for its upright, quick-hopping gait. Newly fledged birds lack orange and are mottled brown with golden spots, a less conspicuous pattern that blends into leaf litter. In a partial post-juvenile moult during summer, some feathers are replaced and orange-red feathers begin to appear on the breast. The sexes remain difficult to tell apart by sight.

Robins use cool, shaded places with low cover, such as deciduous woods, hedges, scrub, parks and gardens. Dense vegetation gives shelter and song perches, while patches of open soil or leaf litter make small prey accessible. Nests occupy sheltered sites, from natural cover to unusual human-made places such as flower pots. Their comfort around people is especially familiar in Britain and Ireland; elsewhere in Europe they can be more wary, so garden behaviour is not universal.

Most of the year, robins hunt small invertebrates such as insects and earthworms at ground level. From a low perch, one may drop onto visible prey and return to cover, or hop across litter and seize prey after a brief pause. In autumn and winter, berries and other fruits can also supplement animal food; the balance varies by season and region.

Outside breeding season, a robin is usually solitary and defends feeding space from others. Both sexes can hold territories and sing during winter, when the song is often more plaintive and drawn out than the breeding song. This year-round defence helps secure familiar cover and safe feeding patches as well as food. The species is partly migratory: some populations are resident, some move only in part, and northern or eastern breeders travel to western Europe and North Africa. In Britain, local birds are joined by winter visitors from farther north and east; migration varies among populations.

The female builds a cup of moss, leaves and grass, lined with hair or plant fibres, in a cavity or other sheltered site. In Britain, four or five eggs are typical; she incubates them for about 14–16 days. The chicks are altricial, meaning they hatch helpless and need parental warmth and food. Both parents feed chicks until they fledge at about two weeks; the male may keep feeding them when the female starts a second brood. A pair often raises a second brood when conditions permit.

By taking insects and other invertebrates, robins are small predators in leaf litter and low vegetation; adults can in turn be hunted by birds of prey. A Lithuanian nest-box study recorded pine martens and dormice as nest predators; other observations describe cuckoo chicks ejecting host eggs or young. In southern France, a winter study documented seasonal fruit eating and inferred that robins may contribute to seed dispersal in Mediterranean scrub. When gardeners dig, robins seize worms and grubs exposed in the soil.

BirdLife International’s 2018 global assessment classified the European robin as Least Concern, reflecting its very large range and population. Global security does not mean every local population is stable. In the UK, Birds of Conservation Concern 5 (2021) places the robin on the Green List. Monitoring shows a long-term increase, interrupted by falls after severe winters and local declines in earlier atlas comparisons. Cold spells can reduce survival by making food harder to find.

Rock pigeon
Columba livia

The Rock Pigeon is a dove that nests on natural cliffs and city ledges. Its close association with people began through domestication thousands of years ago; the familiar urban bird is usually descended from domestic pigeons that escaped or were released. This history has carried feral populations around the world, while genuinely wild populations retain a much narrower native range. The distinction matters because plentiful city flocks do not by themselves show that wild cliff populations are secure.

A typical wild adult is blue-grey, with two black bars across each wing, a white patch on the lower back, and a dark band near the tail tip. Green and purplish iridescence flashes on the neck as the bird turns in the light. Adults usually measure 30–36 cm, weigh 265–380 g and span 50–67 cm; sex and population cause variation. Domestication has produced many colours and patterns, and feral birds may show them too, so a grey, barred individual is not automatically a wild Rock Pigeon.

The wild native range extends across parts of Europe, North Africa, the Middle East, Central Asia and South Asia, but millennia of domestic movement blur its limits and make some remnant wild populations hard to distinguish from feral birds. Rock Pigeons nest in cliff crevices, usually near open ground where seeds are accessible. Farms provide grain and water, while cliffs offer protected roosts and nest sites. In towns, roofs, bridges and ledges provide similar shelter, explaining urban success without making cities the species’ original home.

The bill picks up seeds and grains from the ground, along with small fruits, green plant material and occasional invertebrates. A pigeon can drink by immersing its bill and drawing water continuously, an unusual ability among birds that avoids repeated head tipping. Swallowed food may pause in the crop, an expandable part of the oesophagus that stores and moistens it. In the glandular stomach (proventriculus), hydrochloric acid activates pepsin for chemical digestion; the muscular gizzard grinds seeds, often aided by swallowed grit, before the small intestine completes digestion and absorbs nutrients. Urban scraps broaden the menu but do not erase the species’ seed-eating biology.

Outside the breeding season, pigeons often gather to feed and roost. Males bow and coo during courtship, and may regurgitate food to a partner. Experiments on trained homing pigeons show a sun compass corrected by the internal clock and olfactory map cues for locating home after unfamiliar releases; the strength of odor-based navigation varies among regions. GPS-tracked pigeons also follow learned visual routes over familiar terrain. When the sun compass is unavailable, tests support a magnetic compass; these experiments study domestic birds released away from their loft.

Pairs may keep the same partner through successive nesting attempts, but long-term bonds can break when breeding conditions change. The male brings twigs while the female arranges them into a loose platform on a ledge or in a cavity. A clutch is usually two white eggs; both adults share incubation for about 18 days, with the male commonly taking the middle of the day. Hatchlings are helpless, sparsely downy nestlings that remain in the nest. Both parents feed crop milk: prolactin stimulates crop-lining cells to multiply and shed, producing a secretion rich in protein and fat but poor in carbohydrates, not milk from mammary glands. Parents gradually add softened or regurgitated seeds as chicks grow. Young usually leave the nest at 25–32 days and continue to be fed as they learn to forage.

By eating seeds on open ground, Rock Pigeons link wild plants and cultivated grain to the animals that prey on birds. They are themselves taken by predators including Peregrine Falcons; in cities, these raptors sometimes nest on tall buildings and hunt pigeons among the rooftops. Nesting colonies leave conspicuous droppings on building ledges. Their broad diet also lets them exploit food discarded or provided by people, tying local flocks to human activity.

The IUCN lists the Rock Pigeon globally as Least Concern. The cited assessment is the 2016 version amended in 2019. That broad category can obscure a problem for wild birds: domestic and feral pigeons interbreed with cliff-dwelling Rock Pigeons, introducing genes and sometimes replacing local ancestry. Research in Britain and Ireland found the least introgression in the Outer Hebrides and varying admixture elsewhere; plumage alone cannot reliably identify an individual’s ancestry. The 2021 European Red List assessment classed the species as Least Concern but its regional population trend was unknown. Cornell’s North American summary reported a 46% decline from 1966 to 2015, a regional signal rather than a global estimate.

Rook
Corvus frugilegus

The rook is a social Eurasian crow of open farmland, ranging from western Europe across northern Asia to eastern Siberia. Most western populations stay near their breeding grounds, while birds farther north and east move south for winter.

Adults measure about 44–46 cm long, with a wingspan of 81–99 cm; their black plumage often shines blue or violet in sunlight. Bare pale skin around the slim bill distinguishes adults from carrion crows; juveniles retain facial feathers until roughly six months old.

Rooks are most common in rural fields and villages, nesting in mature trees between farmland; they also enter towns when suitable habitat is available. They use parks and churchyards where large trees provide nesting sites.

As an omnivore, the rook eats earthworms and insect larvae, while grain and other plant foods also make up a major part of its diet. In spring it may pull up germinating crops, and occasionally eats small vertebrates, eggs or carrion.

Rooks feed in noisy flocks and gather at dusk before flying to communal night roosts, sometimes alongside jackdaws. Their varied calls signal recognition between mates or aggression, while long-term pair bonds persist within the colony.

Established pairs build or repair a cup of twigs high in a tree, often reusing a site in a rookery that may persist for years. The female usually incubates three or four eggs for about 15–16 days while the male brings food; after hatching, both parents feed the helpless chicks. Young leave the nest at about 32–34 days but remain dependent on parental feeding for some time before becoming independent.

By eating soil invertebrates, rooks remove some crop pests, yet their taste for newly sown grain and emerging seedlings can bring them into conflict with farmers. Their feeding therefore links the seasonal supply of field prey and seeds with both agricultural benefits and losses.

Its global conservation status is Least Concern, although local fortunes differ. In Britain, breeding numbers have declined since around 2000, while the causes remain unclear. Across its range, changing farmland, pesticide-treated seed and persecution are documented pressures.

Desert rosy boa
Lichanura trivirgata
The desert rosy boa, Lichanura trivirgata, is a small boa native to the southwestern United States and northwestern Mexico.

Females are generally larger than males. Arizona individuals reach 95 centimetres; three dark lengthwise bands and vertical oval pupils are characteristic. The head is small and the tail relatively blunt. A stout body usually has a pale grey background with brown or orange bands.

Its range covers western Arizona, Sonora and most of Baja California; California records are limited to far southern San Diego County. It shelters in rocky desert foothills, scrub and canyon crevices, and may use burrows where surface cover is scarce. Coastal California populations formerly grouped with this boa are now treated as Lichanura orcutti.
Small mammals and birds are its main prey. It subdues them by constriction, wrapping its body around the animal.

Usually solitary, it moves slowly and stays sheltered under rocks, in crevices or inside burrows. In Arizona it is mostly nocturnal or crepuscular, yet may move on spring mornings and on mild or overcast days.

During spring courtship, a male follows the female’s scent, tongue-flicks over her body and strokes her flanks with pelvic spurs before mating. After several months of internal development, females bear live young that soon become independent. In Arizona, births occur in late summer or early autumn, with three to fourteen young recorded per litter.
It hunts rodents in rocky desert habitats, acting as a ground-level predator in arid food webs.
Wild collection for pets occurred historically, while captive breeding later met much of the demand. An IUCN assessment published in 2007 classified the species as Least Concern.

Sable
Martes zibellina
The sable is a forest marten of northern Eurasia, widespread from the Urals through Siberia to the Pacific. It also occurs in China, Mongolia, North Korea, Kazakhstan and Hokkaido.

Adults have a long, flexible body, short feet and a bushy tail. In broad Russian samples, males measured 32–53 cm from head to body and weighed 1.15–1.85 kg; females measured 30–48 cm and weighed 0.65–1.60 kg. These observed ranges vary geographically, and adult males are usually heavier than females. Winter fur is dense and silky; the summer coat is shorter and coarser. Across populations, fur ranges from sandy brown to nearly black, sometimes with a pale throat patch. The sable resembles the European pine marten, Martes martes, but is usually darker, has a shorter tail relative to its body, and hunts more often on the ground.

The sable inhabits coniferous taiga and mixed forests on plains and mountains, hunting mainly near the ground. In Hokkaido, tracked animals rested in dense stands with fallen wood and foraged in mature forest where rodents were plentiful.

The sable is an adaptable predator, and its diet shifts with season and local prey. In eastern Hokkaido, voles occurred most often in samples, followed by Siberian chipmunks and wood mice. The same study recorded birds, eggs, insects, fish, amphibians, reptiles and crustaceans; fruits were more frequent in autumn and winter, when plant foods can supplement mammal prey. In Barguzin, sables hunt pikas beneath snow and scavenge carrion. This broad menu may help sables compensate when mammal prey fluctuates.
Sables are generally solitary, use individual ranges, locate prey by hearing and smell, and mark their surroundings with scent. In storms or during human pursuit, they may hide in dens for days.

Mating takes place mainly from mid-June to mid-August, though dates vary by region. In sparse populations, courtship may involve chasing, jumps and low rumbling; males may fight where their ranges overlap. After fertilization, the embryo remains dormant for 7.5–8 months before attaching to the uterine lining; it then develops for about 30–35 days, with births from late March to early May. Litters contain one to seven kits, often about three. Newborns are helpless and blind; they open their eyes around one month, leave the den soon afterward, and are weaned at about seven weeks, when the mother begins providing regurgitated food. Young disperse in August.

Forest structure shapes shelter and hunting: in Hokkaido, sables rested under dense cover that may reduce exposure to red foxes and wind, then foraged in rodent-rich mature stands. Some tracked home ranges overlapped extensively. Food shortages can enlarge home ranges.

Demand for sable fur drove severe depletion in parts of Russia by the early twentieth century. In 1914, a survey found only about 20–30 sables across the future Barguzin reserve; established in 1916 with a hunting ban, it enabled the population to recover. An IUCN assessment dated 3 March 2015 and published in 2016 classified the species globally as Least Concern, reflecting its large, widespread population.

Senegal galago
Galago senegalensis

The Senegal galago, also called the northern lesser galago or Senegal bushbaby, is a small strepsirrhine primate in the family Galagidae. Despite its name, it ranges far beyond Senegal across sub-Saharan Africa, from western regions toward the Horn and East Africa. Four subspecies are commonly recognised, though boundaries and some taxonomy remain under study. It is a nocturnal, tree-living primate, but regularly descends to the ground.

This galago has a compact body, soft grey to brown fur, a pale stripe down the nose, very large mobile ears, and forward-facing eyes that reflect torchlight. A reflective layer behind the retina returns some incoming light through the photoreceptors, improving the chance of detecting photons in dim conditions; it does not create light. Long fingers and toes end in broadened, grippy pads for holding branches. A comb of lower front teeth and a narrow grooming claw on the second toe of each hind foot help maintain the coat.

Across its broad range, the species uses woodland, bushland, savanna and some montane habitats rather than one uniform forest type. Local observations illustrate this flexibility: the Senegal subspecies occurs in open Acacia–baobab woodland in The Gambia, while populations elsewhere use moist woodland, riverine forest and wooded grassland. In northern Tanzania, researchers found sleeping sites with dense canopy and connected neighboring trees. Such cover can hide a resting animal from aerial predators, while connected branches provide escape routes; cooler, more humid sleeping locations also support a thermoregulatory explanation. These results describe one Tanzanian site and season, not every population.

The Senegal galago eats arthropods and tree exudates such as gum. At a northern Tanzanian site, researchers directly observed both foods but did not collect enough data to estimate their dietary proportions. During a separate dry-season study at Fongoli in southeastern Senegal, they did not see fruit eating; fruit has been recorded in The Gambia. These observations suggest local and seasonal flexibility, not one universal menu. Gum is an energy-rich plant secretion, often released after insect damage to bark, and gives the galago a food source distinct from mobile insect prey.

The galago’s night is divided between travel, feeding, pauses and self-maintenance. Powerful hind limbs and elongated ankle and foot bones help it cling upright to a trunk, then launch into a leap; elastic tendons and connective tissues store energy during crouching and release it rapidly at take-off. This spring-like mechanism amplifies muscle power, while the long tail helps stabilize the body in motion. Grooming combines licking and combing with the lower toothcomb and hind-foot grooming claw. Social life is neither strictly solitary nor continuously group-based: individuals often forage alone, but may sleep together and keep contact by calls. A Tanzanian study found social patterns differed substantially among sites.

Females bear dependent young that require milk, warmth and protection while their coordination develops. A mother may carry an infant in her mouth or let it cling to her fur, and may leave it concealed while she forages. A 1960 study of the nominate subspecies in Sudan described oestrous cycles lasting four to six weeks throughout the year, with a local peak of sexual activity in mid-December in the Nuba Mountains. This did not establish a fixed breeding season across the species. Maternal care is central; reproductive timing and male involvement remain less well documented across populations.

By eating arthropods, galagos are predators of small invertebrates, although their effect on prey populations has not been quantified well enough to claim broad ecosystem control. They also exploit gums produced when insects damage Acacia trees, linking the primate’s feeding to a plant’s response to injury and to the insects beneath the bark. A striking predator–prey interaction was documented at Fongoli, Senegal: chimpanzees sometimes probe tree cavities with sharpened sticks to capture sleeping galagos. This is a local hunting technique, not a general account of chimpanzee diets or of galago mortality across Africa.

The IUCN’s global assessment conducted in 2016 and published in 2019 classified Galago senegalensis as Least Concern, consistent with its extensive range. This category is a global risk assessment, not proof that every local population is stable or that habitat change is harmless. Nocturnal galagos are difficult to detect, and information remains sparse for many populations, making local abundance hard to establish. Woodland conversion and degradation can remove sleeping cover and feeding trees locally; the degree of risk depends on the site. The category alone does not establish the condition of any particular population.

Balaeniceps rex

The shoebill is a wetland bird and the sole living member of Balaenicipitidae. Despite its stork-like silhouette, it is neither a stork nor a heron: evidence places it closer to pelicans. Its slate-grey body, long legs, and broad, shoe-shaped bill mark this marsh hunter.

Adults are mainly blue-grey, with darker flight feathers, a pale eye, and long, widely spread toes suited to walking over floating vegetation. The enormous bill has a deep, bulbous base, sharp cutting edges, and a hooked tip; males average slightly larger.

It occupies freshwater swamps and seasonally flooded marshes across central and eastern Africa, from South Sudan south to Zambia. Dense reeds, sedges, or papyrus provide cover, while small open patches and floating plant mats offer places to fish and nest.

Fish dominate its diet, especially lungfish, bichirs, and catfish; it also takes water snakes and frogs, with other aquatic vertebrates reported less often. The bird waits motionless or walks slowly, then lunges down in a forceful forward collapse to seize prey in its bill.

Usually solitary, shoebills keep space between feeding birds, even when a pair is nesting. A successful strike may bring up fish tangled with vegetation; the bird shakes plant matter free before swallowing. It is largely sedentary, though changing water levels can prompt local movements.

Pairs nest far apart, building broad platforms of wetland vegetation on floating mats or small mounds. Clutches hold one to three eggs, commonly two; both parents incubate and tend young. Often only one chick survives, as food shortage or sibling aggression limits the brood.

The shoebill depends on a shifting mosaic: dense cover for concealment, fish-rich water, and open footing where it can recover after a lunge. In Bangweulu, Zambia, tracking found mostly short daily movements, linked to feeding and the search for suitable wetland patches.

In its profile consulted in October2026, BirdLife International lists the shoebill as Vulnerable and reports an estimate of3,300–5,300 mature individuals. These are assessment estimates, not a new census. Wetland loss, hunting, nest disturbance, illegal capture and drought are identified pressures.

Siamese Fighting Fish
Betta splendens
Native to Thailand and nearby Indochina, wild B. splendens is short-finned and subdued; ornamental colours and flowing fins reflect selective breeding.
Adults average about 6.5 cm; males are often slimmer, longer-finned, and brighter, while females have shorter fins, especially in domestic strains.
It inhabits Thailand’s central plain and nearby Indochina, in shallow marshes, floodplains and rice fields with warm, slow water and vegetation.

It snaps up small animal prey among plants or at the surface, especially zooplankton and mosquito or other insect larvae. Small crustaceans and insects that fall onto the water also provide food, so access to animal prey is a central part of its natural feeding ecology.

Territorial males spread fins and flare gill covers to warn rivals; clashes can cause bites and injury. Aggression varies, and females can also be territorial. Domesticated fighting strains were selected for persistent aggression, whereas ornamental breeding later favoured elaborate fins and colours; the intensity of fighting therefore differs among strains.

The male courts beside a floating bubble nest. During an embrace, female eggs meet male sperm in water: fertilization is external. He gathers sinking eggs and guards them; after hatching, he tends larvae until they swim freely. Keeping eggs in a surface bubble nest improves their access to oxygen in warm, poorly oxygenated water, while the male repairs damaged bubbles. Incubation typically lasts about 24–36 hours, followed by two to three days in the nest while larvae absorb their yolk reserves. Young fish initially rely on their gills, because air breathing develops later; growth rate influences this transition and the age of maturity.

It eats insect larvae and feeds larger aquatic predators. A blood-rich labyrinth above the gills absorbs surface air in oxygen-poor water; gills still exchange gases underwater. The labyrinth contains folded bony surfaces lined with respiratory tissue, giving inhaled air a large exchange surface above the gills.
The IUCN’s 2011 assessment classifies wild populations as Vulnerable, citing wetland loss and pollution. Captive abundance does not secure native fish.

Snowshoe hare
Lepus americanus

This North American hare inhabits boreal and mountain forests, from Alaska and Newfoundland south to the western mountains and Appalachians. Its name recalls broad, furred hind feet that aid travel over soft snow. Herbivorous, it also feeds many mammalian and bird predators, so its abundance affects other populations. Northern numbers cycle strongly, while many southern populations fluctuate less.

Adults average 46–51 centimetres and 1.4–1.8 kilograms in Alaska; size varies regionally, so these are indicative figures. The coat usually changes from brown or grey-brown in summer to white in winter, with dark ear tips and a small tail. Large, furred hind feet spread weight over snow and reduce sinking. On coastal parts of British Columbia, Washington and Oregon, where snow is scarce, hares may remain brown year-round. Females are often slightly larger than males.

Across most of its range, the hare favors boreal or upper-montane forest with dense understory, where shrubs provide food and concealment. In California it also uses dense conifer stands, high-elevation riparian woods and chaparral. It rests in a shallow ground hollow called a form, often beneath brush, ferns or fallen timber, rather than digging a burrow. Well-used runways connect feeding patches and shelter; snow makes them conspicuous and can preserve summer routes.

In California, grasses, forbs and succulent plants are important summer foods; in snowy winters, hares there rely mainly on conifer needles and evergreen shrub leaves. Newfoundland menus include birch, willow, maple, balsam fir, grasses and fireweed, illustrating regional variation. Like other lagomorphs, hares re-ingest soft nutrient-rich droppings called cecotropes, passing food through the gut again so more nutrients can be absorbed. This helps recover nutrients from fibrous plants, while nutritious young growth remains valuable when available.

Snowshoe hares are generally solitary outside breeding, although overlapping home ranges and temporary feeding aggregations occur. They are active mainly at dusk and night, resting by day in sheltered cover. Individuals communicate partly by thumping their hind feet, a reported warning or contact signal, and may squeal when captured. Females and males may each have several mates; this does not make hares a stable social group.

Breeding dates vary with latitude and local conditions; in many northern populations, mating begins in late winter or spring and continues into summer. Gestation lasts about 36–37 days; litters range from one to six leverets and average three, with counts varying locally. A female may conceive again before her previous litter is born, allowing several litters in a long season. Leverets are born fully furred, open-eyed and mobile; they nurse once daily and become self-supporting at three to four weeks.

Lynx, coyotes and foxes hunt snowshoe hares, as do numerous hawks and owls; no single predator explains every local trend. Yukon field experiments found that reducing mammalian predation and adding food each raised hare density, while doing both had a larger combined effect. Predator numbers often follow hare abundance with a delay, and may shift to other prey when hares become scarce. At population peaks, browsing can reduce young shoots, linking plant availability with predation.

The species is widespread and classified as Secure in Canada in the 2020 General Status assessment, a national screening rather than legal protection. In California, where it occupies a limited set of high-elevation regions, the wildlife agency lists it as a Species of Special Concern. In Alaska, the wildlife agency lists development, mining and fuel exploration as habitat threats. Shorter snow seasons can leave winter-white hares conspicuous against bare ground. Montana research found mismatches during spring and autumn molts; spring color change can respond to snow conditions, but does not track every local change perfectly.

South American coati
Nasua nasua
The South American coati is a procyonid mammal of tropical and subtropical South America. Its daily life combines solitary feeding, group travel by females and young, and seasonal reproduction.

An adult measures about 41–67 cm from head to rump, with a separate 32–69 cm tail; reported mass is 3–6 kg. In a wild adult sample from three parks in Minas Gerais, Brazil, males averaged 4.36 kg and females 3.53 kg; this difference was not statistically significant. Fur ranges from grey-brown to rusty red, and the brown, flexible muzzle turns slightly upward. The ringed tail balances the animal but cannot grasp; five clawed digits and strong forelegs dig through soil and rotting wood. Mobile ankle joints let it turn its hind feet outward to climb down a trunk headfirst.

The range stretches from Colombia and Venezuela south through Ecuador and Brazil to Uruguay and northern Argentina, reaching about 2,500 m on Andean slopes. Coatis use evergreen and deciduous forests, cloud forests, riverine woods, dry scrub, Chaco, and Cerrado, with forest cover remaining central. In an urban Cerrado park in Brazil, seasonal food availability shifted coatis’ movements and daily activity.

Fruits and invertebrates are major foods, but their importance shifts with season and local availability. In Paraná, 426 scats contained frequent fruit, especially figs and Prunus brasiliensis, as well as leaves and beetles; winter samples held more invertebrates, plant matter, and vertebrate prey. It noses beneath leaf litter and claws into rotting wood for insects, larvae, ants, and termites, while also searching trees for fruit. Eggs, small vertebrates, and carrion broaden the menu when available. At Brazilian visitor sites, processed food and refuse have also appeared in coati diets.

Coatis are chiefly diurnal, foraging mostly on the ground but climbing to sleep, nest, and move through trees. Females and immature animals travel in bands, while adult males often live alone; a field study at Iguazú, Argentina, also recorded males staying with bands year-round. In a Cerrado population, seasonal food supply shifted movements and daily activity, showing that group life and space use are flexible. Members keep contact with calls and touch, groom one another, and retreat into trees or flee over ground when disturbed.

Breeding is seasonal; solitary males may temporarily join female bands to mate. Females may become receptive within a synchronized one- to two-week period; males compete, while genetic work has found some young fathered by males from outside the group. After mating, pregnant females build tree nests and raise the litter apart from the band. Gestation lasts about 74–77 days, with three to seven young; mothers reunite with the band after five or six weeks and nurse until weaning near four months. Young open their eyes at around ten days, walk at three to four weeks, and climb soon afterward; females mature near two years and males around three.

The coati consumes litter-dwelling invertebrates and is itself prey for large cats, raptors, and boas. Fruit-eating also moves seeds away from parent plants: a 33-month study in southeastern Brazil recorded fruits from 53 plant species and seeds from at least 49 in coati diets and scats. Gut passage left germination unchanged for most tested plants, but improved it for one species after pulp removal. Seed dispersal by coatis may help connect forest patches and support plant recruitment, alongside the partly overlapping services of other fruit-eating animals.

The IUCN’s global Red List assessment, published in 2016 and conducted in 2015, classified Nasua nasua as Least Concern. Its wide range and presence in protected areas support that status, though habitat loss and hunting threaten coatis locally. Near settlements, coatis may raid crops or take poultry. Studies at Brazilian visitor sites have also found human food and refuse in their diets, evidence that contact can alter foraging. Nasua nasua solitaria is listed in CITES Appendix III at Uruguay’s request.

Spring peeper
Pseudacris crucifer

The spring peeper is a tiny chorus frog native to eastern North America, from southeastern Canada through much of the eastern United States. Its shrill, repeated peep is among the first frog calls heard as spring approaches.

Adult males are often 20–30 mm long and females 30–40 mm; measurements vary among populations. Tan, brown or grey skin usually bears a dark X-shaped mark; the forefeet have four digits and the hindfeet five, tipped with adhesive pads.

It can climb but often stays near the ground, hiding in leaf litter in marshy woods or lowlands near ponds and swamps. It breeds in shallow freshwater pools, often temporary, where plants or debris can hold eggs.

Adults catch small live insects and other arthropods visually, using a sticky tongue; prey includes ants, beetles, flies and spiders. Tadpoles graze on algae and consume detritus and microorganisms in the pond.

Male spring peepers call at breeding pools at dusk and on spring evenings; the throat vocal sac is an expandable pouch that inflates and deflates during the repeated peep. In northern populations, some individuals can survive partial freezing during winter dormancy, but this tolerance is not universal.

After winter, males call at breeding sites and clasp females in amplexus, the mating hold. They externally fertilize several hundred eggs as females lay them; eggs attach singly underwater and hatch within days. Larvae usually metamorphose after roughly 45–90 days, with development partly dependent on water availability.

Spring peepers use fishless pools and also breed in temporary ponds that may dry after tadpoles transform, linking successful development to water persistence. Predators include aquatic beetle larvae for tadpoles and snakes, skunks and larger frogs for adults.

The IUCN assessed the species as Least Concern in 2020, citing its broad range, large presumed population and use of varied habitats. Wetland drainage is a minor threat globally, while intensive urbanization and agriculture can make some areas less suitable.

Stoat
Mustela erminea

The stoat is a small mustelid with a long, slender body, short legs and a black-tipped tail. It searches covered ground and follows prey into burrows. Its coat moults seasonally, but winter whitening varies with local climate and snow conditions.

In Britain, adult males measure about 27.5–31 cm and weigh roughly 200–450 g; females are about 24–29 cm and 140–280 g. Tails measure 9.5–14 cm in both sexes. In summer the back is chestnut to reddish brown and the underside pale; the black tail tip remains in winter. The smaller least weasel, Mustela nivalis, lacks this black tip. Stoats moult twice yearly: day length helps set the seasonal timing, while temperature affects whether winter fur becomes fully white or stays mottled. A study of Dutch pelts found full winter whiteness more often in colder regions. When snow disappears, a white coat can stand out against bare ground.

Stoats occupy a broad range of covered habitats, from grassland and farmland to woodland, marsh and upland; in Britain they travel along hedgerows, ditches and stone walls. A 2021 genetic and morphometric revision assigns M. erminea mainly to the Old World and Beringia into Alaska; most continental North American populations are M. richardsonii, while Haida Gwaii and Alexander Archipelago island populations are M. haidarum.

Small mammals, especially rabbits and water voles where abundant, are staple prey; stoats also take rodents, birds and eggs. A British stomach-content study found lagomorphs most often, followed by rodents and birds or eggs; in that sample, males ate more lagomorphs and females more small rodents. Stoats enter wider prey tunnels, such as rabbit, rat and water-vole burrows, and climb to reach birds’ nests. Most prey are killed with a bite to the back of the neck. Stoats cache surplus prey and reuse former prey nests as dens, sometimes lining them with fur in cold regions.

Stoats are mostly solitary: adult males and females occupy separate territories, and males range more widely when searching for mates. Scent marks communicate territorial presence and social status. At about eight weeks, kits begin hunting alongside their mother.

In wild stoats in New Zealand, females mate in September–November and give birth the following September–October. The fertilised egg remains dormant in the uterus for about eight to nine months before implantation. After implantation, active pregnancy lasts about four weeks. Spring litters usually contain six to twelve young, born blind, deaf and sparsely furred. Mothers care for the kits until they become self-sufficient at around twelve weeks. Female kits can mate at only two or three weeks old, before leaving the nest.

In Britain, stoat abundance often tracks prey populations, especially rabbits; myxomatosis-driven rabbit crashes coincided with sharp stoat declines in the 1950s and 1960s. A recent climate projection for the Italian Alps suggests its local range may contract as snow cover declines and snow voles shift distribution, but this is a regional forecast rather than a measured global trend. On Orkney, introduced stoats prey on endemic voles and ground-nesting birds, and compete with native raptors for voles. New Zealand stoats were introduced from Britain in the nineteenth century to control rabbits, but they have had a devastating effect on native birdlife.

England’s 2021 mammal assessment classed the stoat as Least Concern but also described its population evidence as highly data deficient. In Britain, hedgerow loss and rabbit declines may reduce habitat or food. On Orkney, where they were first recorded in 2010, an eradication programme targets this introduced predator to protect native wildlife.

Tawny owl
Strix aluco

The tawny owl is a stocky, resident woodland owl of much of Europe and parts of Asia and North Africa. It hunts mainly at night, often from a perch, and stays close to a familiar territory through the year. A rounded head without ear tufts, dark eyes and richly patterned brown or grey plumage make it recognizable even when its bark-like colours conceal it against a tree. The North African form mauritanica, sometimes separated as the Maghreb owl, is included within Strix aluco by the 2025 Clements checklist.

Adults have a rounded head, a plain facial disc, a short hooked bill and no raised ear tufts. The eyes are dark brown to nearly black and face forward. Across Europe, plumage ranges from chestnut red-brown through grey-brown to paler grey; these are colour forms within the species, not separate sexes. Males and females look alike, although females are larger on average and the size ranges overlap. Fine streaks and mottling break up the outline against bark. The broad, rounded wings and compact body suit manoeuvring among trees.

Broad-leaved and mixed woodland provide mature trees, sheltered roosts and cavities for nesting. Tawny owls also occupy conifer plantations, wooded parks and large gardens, provided that trees or nest boxes offer a suitable cavity and nearby ground supplies prey. They avoid extensive open country and uplands without tree cover. Adults remain on established territories year-round; young birds usually disperse only a few kilometres, and large stretches of water can impede their spread. Habitat quality therefore depends on both nesting sites and connected, huntable cover.

Small mammals, especially mice and voles, are common prey, but the owl takes whatever suitable animals are available: small birds, amphibians, large insects and earthworms. On damp nights it may catch worms on lawns; observations also include bats near roosts. Pellet studies show why a single menu cannot describe every pair: prey remains vary with season, habitat and local animal abundance, and the owls can switch to other prey when rodents are scarce. Fur, feathers and bones that cannot be digested are regurgitated as compact pellets, which let researchers reconstruct local feeding patterns.

This is a mainly nocturnal hunter that often waits on a perch, watches for movement, then glides down to seize prey with its feet. Its broad facial disc helps collect sound, while forward-facing eyes provide overlapping vision for judging distance. Tawny owls can locate prey by listening as well as looking. Their flight is very quiet, though not literally soundless: experiments on tawny owl wings found that removing leading-edge feather serrations increased noise shortly before landing, showing that the effect depends on flight phase. A male’s territorial hoot and a female’s sharper “keewik” may overlap as a pair duet. The familiar “twit-twoo” is therefore often two birds’ calls, not one individual producing a single phrase.

Pairs nest in tree cavities or nest boxes and may lay their first eggs as early as February in Britain, although many begin in March or later. Incubation starts with the first egg, so chicks hatch at different times; when food is limited, this can allow at least some of the brood to survive. Young leave the nest while still unable to fly. During this “branching” stage they climb, hop and flutter around nearby branches, calling to adults, which continue to find and feed them outside the cavity. Leaving the nest is thus a normal developmental step, not proof that a chick has been abandoned.

By feeding on small mammals and changing prey when their numbers fluctuate, tawny owls link woodland food webs to local prey communities. Pellet contents offer a practical record of that relationship: a two-territory study in Ukraine found seasonal, annual and habitat variation in mammal remains, with alternative prey represented as well as rodents. The owl’s dependence on cavities also ties its breeding distribution to the supply of old trees and nest boxes. Because established pairs defend territories through the year, suitable nesting cavities and hunting ground must occur within the same local landscape.

BirdLife International’s global owl-species account consulted on 11 October 2026 lists the tawny owl as Least Concern. That global category does not mean every national population is secure: in Britain, the British Trust for Ornithology reports that the species has been Amber-listed since 2015 because of concern about long-term decline. British monitoring remains incomplete because a nocturnal bird is difficult to survey, and the BTO identifies population change, breeding success and survival as continuing knowledge gaps. Availability of nest cavities and prey also shapes local suitability, so national concern and global category describe different geographic scales.
