Common starling
Sturnus vulgaris

The Common Starling is a medium-sized, adaptable songbird native across much of Europe and temperate Asia. It moves between open feeding grounds and sheltered roosts, and often nests in cavities in trees or buildings. Its seasonal plumage, varied calls and large coordinated flocks make it conspicuous, while its ecological effects depend strongly on whether it lives within or beyond its native range.

Adults have a compact, dark body, short tail, pointed wings and a slender bill. The apparent blackness is broken by green, blue and purple iridescence: ordered melanosomes beneath a thin keratin layer in feather barbules produce structural colour whose hue changes with illumination and viewing angle. After the annual moult, fresh feathers carry pale tips that create conspicuous winter spots; abrasion gradually removes the tips towards spring, exposing the darker glossy feather. The bill is dark in winter and becomes yellow as breeding approaches. In breeding condition, the lower bill base is usually blue-grey in males and pink in females. A late-winter bird can therefore show both residual white spots and a yellow bill.

Starlings use open country with short vegetation, including pasture, lawns, parks and cultivated fields, where the ground is accessible for probing. Trees, reedbeds and buildings provide night roosts; nest sites are cavities such as old woodpecker holes, tree hollows, nest boxes and gaps in structures. Their broad use of human-shaped landscapes helps explain successful establishment in several introduced regions, but does not make every introduced population equally damaging.

The diet shifts with season and opportunity. During much of the breeding season, adults search soil for invertebrates such as beetle larvae and other prey, which also provide protein for growing chicks; in other periods they take fruit, seeds and other available foods. A characteristic feeding sequence is to insert the closed bill into turf or soft soil, then force it open to widen the gap and expose hidden prey. This probing-and-gaping action reaches food beneath the surface, unlike simple picking from foliage.

They forage in loose groups and gather in larger flocks at communal roosts, especially outside the breeding season. Before settling, flocks may wheel in dense aerial displays called murmurations. Measurements and models of starling flocks show that birds adjust direction and speed in response to nearby flockmates; local reactions can spread through the group, so no central leader is needed. Rapid turns propagate as birds respond to nearby flockmates and predators. Starlings also produce whistles, rattles and imitations within their vocal repertoire.

Starlings nest in cavities, where the male begins a nest of grasses and other material and the female helps finish it. A clutch usually contains three to six eggs; both parents incubate, and both feed the helpless hatchlings. Chicks remain in the nest for roughly three weeks before fledging, then continue to depend on adults while learning to forage. Some populations can raise a second brood when conditions allow. Nest cavities are a limiting resource in many landscapes, so competition for them can be intense.

Within its native range, the starling consumes soil invertebrates and fruit and also supplies prey to predators. Its probing can affect the availability of pasture invertebrates, while large feeding flocks may concentrate pressure on particular fields. In North America, where it was introduced, competition for nest cavities can displace native cavity-nesting birds; a 2003 analysis of 27 native North American cavity-nesting species detected few population declines potentially attributable to starlings. The balance of effects is therefore local and evidence-dependent, rather than a universal property of the species.

Global assessments classify the Common Starling as Least Concern because of its very large range and population. That category masks substantial regional differences. In the UK, the species is Red-listed: the British Trust for Ornithology reports a 61% decline in the breeding population from 1995 to 2024, and links concern to losses in pastoral farmland and reduced access to food. In North America and parts of Australasia it is introduced and can compete for nest cavities or cause agricultural problems, leading to local control policies. Conservation status and management therefore need a stated geography; a global category does not describe the condition of every regional population.

Tiger
Panthera tigris
The tiger is Asia’s largest wild cat, surviving in populations from the Russian Far East through South and Southeast Asia to Sumatra.

Its orange coat carries dark vertical stripes, a pale underside and conspicuous white marks behind the ears. The pattern is individual, so researchers can identify tigers in repeated photographs. Across populations, reported adult head-and-body lengths span about 150–230 cm, with tail length reported separately at 90–110 cm, and masses 75–325 kg; this broad interval is not one average or a record size. Males are larger than females, and large continental animals are not representative of every population. A broad skull, long canines and powerful jaw and forelimb muscles help seize and control heavy prey.

Tigers occur in tropical rainforests and mangroves, dry forests and scrub, grasslands, and temperate forests with heavy snow. This breadth reflects ecological flexibility, but climate alone does not make a site suitable: adequate cover, water and large wild prey are essential, and prey availability influences how much space a tiger needs.

Deer and wild pigs make up much of the diet; gaur, banteng and buffalo are important prey in some regions. Tigers also take smaller mammals, birds, reptiles and fish. Livestock may be taken where people and tiger habitat overlap. A semi-arid forest study at Ranthambhore, India, found that sambar and chital supplied most recorded prey biomass, while livestock still contributed a smaller share. That local result shows why prey choice and reliance on domestic animals should not be generalized across the range. The tiger usually stalks under cover and attacks at close range instead of pursuing prey far. Its weight and forelimbs knock an animal down; a nape bite can damage the spinal cord of small prey, while a throat bite can suffocate larger prey. After a kill, the tiger may drag the carcass into cover, tear off meat with its carnassial teeth and return to feed over several days.

Adults generally live alone. Males tend to occupy larger ranges that overlap several females; in one Thai population, neighboring females’ ranges overlapped little, while males’ ranges covered most of the female ranges they overlapped. Female home ranges tend to be smaller where prey is more abundant, though their exact area varies by landscape. Scent marks, ground scrapes, claw marks and calls let tigers exchange information without frequent direct encounters; roars, grunts and softer contact sounds serve different social purposes. Their muscular forelimbs support movement on land and help control prey. They swim well and have even been recorded hunting in water.

Breeding can occur in any season. After several receptive days, gestation lasts about 100 days and usually produces two or three cubs, though litter size varies. Newborns are blind and helpless; their mother nurses them in a den and protects them alone. Cubs begin following their mother at about two months; weaning generally occurs between three and six months. They join hunting trips at five or six months. Young gradually become independent; in a Chitwan field study, they left their natal ranges at 19–28 months. In Ranthambhore, males dispersed later on average than females. Females mature around three to four years and males around four to five.

Prey-rich areas can support denser tiger populations and smaller female home ranges than landscapes where ungulates are scarce, linking tiger distribution to the prey base. Predation can shape herbivore communities, but wider effects depend on local food webs. A field experiment in northeastern China found that birds including crows, jays and woodpeckers used simulated remains of Amur tiger prey, showing how kills can also provide carrion to scavengers.

The IUCN assessed the tiger on 15 December 2021 and published its Red List account in 2022, classifying the species as Endangered. The estimate was 3,726–5,578 wild individuals, excluding cubs, with 3,140 mature individuals as the best estimate. It combines national data collected in different years and with different methods, so it is not a synchronized census and its higher value than older editions alone does not prove growth. The assessment reports that occupied range contracted by more than half over three generations. Poaching for illegal trade, hunting of prey, habitat conversion and fragmentation remain major pressures; prey depletion and conflict with people also cause local losses and retaliatory killing.

Eurasian water vole
Arvicola amphibius

The Eurasian water vole, Arvicola amphibius, is a wetland rodent widespread across Europe and northern Asia. Its range reaches from Britain east through Russia to Siberia, and south into the Middle East. Most populations live beside water, while some use damp grasslands and other less aquatic habitats. The IUCN classified it as globally Least Concern in 2023, despite regional declines.

Adults are usually 14–22 cm long, with a 9.5–14 cm tail, and weigh 150–300 g. A blunt muzzle, fur-hidden ears and furry tail distinguish it from the brown rat, which has a pointed face and bare tail. The coat is usually chestnut or dark brown above, greyish below; some populations are entirely black. Continuously growing incisors cut vegetation, and broad molars grind it.

The waterside form favours slow streams, ditches, ponds, marshes and reedbeds with soft banks and dense cover. It stays near water but travels and feeds mostly on land, often under grass. Bank burrows contain nest chambers and may open both above and below water, offering escape from danger. Some northern and upland populations also occupy wet grassland or moorland away from rivers.

It is chiefly herbivorous and may eat plant matter approaching 80 percent of its body mass daily. Grasses, sedges, rushes and waterside herbs dominate, supplemented by roots, bulbs, shoots and fruit. It carries cut stems to feeding spots and stores vegetation underground for lean periods. Pregnant females sometimes seek protein-rich snails or flowers. In captive water voles, the caecum, a pouch in the large intestine, enlarged on cellulose-rich food; pellet-eating (coprophagy) also became more frequent.

It swims and dives over short distances but is no aquatic specialist: it breathes air with lungs, and its coat can become waterlogged. A compact body and burrows help it escape predators; most feeding and resting occur on land. Activity peaks by day and at twilight, varying with season. Along streams, females often defend breeding territories while males range farther and overlap several females; studies in other habitats find looser boundaries. Scent marks and latrines advertise territories.

Breeding in temperate Europe usually lasts from spring into early autumn, with a shorter season in colder regions. Gestation is about three weeks; litters commonly contain four to six pups, and females may produce several. Newborns are hairless and blind, sheltered in a grass nest; their eyes open within days. They are weaned at two to three weeks, leave the nest soon after, and may mature in their first year.

By burrowing, feeding and moving through wetlands, the vole helps create conditions that other plants and animals can use. Burrowing and droppings alter soil structure and nutrient cycling. It is prey for native predators and, in Britain, introduced American mink. Dispersing juveniles can recolonize empty patches, linking local populations across wetlands.

The IUCN’s 2023 Least Concern assessment reflects the species’ broad range and mostly stable global trend, while recognizing regional declines. In Britain it is Endangered in England and Great Britain, and Near Threatened in Scotland. Agricultural intensification, pollution and watercourse development have destroyed and fragmented British water vole habitat. Introduced American mink can enter burrows and intensify predation; river restoration and mink control are part of recovery work.

Western gorilla
Gorilla gorilla

The western gorilla (Gorilla gorilla) is one of two gorilla species; the eastern gorilla (G. beringei) lives farther east. Western gorillas inhabit west-central equatorial Africa and comprise western lowland and Cross River subspecies.

Adults have dark hair, long arms and broad chests; males are much larger. Mature males develop a silver saddle, sometimes extending to rump and thighs in western lowland gorillas. Infants have a pale rump tuft. Gorillas knuckle-walk; skull crests anchor jaw muscles.

Western lowland gorillas inhabit swamp and terra firma forests across the Congo Basin; Cross River gorillas occupy fragmented forests on the Nigeria–Cameroon border. Gorillas spend much time on the ground, but also climb and nest in trees or on the forest floor.

Leaves, stems, shoots and fruit dominate, but proportions vary by season and site. At three western lowland sites, fruit made up about 35% of feeding time and leaves plus herbs about half; plant species differed. Some populations also eat nuts or insects, so these figures are not universal.

Groups often include a mature silverback, females, young and sometimes other males; membership changes. Gorillas forage, rest and nest by day, communicating through calls, posture and chest-beating. Females leave their birth group; young males may live alone or in bachelor groups for years.

Western lowland gorilla pregnancy lasts about eight and a half months; usually one infant is born, with no fixed season. It grasps its mother, who carries it; young may ride on her back for years. Females change groups as they mature, and births are years apart. These observations concern this subspecies.

Fruit-eating western lowland gorillas pass many seeds intact in their dung, carrying them from parent trees. Studies in Gabon and Cameroon found seeds from many fruit species, some able to germinate. Dispersal and germination effects vary with diet, site and plant.

The IUCN’s 2016 global assessment classified western gorillas as Critically Endangered, citing losses from illegal hunting, disease and habitat loss. Logging roads expose remote forests to hunters. This is a dated assessment, not a new census. Cross River gorillas have a particularly restricted, fragmented range; pressures vary regionally.

Whale shark
Rhincodon typus

The whale shark is the largest living fish, a slow-moving shark whose immense size comes with a specialised way of feeding on small prey. It ranges through tropical and warm-temperate seas, crossing ocean basins while repeatedly visiting some seasonal feeding sites.

Its broad, flattened head bears a very wide mouth at the tip of the snout; five pairs of large gill slits open behind it. Pale spots and bars form a checkerboard over the dark back, and the pattern is distinctive enough for researchers to identify individuals in photographs. Individuals recorded at feeding sites often measure around 4–10 m, but this is an observation range that includes juveniles, and many coastal sites are dominated by young males. The 2025 IUCN assessment estimates male maturity at 6.8–9.2 m by region and female maturity at about 9–10 m. A Ningaloo re-sighting model estimated average eventual lengths—the limits approached as growth slows—of 8.5–9 m for males and 14.5 m for females; rare records approach 18 m, and these modelled averages are not maximum lengths.

The species occurs in coastal waters and the open ocean, usually in warm seas, and spends much of its time near the surface. It can also dive into cold deep water; a satellite-tagged shark off Yucatán reached 1,928 m, although the purpose of such exceptional dives is not settled. Seasonal prey pulses bring sharks together at regional feeding sites, but their movements differ among regions and individuals.

Its food includes zooplankton such as copepods and sergestid shrimp, as well as fish eggs, larvae and small fish; the menu depends on what is locally abundant. In a feeding bout it may cruise with its mouth open, draw water in by suction, or feed nearly upright while stationary. Water exits through the gills after prey is retained by filtering pads in the pharynx. Motta and colleagues proposed that tangential cross-flow across the pad mesh may limit clogging, but described this as a mechanism rather than directly demonstrating that effect. Indirect biochemical evidence from tissues, faeces and prey at Ningaloo suggests floating Sargassum and its small associated animals can contribute to the diet there; this does not establish plant feeding as universal.

At the northeastern Yucatán feeding area, hundreds of sharks gather in summer and disperse between August and October. A female tracked from Mexico travelled at least 7,213 km in 150 days. In Qatar, tracking showed that many tagged sharks returned to the same feeding area. Dives vary with region and prey: most tagged sharks spend much time in shallow water, yet some make deep excursions.

Reproduction remains poorly observed: the only confirmed pregnant female was a 10.6 m shark caught off Taiwan in 1995. She carried 304 embryos at different stages, including some still enclosed in egg cases and others already hatched; this showed aplacental yolk-sac viviparity, in which eggs hatch inside the mother and embryos develop without a placenta. The litter is an exceptional documented case, not a typical or known universal litter size. Newborns are rarely seen, so their birth size, nursery grounds and early growth in natural habitat remain uncertain.

By filtering plankton and fish eggs, whale sharks feed on concentrated pulses of production and connect tiny prey to large marine predators. In the southern Gulf of California, seasonal plankton blooms draw juvenile sharks to feeding areas, where they can also become prey for large sharks and killer whales. Predation by killer whales is documented there: observations recorded four events of killing and consumption between 2018 and 2024, evidence that does not show orcas commonly hunt the species everywhere.

Targeted fisheries once supplied meat, oil and fins, and some fisheries closed in the 1990s and 2000s; incidental capture in nets continues in parts of the range. The global IUCN assessment, assessed on 31 March 2025 and published in 2025, lists the species as Endangered and infers a 50–79% population reduction over three generations (120 years), with declines especially severe in the Indo-Pacific. Serious vessel strikes are another major threat because sharks cross shipping routes and aggregate predictably near the surface.

White stork
Ciconia ciconia
The white stork is a large wading bird that breeds across Europe, North Africa and western Asia, then winters in Africa or nearer regions.

Adults are unmistakable at a distance: most of the body is white, the flight feathers are black, and the long bill and legs are red. The recorded maximum height is about 1.15 metres and maximum wingspan 2.15 metres. Males average slightly larger, although the sexes share the same plumage. Newly hatched young have dark bills and dull yellow-grey legs, which turn red as they mature.

The species favours open landscapes where it can see and reach prey: floodplains, marsh edges, wet meadows, pastures and cultivated fields. In Alsace, Rhine-valley ried meadows are characteristic; across its range, nests also stand on trees, roofs, chimneys and purpose-built platforms.

As it walks, the stork spots prey, snaps it up in a bill thrust and regurgitates food for chicks. Its menu is opportunistic rather than frog-centred: earthworms, insects, small mammals, amphibians, reptiles and fish all feature. In dry conditions insects and mice may dominate, whereas wetter seasons make aquatic prey more available. A Polish study found that grassland and uncultivated margins supplied much of the food, alongside prey from fields and wetlands.

Adults are quiet compared with many birds: they greet a mate or warn rivals with loud bill-clattering, raising and lowering the head and neck. Pairs also use postures and wing movements during courtship and nest defence. On migration, the stork saves energy by circling in rising columns of warm air called thermals, then gliding as the air carries it forward. Because thermals weaken over open sea, European birds funnel around the Mediterranean through the Strait of Gibraltar or the Bosporus rather than crossing directly. Migration differs among individuals and regions: many western and central European birds travel to Africa, while some winter in Iberia or southern France and some remain near reliable food. Landfills have helped sustain resident groups in Iberia, changing local movements without making every population sedentary.

Pairs reuse and enlarge bulky nests of sticks, often on high structures; the female usually lays three to five eggs, incubated by both adults for about a month. Incubation starts before the clutch is complete, so chicks hatch asynchronously; both parents feed them, and the young begin flying at about eight to ten weeks.

Storks consume insects such as grasshoppers, which farmers may regard as pests, as well as rodents and other prey. Eagles and other large raptors may prey on young storks. GPS tracking in Spain and Morocco shows birds moving from landfills to wetlands and rice fields, linking separate habitats. These journeys create a possible route for litter or contaminants to move between waste sites and wetlands in droppings or regurgitated pellets.

BirdLife International’s global IUCN assessment, published in 2025 after assessment on 5 June 2025, lists the species as Least Concern and increasing, with an estimated 526,000–588,000 mature birds. This is a global risk category, not a claim that every regional population is secure. In Alsace, numbers fell from about 145 breeding pairs in 1960 to only nine in 1974, amid deaths during migration and on African wintering grounds, as well as drought and habitat pressures. From the early 1970s, local groups held storks in enclosures for three years before release, encouraging them to settle and breed locally; later nest platforms and habitat work helped the population expand. Current hazards include wetland loss, intensive land management, electrocution and collisions with overhead wires, as well as hunting along some migration routes. A newer localized concern is landfill feeding: litter may be ingested, and movements between waste sites and wetlands create a possible transfer route.

Whooper swan
Cygnus cygnus
The whooper swan is a large migratory waterbird of northern Eurasia, with white plumage, a long upright neck and ringing calls; it breeds from Iceland to Siberia and winters farther south.
Adults measure about 140–165 cm long and span 205–275 cm; males are heavier, and their black bill bears more yellow than the smaller, mostly black-billed Bewick’s swan.
It nests beside shallow lakes and marshes in Eurasian taiga and subarctic tundra, where waterside vegetation offers cover; wintering birds also use estuaries, sheltered coasts and farmland.

It feeds mainly on aquatic leaves, shoots, stems and roots, reaching plants with its long neck or by tipping forward; in winter it also grazes grass and crops, while small invertebrates are a minor food.

Pairs defend territories while breeding, then gather in flocks; deep trumpet-like calls keep family members in contact, and head-bobbing can signal that birds are ready to take flight. Pairs usually remain together for life, and winter flocks contain families whose young migrate with their parents until the following breeding season.

Females lay four to seven eggs and incubate them about 35 days while males guard; downy cygnets leave the nest and fledge at roughly 78–105 days, depending on region. The nest is a mound of vegetation beside freshwater; the mobile young are nevertheless dependent on parental protection and help with feeding during their early development.

Natural predators in northern Russia include red foxes, white-tailed eagles and golden eagles. Open water also supplies communal roosts for winter flocks. Predation affects eggs and small young most strongly; adults can retreat into water to escape terrestrial predators, while the parents’ vigilance protects the brood.

The global IUCN assessment of 5 June 2025 lists the species as Least Concern, estimates 176,000 mature individuals and an increasing trend, while identifying wetland loss, disturbance, hunting, lead poisoning and power-line collisions as threats. Persecution reduced numbers and range in the 19th and early 20th centuries; bans on hunting later brought recovery.

Wild boar
Sus scrofa

The wild boar is native to much of Europe, North Africa and Asia, reaching eastern Siberia and Southeast Asian islands. Feral populations also occur in the Americas and New Zealand, where pigs introduced by people established in the wild. Body size and coat vary widely, and escaped domestic pigs can alter local populations.

Adults have a muscular body, short muzzle and coarse bristles; their brown to nearly black coat often greys with age. Piglets\' dark stripes fade within months. Both sexes have curved canine tusks, usually larger in males. A study of 403 boars in two Spanish districts found canine thickness chiefly related to sex and age.

Wild boars inhabit forests, scrub, grassland, wooded savanna and farmland. They rest in cover and feed in open areas; in Singapore they also forage at urban edges. Habitat use shifts with season, food and disturbance. Their native range spans diverse climates; introduced populations do not extend it naturally.

This omnivore finds food mainly by smell and roots through soil with its mobile snout. Depending on season and place, it eats roots, tubers, grasses, nuts, berries, crops, insects, worms, small reptiles and carrion. Plants often dominate. Rooting also disturbs soil and seedlings.

Females and young often form family groups; adult males are usually solitary outside mating periods. Boars may be active by day but become more nocturnal under human disturbance. Their keen smell locates food. They push soil aside while rooting and wallow in mud to help regulate body temperature. Grouping varies locally.

Breeding follows climate and food: it can occur year-round in the tropics, while births in temperate regions often peak in spring. Gestation lasts about 108–120 days, and litters commonly have five or six piglets, with local variation. The sow makes a sheltered nest; piglets\' stripes fade as they grow.

Rooting turns over vegetation, litter and soil; effects depend on habitat and intensity. In 22 Berlin dry grasslands, plant diversity declined with rooting, while grasshopper diversity and sand-lizard abundance were positively associated. Forest studies report damage to understory plants and regeneration. Outcomes vary locally.

The species remains widespread in much of its native range, though habitat loss, hunting and interbreeding with free-ranging domestic pigs threaten some populations. In introduced regions such as North America, rooting can erode soil, hinder forest regeneration, compete with native wildlife and disturb nests. Such impacts are documented especially in the United States.

Wild turkey
Meleagris gallopavo

The wild turkey is a large North American forest bird that moves between woods and clearings. It walks and scratches for much of the day, yet flies strongly enough to reach night roosts in trees and escape danger.

Adult males are substantially larger than females: usual masses are about 6.8–11 kilograms for males and 3.6–5.4 kilograms for hens, varying among populations and seasons. A male’s bare blue-red head bears small fleshy caruncles; a soft flap called a snood hangs above the bill, red throat wattles and a black bristly breast beard stand out, and long legs carry sharp spurs. Hens are smaller and browner, usually without a beard. Both sexes have barred wings and a broad rounded tail, closed at rest and fanned during display.

Across much of North America, turkeys use mature mixed or hardwood forest with fields and grassy openings. In the southeastern United States, trees supply roosts and acorns, while open low cover helps birds spot predators and shelters nests and insect-rich brood habitat.

Turkeys are omnivores, though plant foods dominate: they eat seeds, acorns, nuts, berries and green plants, plus insects and other invertebrates, especially when young. They scratch leaf litter and peck food from the ground, sometimes reaching fruit in shrubs. They swallow grit; in the muscular gizzard, contractions and hard particles grind coarse seeds and plant matter into smaller pieces for digestion.

Turkeys are social, but flock structure varies by season and sex: males often associate together outside breeding, while hens travel with young and may join other families. At dusk, birds fly up into sheltered trees to roost; their powerful burst flight also helps them escape danger. Many broad-breasted commercial strains have been selected for heavy bodies and have limited flight ability. In spring, males gobble, strut with lowered wings and fan the tail, using sound and plumage to attract females and signal to rivals.

A male may display to several females and does not help build the nest or raise young; females visit display grounds to mate. A genetic study of eastern wild turkeys in Georgia and South Carolina found that some clutches had multiple fathers. The hen scratches a shallow nest in leaf litter or low cover and usually lays one seasonal clutch of roughly 4–17 eggs; she incubates for about 25–31 days. The down-covered poults hatch well developed, leave the nest within about a day, and follow their mother, who broods and protects them. They feed themselves early, often taking many insects, and typically can fly to tree roosts at two to three weeks; this is a vulnerable transition because they sleep on the ground before then.
Turkeys eat seeds and nuts, and their young consume many insects; they in turn feed predators such as coyotes, bobcats, eagles and owls, while raccoons and snakes take eggs and young.

The IUCN global assessment completed on 9 August 2018 and published in 2018 classified the wild turkey as Least Concern; this worldwide category is not a guarantee that every local population is secure. Hunting and forest clearance caused severe declines in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Early releases of farm-raised birds often failed, but wildlife agencies later restored populations by trapping wild birds and moving them into suitable habitat; New York’s program began in 1959 and supplied other northeastern states and Ontario. The bird is also the ancestor of domestic turkeys: Indigenous peoples in Mexico domesticated it centuries before Europeans carried domestic birds to Europe. Hunting remains an important human use and a management consideration, with seasons and rules determined locally.

Wild yak
Bos mutus

Wild yaks inhabit the cold, high Tibetan Plateau. The wild species is Bos mutus; the domestic yak, Bos grunniens, is its close relative, raised by people on the Asian highlands. Its remaining range is concentrated in northern Tibet and western Qinghai, with a small, documented occurrence in Nepal.

A mature wild yak has a deep, compact body, short sturdy legs, small ears and broad rounded hooves. Long coarse guard hairs hang from the chest, flanks and thighs over a dense insulating undercoat; large lungs and a strong heart, alongside abundant red blood cells, help it obtain oxygen in thin air. Adult bulls stand about 175–203 cm at the shoulder and weigh over 800 kg, with estimates reaching 1,200 kg; cows stand 137–156 cm and average about 350 kg.

Wild yaks occupy alpine meadows, cold steppe and high-desert grassland, generally between about 4,000 and 6,100 m. The plateau is windy and arid, with temperatures below −40 °C in some areas; yaks shift to lower valleys in winter. Field research in Arjin Shan found seasonal habitat choices, including use of rugged, higher ground during summer.

The wild yak grazes grasses, sedges and other low alpine plants, with the mix changing as plants mature and snow limits access. It is a ruminant: swallowed vegetation is first fermented by microbes in the rumen, then brought back to the mouth as cud and chewed again; later stomach chambers digest and absorb the released nutrients. This microbial fermentation makes fibrous cell walls usable as energy. A 2025 field study using DNA from wild-yak droppings found clear seasonal shifts in plant foods, consistent with flexible foraging through the short growing season and lean winter.

Wild yaks are social: females and calves form nursery groups, while adult males may join them, remain solitary or gather in small bachelor groups. In the summer rut, bulls join female herds, compete for mates, display and fight. Wild yaks vocalize and can be noisy. In the growing season, they use higher, more rugged ground; seasonal habitat use shifts with climate and snow.

Mating occurs in summer, and calves are born from April through June, with timing varying with elevation and seasonal food. After about 258–270 days of gestation, a cow usually gives birth to one calf; wild females commonly calve every two or three years, depending partly on forage and weather. A calf can stand soon after birth and learn to walk within hours; it soon follows its mother back to the herd. The maternal group offers protection while the young animal begins to graze and grow.

As a large grazer, the wild yak shares alpine forage with Tibetan wild asses, argali, blue sheep and other plateau herbivores. In summer, movement into higher meadows can reduce overlap with animals using lower ground; competition becomes more consequential where domestic livestock concentrate on the same productive pastures. Its need for connected ranges ties survival to highland land use.

The IUCN assessment published in 2016 is based on a global assessment dated 9 July 2014: it classifies Bos mutus as Vulnerable and estimates 7,500–9,999 mature animals, with a continuing decline projected. Earlier surveys placed about 15,000 wild yaks across the plateau in 1995, while the Wildlife Conservation Society later reported imprecise global estimates of 15,000–20,000; these figures come from different dates and methods. Poaching for meat, shrinking and fragmented habitat, competition with livestock, and hybridization with domestic yaks threaten the species. Nepal’s presence was confirmed again in 2014 after decades without records. China’s nature reserves and anti-poaching protection offer important refuges, but the global trend remains uncertain and negative in many areas.

Grey wolf
Canis lupus

The grey wolf is a highly adaptable wild canid whose former range covered much of the Northern Hemisphere. It persists in parts of North America, Europe and Asia. Populations differ in size, coat and prey with local climate, food and human pressures.

This large, long-legged canid has a broad muzzle, upright ears, powerful jaws and a bushy tail. Dense underfur insulates it in cold conditions. Coat shades range from white through grey, brown and cinnamon to nearly black; northern populations tend to be larger.

Wolves occupy Arctic tundra, forests, grasslands, mountains and some arid landscapes. They need prey and room to move, but not only untouched wilderness; some populations live near settlements. Abundance tends to track prey availability, while roads and development can fragment habitat.

Wolves mainly eat mammals. Packs hunt ungulates such as deer, elk, moose, reindeer or bison; lone wolves also take beavers, rabbits and small prey. They scavenge too. Diet shifts seasonally: elk dominate winter prey in Yellowstone, deer more in summer.
A wild pack is usually a family: a breeding pair and offspring, some helping care for pups. Young wolves may disperse to form packs. Howling and scent marks signal territory.

Breeding is seasonal and timing shifts across the range; Yellowstone wolves usually mate in February. After 62–63 days, a female gives birth in a den. Newborns are blind and deaf; their eyes open at about two weeks. Adults bring food as they grow.

Wolves affect prey through hunting, but effects depend on prey vulnerability, weather, other predators and human hunting. Carcasses also feed scavengers: Yellowstone observations record ravens, magpies, coyotes, bears, eagles and invertebrates at wolf kills. These relationships vary over time and place.

The global IUCN assessment dated 30 August 2018 classified the species as Least Concern and noted competition with people over livestock and game, persecution and habitat fragmentation. A global category can conceal regional decline or recovery: legal protection, prey, connectivity and conflict differ among populations.

Wolverine
Gulo gulo

The wolverine is a wide-ranging member of the weasel family found across northern Eurasia and North America. It occupies boreal forest, tundra and mountains, usually at low density and across large individual ranges.

The wolverine has a broad head, small rounded ears, a stout neck, short powerful legs, large feet and a bushy tail. Adults measure about 65–105 cm from nose to rump, with a 13–26 cm tail. In Alaska, adult males are reported at 11–18 kg and females at 6–12 kg. Dense, coarse fur is usually dark brown, often with pale face or throat markings and lighter bands along the flanks. Its broad skull and strong teeth can crush bones.

The circumpolar range extends from northern forests and taiga to Arctic and alpine tundra. In Canada, wolverines occupy northern and western forests, western mountain tundra and Arctic tundra. At the southern edge of the North American range, populations are sparse and fragmented in mountain landscapes. Individuals travel among forest, open slopes, rock and tundra as seasons and prey change. Low natural densities and large home ranges make connected habitat important.

Wolverines are primarily scavengers, often using ungulate carcasses left by wolves and other predators. They also hunt small mammals and birds and occasionally kill larger prey, including moose or caribou calves. In the studies synthesized by USFS, hunts for large ungulates were most successful in early spring, when deep, soft snow limited their movement. Diet shifts with season and local prey. In Arctic Alaska, cached ground squirrels and caribou remains were important winter foods. Surplus meat is cached under snow, in soil or trees.

Wolverines are mostly solitary and active throughout the year, by day or night. Adult ranges can be very large; a male’s range may overlap those of several females, while same-sex overlap is more restricted in some studied populations. A 12-year analysis of genetically identified scats in central Norway found larger male than female ranges and avoidance between same-sex individuals; avoidance weakened after a territory holder died. A USFS review describes scent marks as advertising an animal’s current position.

Mating takes place in the warm season, commonly from late spring into summer. After fertilization, the embryo may pause before implanting, so birth follows months after mating. Active gestation lasts 30–40 days. Females give birth in late winter or early spring, usually to two or three kits, in a sheltered den. Snow tunnels are common in northern and mountain settings, but roots, logs and rocks also provide den sites. Newborns depend on their mother’s milk and protection; she may move them among dens as they grow. Young leave dens in spring and continue learning to forage before dispersing. In the Scandinavian population studied, females first reproduced at about three years.

Carrion creates a feeding link with larger predators and human hunting of ungulates. In eastern Finland, moose killed by people or wolves made up 55% of diet occurrences in samples from four breeding females; mountain hare was most frequent among males and non-breeding females. This small study is a regional example. A Swedish monitoring study recorded 1,589 reproductive events from 2000 to 2018 and found events expanding into areas with less persistent spring snow. Associations differed among regions and periods: April snow depth remained positively associated with reproductive-event occurrence in the Alpine-Reindeer region, while the snow-cover relationship changed in other regions.

The IUCN global assessment completed on 15 May 2015 and published in 2016 classified the wolverine as Least Concern, citing its broad range and large remaining populations while noting decline from persecution and land-use change. This dated global category does not describe every population. Trapping historically removed wolverines from parts of their range; harvest, conflict, roads, development and fragmentation remain concerns in some regions. Canada’s 2014 COSEWIC assessment treated the species as one national population and designated it Special Concern. Southern mountain populations are vulnerable to isolation from the northern core. Long-term monitoring, connected habitat and mortality management matter alongside climate projections.

Common Wood Pigeon
Columba palumbus

A large, adaptable pigeon, the Common Wood Pigeon inhabits European woods, farmland, parks and gardens. Adults measure 40–42 cm long, weigh about 480–550 g and span 75–80 cm. Some European populations stay near their breeding grounds; others migrate, and winter flocks gather where food is abundant.

Its bulky grey body, pink breast, yellow eye and orange-red bill make it distinctive. Adults have white patches on both sides of the neck, edged with green and purple iridescence, and broad white wing bars that flash in flight. Juveniles lack the white neck patches, but show the wing bars. It is larger than the Rock Pigeon, Columba livia, whose wings have dark bars; the smaller Stock Dove, Columba oenas, lacks white neck patches.

It nests in open woods, woodland edges and hedgerows, then feeds in fields, meadows and lawns. In cities, parks and tree-lined gardens offer nesting branches, grass and planted foods; some birds forage there, while others travel to farmland. This flexibility has helped it colonize European cities, though timing varies by region.

It eats mainly plants: seeds, grain, buds, leaves, flowers, berries and fruits. It pecks seeds and cereal grain on the ground, and plucks fruits and buds from trees; crops such as oilseed rape can be important seasonal foods. The crop, an expandable pouch in the lower throat, stores food before it passes to the stomach, allowing quick gathering followed by digestion. Small invertebrates are occasional foods, not a staple.

Pairs keep contact with a deep, repeated coo, often from a perch. In display, a bird climbs steeply, claps its wings loudly and glides down with wings stiff; this signals territory and courts a mate. Outside nesting, loose groups feed together and large flocks use communal winter roosts. Movements vary: some city birds stay near parks, while tracked birds in central Europe fly several kilometres to fields.

Courtship leads to a simple stick platform in a tree, hedge or sometimes building; both parents incubate the usual two white eggs. Incubation lasts about 17 days, and the downy chicks fledge after roughly 33–34 days. Both parents feed the young. In the final days of incubation, cells lining the crop, a food-storage pouch in the lower throat, swell and shed a nutrient-rich secretion called crop milk. Chicks rely on it at first; around day ten, parents add softened seeds and other solid foods. A long breeding season allows one or two broods yearly, depending on place and conditions.

By eating fruit, Wood Pigeons can disperse seeds; in southern Spain, many swallowed cultivated olive seeds passed intact into nearby natural vegetation. Some pairs nest near Eurasian Hobby falcons: although a falcon may take a pigeon, its defense of nearby nests can deter other intruders. Cereal feeding can conflict with farming, and local population growth has accompanied agricultural food access and reduced hunting.

The species has expanded in parts of Europe and was assessed as Least Concern in BirdLife’s 2021 European assessment, which estimated an increasing population. The RSPB estimates around 5.2 million breeding pairs in the United Kingdom, where continental birds add to winter numbers. In northern Algeria, one population grew while hunting pressure fell and agriculture supplied new foods, showing that land use can affect populations differently by region. National and European assessments cover different scales, so their categories may differ.

Yellow-footed tortoise
Chelonoidis denticulatus

The yellow-footed tortoise is a large land tortoise native to tropical South America. Its scientific name is Chelonoidis denticulatus; older names include C. denticulata and Geochelone denticulata. It lives chiefly in humid forest and searches the ground for fallen foods and shelter. Field knowledge comes mainly from a few studied sites.

Its rounded, domed carapace is bone covered by horny scutes, above a flatter plastron. The shell is brown, often with pale yellow or orange scute centers; yellow-orange scales mark the head and limbs. This pattern helps separate it from the red-footed tortoise (Chelonoidis carbonarius), but colors vary and should not be used alone. Adult males have a longer, thicker tail and a somewhat concave plastron. The species is generally larger, though size also varies by region. Elongated prefrontal scales on the head are another useful distinction from the smaller, fragmented scales typical of red-footed tortoises.

The species is associated mainly with humid tropical forests, including Amazonian rainforest. It shelters in leaf litter, beneath fallen logs and among roots or dense plants, which buffer heat and drying. In a six-month Central Amazon study, tortoises usually sheltered when encountered; smaller animals often used leaf litter. Tracked individuals used an average 1.56 hectares, with larger areas used by larger tortoises. This local estimate is not a universal home range.

This opportunistic omnivore gathers food mainly from the forest floor: fallen fruits, flowers, seeds, fungi, invertebrates and carrion. A Brazilian study found seeds of several plants in tortoise droppings, many still viable; a later study of two Chelonoidis species found viable seeds in most samples. Seeds can therefore survive gut passage, but germination and successful plant recruitment are not guaranteed.

Field accounts describe mostly daytime activity, though weather and local conditions affect when tortoises move. As reptiles they depend on external heat; shade, humid refuges and sunlit patches offer different thermal conditions, but detailed seasonal thermoregulation is poorly studied in this species. In Central Amazonia, animals were encountered sheltering much more often than walking or feeding. Studies document individual movements and shelter use, not a stable social-group system.

Wild breeding is opportunistic and seasonal. In 347 adult females from the Peruvian Amazon, reproductive stages occurred through the year, but output varied with climate: follicle growth tracked peak rainfall and laying was estimated mainly in the dry season. Gravid females held an average 3.7 shelled eggs; estimated clutch size averaged 5.1, with a wide range. These figures come from one harvested population. Wild incubation duration and hatchling survival remain poorly documented.

By eating fruit and moving through forest, the tortoise can carry seeds away from parent plants. A 2025 study of two Chelonoidis species combined fecal samples, seed tests and movement data; its models placed many seeds hundreds of metres away, sometimes beyond a kilometre. This supports a dispersal role, but the effect on plants depends on where seeds land and whether they germinate and establish.

The 1996 global IUCN assessment classified the tortoise as Vulnerable, a historical result rather than a recent measurement. In December 2025, the IUCN specialist group listed an Endangered assessment among those submitted and in press, without giving its assessment date. The tortoise is hunted for meat and enters international live-animal trade. A Norwegian scientific review reports depletion and scarcity in some populations, while noting uncertainty about captive breeding in trade. Conditions vary across its range and need local monitoring.
